### 7.2 Release gates — not acceptance of this slice's code

Each gate must exist before the exposure it names. **None blocks the local walk** (S0.70), and the local walk **waives none of them** ([SLICE-000.md](../slices/SLICE-000.md) §7 items 5 and 6).

| Gate| Needed before| What it is| Owner input|
|---|---|---|---|
| **G1**| Production identity use| Signed audit checkpoints with independent storage and monitoring ([audit.md](../../contracts/audit.md) §2.1)| Backend Engineer; storage choice|
| **G2**| External authentication exposure| Edge, trusted-proxy and load evidence; the shared limiter at the deployed topology; the measured capacity values approved (OB-31)| Product Owner approves values|
| **G3**| Staging release evidence| **Prerequisite (OB-36): managed key custody is implemented, with a rotation proof and a recovery proof for every key purpose; until it exists the API refuses a production start.** Real secrets and providers, a restore and key-rotation rehearsal, the controlled real-provider window of [DEPLOYMENT_AND_ENVIRONMENTS.md](../../architecture/DEPLOYMENT_AND_ENVIRONMENTS.md) §4.1 (a non-production credential, allow-listed recipients, a recorded approval; a refused destination is `DESTINATION_NOT_ALLOWED`), and the release inputs: an SMS and an email provider (`OQ-048`), the accepted Android attestation roots, the Rider package name and first signing-certificate digest, the KMS key and the Argon2id pepper| Product Owner; Release owner|
| **G4**| The milestone of each bootstrap waiver| Hosted CI, artifact and branch evidence ([§7.3](#73-inherited-from-the-bootstrap))| Product Owner|
| **G5**| Claiming a client's clauses| The Vendor PWA and Rider app journeys: the clauses of AC-08 to 11, 15, 18, 38, 40 and 47 to 59 that need a client| Frontend Engineer|
| **SW**| Slice acceptance| The Product Owner walks §5 in **Staging** against the substitute verifier and the capture adapter, rows 1, 2 and 12 included, and records it. The Vendor and Rider rows are walked at API level until their clients exist| Product Owner|

**Permitted deferrals — only what an owner decision or waiver names.** These may follow the local walk (S0.70), stay on its record as *deferred*, and are never reported as passed:

**Not deferred.** The bootstrap waivers name existing tests and milestones; they are **not** extended by inference to the worker's `SIGTERM` test (OB-24), the custody-file permission checks (OB-25), the JVM verifier build and tests on Linux or CI (OB-26), or any other evidence this plan creates. The Product Owner decided on 9 October 2026 that they are **required at the gate that names them** (OB-24 at Gate 2, OB-25 at S0.30, OB-26 at S0.55), with no new waiver (§10 row 13); a gate or task that needs them is not passed until the evidence exists. The failure rehearsal (runbook item 2) is open, not waived.

### 7.3 Inherited from the bootstrap

From the runbook's [evidence still owed](BOOTSTRAP_B0_RUNBOOK.md#evidence-still-owed-audit-b-05): the **failure rehearsal** (item 2) is open; the downloaded-build check, the clean supported setup in WSL2 or Linux, the disposable reset and the Linux suite run (items 4 to 7) are **waived until release** and remain unproven; the accessibility passes (item 8) are S0.28. A waiver is not a proof. **A known hazard for every `B` and `D` run:** a Vitest worker that fails to start has recurred on the owner's Windows machine without an explanation; rerun the one project, report both outcomes and never raise a timeout to hide it.

### 7.7 Carried from S0.6

It answers the platform's generic operational failure for `BudgetExpiredError`, `DatabaseDeadlineError`, `PoolSaturatedError`, `AcquireTimeoutError` and `PoolClosedError`, reading the typed error from the rejection of `transactionWithContext` (inside the work, drizzle wraps what a statement throws and keeps it as `cause`). **`CommitOutcomeUnknownError` must not be answered as an ordinary retryable failure:** the transaction may have committed, so a retry is safe only through the operation's idempotency key. ### 7.12 Stage 1 correction batch (10 October 2026): disposition

The owner's review of the Stage 1 report (S0.6 to S0.10) raised six findings and gave directions on the decisions that report listed. This is the disposition of both. **Stage 1 stays under correction until the owner has reviewed this batch's evidence.** Nothing here is a blanket security approval or a statement that Stage 1 is ready for production, and S0.11 is not started. Every finding was reproduced before it was fixed (a unit test that failed on the committed behaviour, or, for F02, a database migrated only to 0004), then fixed test first where a unit test can hold it, and every new guard was broken on purpose, one break at a time, with the file restored and its hash checked. No finding failed to reproduce. A review of the correction (10 October 2026) accepted F01, F02, F03, F04 and F06 on source review, asked for one follow-up, F05 (below), asked that two statements of this record be corrected (the fixtures function's isolation guard; the cause of the timing failures), and made the decisions listed after the limitations.

**Baseline.** Branch `docs/slice-000-reconciliation`, HEAD `fd5f696` (S0.4 and S0.5; everything later is uncommitted), nothing staged; 102 changed paths when the batch began (35 modified, 67 untracked) and 124 when it ended; `melarc_dev` not touched; no dependency changed; no migration that might have been applied was edited (0005 is new, and 0003 and 0004 are uncommitted).

**What kind of evidence this is.** Configuration validation (a setting parsed and refused at start) proves that a value is accepted and nothing about what it bounds; that is how the deployment figures stand until S0.65. *Fixture/platform* evidence is everything below: a real PostgreSQL 18.6, the technical logins, the test fixtures and the kit. *Real-operation* evidence does not exist yet, because no operation of the contract is built (the first route is S0.31): none of this batch is it.

|---|---|---|---|

Reproduced: a unit test saw the value returned, and a real-database test (a row written, an aborting statement caught, a success-shaped return) saw the row absent from a second connection| `database.service.ts` reads the command tag of the COMMIT: `COMMIT` is success; `ROLLBACK` is `TransactionRolledBackError` (definite: nothing kept; the cause is the first statement failure; the connection is destroyed); a missing or unexpected tag is `CommitOutcomeUnknownError` (`unrecognized-completion`); a connection lost or a budget spent in flight is unknown as before. No public error code, no `openapi.yaml` change| `database-deadlines.test.ts`, `database.service.test.ts`, `scope-probe.test.ts`; `test/database/commit-outcome.db.test.ts` (the ordinary commit, the headline case, a refusal the work did not catch, a commit refused by a deferred trigger, a savepoint that recovers). The old behaviour put back by a break is caught by both|

Reproduced on the migrations up to 0004: after the seed, that login, with the `seed` label asserted, inserted a grant into the Ops Staff bundle and committed| Migration `0005_seed_initialization.sql`. The login holds **no privilege** on the seven tables. Two `SECURITY DEFINER` functions owned by `melarc_owner`, executable by that login alone and listed in `APPROVED_DEFINER_EXECUTE`, are the only way in: `melarc.initialize_reference_data` locks the seven tables in one order, counts every one and refuses (`55000`, naming the table) unless all seven are empty, then inserts, in one statement of the caller's transaction; `melarc.add_reason_fixtures` writes `FIXTURE_` codes only. **Decisions of the review (10 October 2026).** Rejecting an arm for an unknown principal type: kept, it fits the closed security-context model. Requiring a non-empty array for all seven seed tables: accepted for this reference seed, every current table has required content. The seed content as JSON: accepted for this gate with the trust boundary stated below. Production fixture protection: `FIXTURE_` is a naming restriction, the limitation is explicit below and production provisioning access is settled before release. The unknown-commit HTTP mapping: due before S0.20 (OB-55). The orphan databases: untouched. Expressionless policies (a policy with no `USING` or no `WITH CHECK`): investigated and ruled out as a bypass, PostgreSQL default-denies when no permissive expression grants access; no repair is requested.

**Review of the batch (10 October 2026) and what it changed.** A read-only reviewer read the whole batch against the registry, the contract and the design (it could run nothing). Nothing it reported was taken on trust: each finding was checked against the code and, where it held, fixed test first, the new test being seen to fail for the stated reason before the change. Eight findings, none critical or high. (1) *Medium, real:* an event the audit writer itself refuses fails before any statement is sent, so the transaction stayed healthy and a caller that caught the refusal committed the act with no record; the writer now aborts the transaction (three cases). (2) *Medium, real:* the limiter's cleanup made admissions for different keys queue on each other's deletes, against its own doc comment; one admission at a time now cleans, by a try-lock (OB-109), shown with a test that failed by timeout and three breaks. (3) *Low, real:* the `authentication` arms of `idempotency_record` were wider than the registry's "erasing the sealed columns only" (read every saved answer, complete any command in progress); the policies now admit it to records that hold or held a sealed replay and the update must erase it (the check clause of the update policy is defence in depth that no test can tell from the guard trigger, an equivalent mutant; the other two clauses are each caught by a test that does not touch the first). (4) *Low, real, not reachable yet:* the audit correlation id is now screened like any text. (5) *Low, real:* a `SYSTEM` transaction can no longer name its own technical identifier as a person. (6) *Low, real:* the handle's context is now the one the database service applied (a regression test over the real service caught a shadowed variable in the change itself; the service also now judges the capability on its frozen copy, not on the caller's object). (7) *Low, real:* a diagnostic sink that throws no longer fails production counting. (8) *Low, real:* the test that claimed different keys do not serialise could not detect one global lock; it is replaced by one that proves both key locks are held at the same moment (a break with one constant key lock is caught). Of the four items the reviewer could not verify: the shared capacity is OB-110, `recorded_at` is OB-111, the fingerprint's path parameters are OB-112, and the reading of `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` was **wrong** (libuv reads it with `atoi`, so `0`, `abc` and an empty value are one thread, not four) and is corrected and measured ([S0.16](#s016--bounded-hash-admission)).

**The gates of the batch, and the three failures to report.** The commands of the Commands section of `CLAUDE.md` ran uncached (`TURBO_FORCE=true`, Node 24.21.0, Windows) twice; the figures are in [§1.2](#12-current-position). The first gate ran on the batch as built. The review above then changed code, so the second ran on the tree that is handed over. (1) **`pnpm test` failed once and then passed unchanged.** On the first gate eleven of the 23 Ops Portal test files ended with `[vitest-pool]: Failed to start forks worker` (the 12 that started passed, 143 tests), and turbo cancelled the API run; the same command repeated alone, with nothing changed, passed in full, and on the second gate it passed at the first run. This is the start-up failure `DEVELOPMENT.md` already describes for this workstation; **its cause is not established here** (nothing was diagnosed, no timeout was raised, and a pass is not a diagnosis), and the open finding about this machine (§1.2, "Open owner items") stands. (2) **`test:db` failed once on the second gate, deterministically, for a defect of the review's own fix.** One test (`lets a SYSTEM transaction record the person it authenticated`) named, as the person, the id that the shared test fixture also gives the `SYSTEM` context as its technical identifier; the fix for finding 5 correctly refuses that. The test now gives that context an identifier of its own, as production does (SECURITY_DESIGN.md §14.16); `format:check`, `lint`, `typecheck` and `test:db` were rerun on the final tree and passed. `build`, `contract:check`, `api-client:check`, `db:check`, `pnpm test` and `test:e2e` were not rerun after that one edit of a database test, which none of them reads. (3) **No `execution-budget.db.test.ts` failure occurred** in the three database-project runs (15 tests passed in that file each time; the whole project passed in two of them), so there was no recurrence to capture; the intermittent timer failures of Stage 1 remain unexplained (OB-91; [§7.12](#712-stage-1-correction-batch-10-october-2026-disposition)), and a pass is not a diagnosis.

**Engineering parameters of the batch and their qualification** (each *development-qualified, not production-qualified*; S0.65 calibrates them): the limiter's window (60 s) is the contract's and not a parameter; the limiter's four constants and the hash admission's slots, memory budget and reserved thread are in the rows and the deployment record above; the audit writer's bounds (`AUDIT_LIMITS` in `audit-vocabulary.ts`: 32 keys, depth 4, 512-character texts, 4096 bytes of structured facts, 1000-character notes) are screening limits of this writer and not product values; the metrics registry's diagnostic interval (60 s) likewise. The idempotency window of a replayed secret is the grant's expiry, which the caller supplies; no figure is chosen here.

**What the batch left for the Product Owner to decide** (the rows above, in the order they bite): OB-102 and OB-100 (before the pipeline, S0.20), OB-96 (before S0.34 and S0.49), OB-93, OB-94 and OB-95 (the audit contract's three disagreements), OB-103 (the metric names), OB-110 (the shared capacity, before authentication is exposed) and OB-111 (`recorded_at`, with release gate G1). No unresolved product decision stopped independent work.

### 7.14 Carried from S0.17 to S0.19 (batch of 10 October 2026)

The owner's instruction of 10 October 2026 authorized S0.17 to S0.19 as one bounded batch on top of S0.11 to S0.16, left uncommitted and unpushed for the owner's review of Stage 2 as a whole. **Gate 2 is not passed and is not claimed:** the worker's real `SIGTERM` stop on Linux, WSL2 or CI has not run (OB-24), and the other Linux, WSL2 and CI checks of [§7.2](#72-release-gates--not-acceptance-of-this-slices-code) and OB-108 remain owed. The evidence is *fixture/platform verified* (a real PostgreSQL 18.6, the technical logins, the kit); no operation of the contract exists, so none of it is *real-operation* evidence. The rows below are what the batch decided on its own authority or found in the documents and did not settle; none is a default for a product value, and none changes an identifier, the OpenAPI document, a generated client or a contract.

Chosen where the documents are silent: the jitter is ±20 %; a stop that gives a lease back (`RELINQUISHED`) **counts as an attempt** and the job is due again at once; a record that cannot be read ends the attempt as `REDEMPTION_UNCONFIRMED`, which waits on the schedule and sends nothing; a provider's `Retry-After` may lengthen a wait up to 2 hours and never removes the bound. **The schedule is six attempts, and a lease taken over after a crash and a lease given back at a stop each count as one:** a message claimed a seventh time is asked about once more (the provider may hold it) and then ends as `SCHEDULE_EXHAUSTED`, and nothing is sent. A job given back at its sixth attempt can therefore end without a sixth real send; the owner may prefer that a lease given back before the provider was asked not count. **Review of the batch (10 October 2026) and what it changed.** Two read-only reviewers read the batch against the registry, the contract and the design, one the database side and one the worker, the process, the configuration and the documents (they could run nothing). Nothing they reported was taken on trust: each finding was checked against the code and the documents and, where it held, fixed test first, the new test being seen to fail for the stated reason before the change, or replaced if it could not fail. What held:
- *Medium, both reviewers:* the six-attempt bound was applied only when an unknown outcome was recorded, so a lease taken over after a crash at the sixth attempt, or given back at the sixth at a stop, led to a seventh send, and again for each lease that ended until the credential expired. A message claimed after the last attempt is now asked about and ends, and nothing is sent (OB-118).
- *Medium:* a payload that only this worker could not open (a key, envelope or layout version it had not been given: a rotation under way) was erased and its job failed for good. It is kept and tried again on the schedule; only a payload no worker can open ends the job.
- *High, worker reviewer:* a call was declared late by a timer of its own, which can fire a millisecond before the budget's monotonic clock agrees, so that the next call could start on time that was spent (a test of that case could fail where timers are precise, as on Linux, which was not run), and the signal of the abandoned call's budget was never aborted. A call is now late when its budget says so (shown with a clock that runs at half speed), and the signal is aborted.
- *Medium:* after a shutdown had given a lease back, a lane it had given up on could go on to send (a status query that answered late, then a send) from a process that had reported that it stopped. The budget every job hangs from is finished at the stop and the calls the lanes wait on are let go.
- *Low, real:* `REDEMPTION_CLOSED` read the database clock twice (the state and the class could disagree on either side of the moment the credential ended, and the table refuses the pair); the job's time was counted from the end of the claim though the lease begins inside it; the record was read before the provider's status query and not just before the send; the cleanup ran under no budget of its own and did not leave off at a stop, and a lease that ended on a job the cleanup expired was never counted; `enqueue` and `cancel` under another context than the issuing capability's returned as if nothing was live; the guard let an outcome replace a payload, let the worker's capability cancel jobs it never leased and take a lease of years, and the erase policy of sealed replays did not keep to the window; the API held `SELECT` on the job's identifier, which none of its statements reads (OB-115); the capture sink's folder was judged on its written path (a link into the checkout passed) and its mode was not checked; a configuration made by hand skipped the refusals the loader makes; the shutdown report counted every lease unconfirmed if one could not be given back, could go negative, and an unreadable claim was recorded after the stop; a refusal of `NODE_ENV` told the operator to choose among three modes; and four statements were stale (the number of tests Windows skips, "the only code that opens the capability", a refusal missing from `.env.example`, and "exercised by" cells that no test supported).
- *Test quality, real:* a test that could not fail (a fence phrased with the wrong version), a claimed catch that no test made (an outcome that changes who holds the lease), a test named for a case it did not attempt, "never touches the redemption record" assertions that no code could break (replaced by the shape of the table), a fake queue that never read the budget it ran under, claim and outcome budgets and the back-off cap exercised by no test, a lease-arithmetic test that compared the function with itself, and an assertion that accepted either of two outcomes for a case that has one.
- *Reported and not built:* the worker, not the consuming operation, ends a job whose record closed (OB-126); Local and CI use only the capture adapter by §13.9a, and the loader allows a real provider in a local run (OB-127).

**Targeted breaks of the review's changes.** 61 single breaks (the late call, the stop, the attempt limit, the claim's anchor, the version skew, the periodic task's budget and stop, the shutdown report, the statements of the store, the guard's new rules, the grant, the queue's check of the context, the erase window, the count of leases, the sink's links and permission bits, the configuration's relations, and the runtime's wiring): 55 were caught at first; four gaps (the release of a lane the stop gave up on, a lease that was no longer the worker's, a claim that comes back after the stop, and the group-write bit of the sink's folder) were closed with tests and caught on a second run; two are equivalent mutants (the check of the principal's type, which the check of the capability implies, and the lexical comparison of the sink's path, which the resolved one subsumes wherever the operating system can resolve it).

**One observation of the environment, not of a reviewer.** The database container's clock was ahead of the host's by about 76 ms (75.3 to 76.2 over 40 round trips, measured on 10 October 2026), and one test of this batch that compared the host's `Date.now()` with a time the database wrote, with 50 ms of slack, failed on it; it now compares on the database's clock. Any test that compares the two clocks is sensitive to that offset on this machine. The cause of the intermittent `execution-budget.db.test.ts` failures (OB-91) is not established here, and this is not offered as it.

**The gate of the batch, and the one failure to report.** The commands of the Commands section of `CLAUDE.md` ran uncached (`TURBO_FORCE=true`, Node 24.21.0, Windows) once, on the tree handed over, after the review's changes; the figures are in [§1.2](#12-current-position). (1) **`pnpm test` failed once and then passed unchanged.** In the first run eleven of the 23 Ops Portal test files ended with `[vitest-pool]: Failed to start forks worker ... Timeout waiting for worker to respond` (the 12 that started passed, 143 tests), and turbo cancelled the API run; the same command repeated alone, uncached and with nothing changed, passed in full. This is the start-up failure `DEVELOPMENT.md` already describes for this workstation and the first gate of the previous batch showed; the batch touches nothing of the Ops Portal, **its cause is not established here** (nothing was diagnosed beyond that, no timeout was raised, and a pass is not a diagnosis), and the open finding about this machine (§1.2, "Open owner items") stands. (2) **No `execution-budget.db.test.ts` failure occurred** (15 tests passed in the full `test:db` run), so there was nothing to capture; the intermittent timer failures of Stage 1 remain unexplained (OB-91; [§7.12](#712-stage-1-correction-batch-10-october-2026-disposition)), and a pass is not a diagnosis. (3) **Skipped, not passed:** eight API tests of `pnpm test` (the five real-`SIGTERM` process tests of Stage 1, the delivery worker's real-`SIGTERM` process test, and the two tests of the capture sink's file and folder modes, which a Windows file system cannot answer) and two of `test:db` (`api-process.db.test.ts` and `delivery-worker-process.db.test.ts`, real `SIGTERM`); they run on Linux, WSL2 or CI, and the worker's two are what Gate 2 waits for (OB-24).

**Engineering parameters of the batch and their qualification** (each *development-qualified, not production-qualified*; S0.65 calibrates them): the worker's lanes (4), poll interval (2 s), lease base (30 s) and margin (5 s), claim and outcome budgets (10 s and 5 s), capture-call bound (5 s), relinquish reserve (2 s) and back-off cap (30 s), the schedule's jitter (±20 %; the schedule itself is the document's), the cleanup's batch (200), interval (60 s) and rounds (20), the allow-list's bound (50 entries), and the limits on a destination and a link (`delivery-payload.ts`). They are capacity and screening limits chosen here and not product values. The measured figures, with the machine and the tests that exercise each, are in DEPLOYMENT_AND_ENVIRONMENTS.md §12.5.

**What the batch left for the Product Owner to decide** (the rows above, in the order they bite): OB-113 and OB-114 (which identity may delete, and the periods: before the first operation that stores an idempotency record is exposed, and before any finished-job metadata is to be deleted), OB-115 and OB-116 (the registry's wording; the outcome-class names), OB-117 (the worker's setting names), OB-118, OB-124, OB-125 and OB-126 (the points the schedule's document is silent on; the capture sink's place and form; whether the cleanup has a capability of its own; who ends a job whose record closed) and OB-127 (whether a local run may use a real provider, before G3). OB-102 and OB-100 of [§7.13](#713-carried-from-s011-to-s016-batch-of-10-october-2026) remain the ones that bite first (before S0.20). No unresolved product decision stopped independent work.

### 7.15 Gate 2 audit corrections (11 October 2026): disposition

The audit of S0.11 to S0.19 (the supplied review; no separate audit file exists in the repository) found eight defects and five small gaps; a final bounded follow-up (below) closed what they left open. This section is the one record of what was reproduced, what was changed, what proves it and what remains. It is a correction batch on the tree of the two batches above: nothing is staged, committed or pushed, S0.20 is not started, no dependency changed, `melarc_dev` and every local secret were left alone. **Gate 2 is not passed and is not claimed**: the worker's real `SIGTERM` stop and the capture sink's mode tests are Linux evidence that has not run on this tree (OB-24, no waiver).

**Method.** Each defect was reproduced against the real code before it was changed (a failing test, or a plan taken from the real database), and fixed at its cause. Deliberate breaks of each new guard were run and restored by hash. Three of the breaks were *equivalent mutants* and are named as such below, not counted as caught.

**The owner's decisions of the brief, and what each did.** A (architecture kept): nothing was redesigned; the worker, the queue, lease fencing and purpose-separated keys are as they were. B (Local and CI capture only): §11.A below; closes OB-127. C (the limiter stays database-authoritative): G2-04, G2-05, §11.B; no per-process limiter exists. D (missing key or version support is operational): G2-03. E (tiers fixed centrally; conditional ones by explicit validated context; a read fabricates no before and after): G2-06. F (event identifiers kept; grammar and counts corrected): G2-06, `audit.md` §3 to §6. G (erasure under `credential_delivery` with narrow column privileges): G2-07, §11.E; no new grant of any kind except the one column `deferred_claims` (G2-03) and the one `SELECT` policy of §11.B. H (nothing chosen for retention periods, deletion, the idempotency HTTP error or other unspecified product values): §11.C to §11.E. I (no authenticated work moved into `SYSTEM` to get past audit permissions): P-1 below.

**The five small gaps.**

Tests: `load-config.test.ts`, `worker-config.test.ts`, `delivery-worker-runtime.test.ts`, `app.module.test.ts`; `DEPLOYMENT_AND_ENVIRONMENTS.md` §12.3 and `.env.example` say so.
- **B. The limiter's six settings.** Migration `0012` adds the policy `setting_rate_limit_read`: the `rate_limit` capability may `SELECT` the six `rate_limit_*` rows and no other row of `setting`, and writes nothing (the runtime login holds no write on `setting`). The limiter reads its limit in its own admission transaction, so an admission takes one connection, not two (`SettingsBucketLimits.limitOf(bucket, transaction)`). `settings-reason.db.test.ts` proves the six are readable, every other setting reads as missing, the visible rows are exactly the six, and insert, update and delete are refused; the policy's names are pinned to `RATE_LIMIT_BUCKETS`. The registry's `rate_limit` row (`data-scope-registry.md` §5.2) is amended. **The brief said "prepare or apply"; this is applied, under it, and is the owner's to confirm or reverse (OB-102).** One equivalent mutant: the policy's capability condition is defence in depth, because the only API-login capabilities are `authentication` (which already reads every setting) and `rate_limit`.
- **C. `recorded_at`.** Closed by the owner's decision on P-2 (F-5, migration `0015`): the value is the moment of the insert. Neither `recorded_at` nor the event `id` is a commit-order cursor for the signed checkpoint chain (membership is explicit, `audit.md` §2.1).
- **D. A command in progress under its key.** SECURITY_DESIGN.md §14.16 now records how `begin`, the business effect and `complete` in one transaction leave no committed `IN_PROGRESS` record; that a legitimate concurrent caller does not observe `IN_PROGRESS` (its `begin` waits on the unique index and then replays or owns the command); that `IN_PROGRESS` can be reported only for a record committed without its `complete`, a defect of whoever assembled the command; that the pipeline of S0.20 must make the three steps one unit of work; and that **the contract code and HTTP answer for `IN_PROGRESS`, and who reclaims a stranded record, remain the owner's decisions (OB-100, section 7.14)**. No error code was invented.
- **E. Retention.** DEPLOYMENT_AND_ENVIRONMENTS.md separates three things: erasing credential material (done), the replay guarantees (a saved answer byte for byte; a sealed replay disclosed only until its window closes) and the retention of metadata (a finished job's state, and the reclaiming of an idempotency record; both periods unset, no deletion granted). **S0.19 is complete for the first and for the sealed-replay half of the second; it is not complete as a whole** while OB-113, OB-114 and `OQ-028` are open.

**The delivery deferral, stated precisely (G2-03).** A claim ends as a deferral only when the worker can confirm that it was unable to ask a provider (it could not open the sealed payload for want of a key, envelope or layout version it was not given, or it could not confirm the redemption record) and says so. Such a claim does **not** spend one of the six sends the Class 1 schedule allows: the sends so far are `attempt_count - deferred_claims`. A claim whose outcome is uncertain (the provider was asked and the answer is unknown, an answer after the call's own deadline, a lease that ended with no outcome, a crash) is counted as a send, conservatively, because it may have sent. The wait after a deferral is bounded (30 seconds doubling to a 10-minute cap, with jitter; development-qualified, S0.65), and the worker slows its own claiming while deferrals follow one another. **A deferred message does not wait for ever:** the job ends when its credential does (judged on the database's clock in the statement that claims it: `EXPIRED`, payload erased) or when it is cancelled (consumed, superseded or invalidated: `CANCELLED`, payload erased). The count of deferrals has no cap of its own, because a cap would be a product value nobody has set. While no redemption reader is built (`consume: false`; the reader arrives with S0.29 and S0.50) the worker claims nothing, so it spends nothing of any queued message. A deferral that persists is visible without a secret: `credential_delivery_jobs_deferred_total{reason}` and the job's non-secret `outcome_class` and `deferred_claims`, never the destination or the token.

**Disposition of P-1 to P-7 (the owner's decisions of 11 October 2026).**

- **P-1. Audit `INSERT` for Vendor and Rider: the narrow direction is approved; it is built by the first consumer, not now.** *Scope as approved.* Today only `STAFF` and `SYSTEM` under `authentication` may insert into `audit_event` (migration `0006`). An authenticated Vendor or Rider operation that must audit in its own transaction (`signOut`; a vendor's `requestAdditionalDeviceGrant` and `revokeVendorDevice`) cannot, and running it as `SYSTEM` is refused (decision I). The approved arms preserve the authenticated actor and the same transaction: in `audit_event_insert`, `WHEN 'VENDOR' THEN actor_type = 'VENDOR_ACCOUNT' AND actor_id = melarc.current_principal_id() AND surface_context = 'VENDOR_PWA' AND event_code IN ('auth.session.terminated', 'auth.setup_grant.issued', 'auth.device.revoked')` and `WHEN 'RIDER' THEN actor_type = 'RIDER' AND actor_id = melarc.current_principal_id() AND surface_context = 'RIDER_ANDROID' AND event_code = 'auth.session.terminated'`; no `SELECT` is added; the registry's `AuditEvent` row (§4.5) is amended to say the two arms. *First consumer:* S0.34 (`signOut`), and S0.49 for the vendor device operations. *Tests owed before that consumer is accepted* (database tests as `melarc_api_runtime`): a vendor or rider inserts only its own listed events, and nothing under another actor identifier, actor type, surface or event code; neither can read, change or remove any row of the ledger; the staff and `authentication` arms are unchanged; the refusal of an event aborts the act's transaction. *Bootstrap identities:* the audit of their creation (`staff.identity.created`, basis `BOOTSTRAP_SEED`) belongs **in the transaction that creates them**, not at their first sign-in. The authority for that transaction to write the event (a `seed` or provisioning insert policy or function, which does not exist and which the provisioning login does not hold) is recorded as a **prerequisite of the bootstrap task (S0.30)**; it is not designed or granted here. Closes the decision OB-96 asks for.
- **P-2. `recorded_at`: applied** as F-5 (insertion time, migration `0015`, existing rows preserved, serialisation version 1). Closes OB-111.
- **P-3. The limiter's throughput: the strict design is kept, provisionally.** Measured on the S0.18 machine (Windows 11, 6 cores and 12 threads, 15.9 GB, PostgreSQL 18.6 in a local container): eight callers with their own keys admitted **100 a second against 233 before the capacity lock**; one admission took 18.3 ms with an empty table and 34.8 ms with 19000 live rows; a refusal at a ceiling takes no lock. That is one machine and one topology, development-qualified and not a deployed figure, and no optimisation was made. If it is not enough at the deployed topology (S0.65, release gate G2), the options are a shared advisory lock while the table is far from its capacity and an exclusive one near it (a design with its own proof, sketched and not built), or a reserved share of the capacity per bucket (a product and capacity decision). Neither is chosen.
- **P-4. The answer for a command in progress (OB-100): still pending, to be decided before S0.20.** No code was written and no error code invented; `STATE_CONFLICT` is the nearest existing code and is not chosen. SECURITY_DESIGN.md §14.16 records how the pipeline must make `begin`, the business effect and `complete` one unit of work.
- **P-5. Enhanced events that change nothing: resolved** by F-3.
- **P-6. The queue's insert: resolved** by F-4.

**The "Timeout waiting for worker to respond" investigation (unresolved).**

- *The command.* `pnpm test` is `pnpm run test:root && turbo run test` (turbo 2.11.7, default concurrency), so the `test` task of four packages runs at once (turbo counts five tasks): `@melarc/e2e` (the node:test harness), `@melarc/api` (vitest, projects `unit` and `process`; the second forks the API and the worker as child processes), `@melarc/api-client` (vitest), `@melarc/ops-web` (vitest 5.0.3, projects `components` on jsdom and `node`).
- *The settings.* `apps/ops-web/vitest.config.ts` sets `testTimeout` and `hookTimeout` to 20 s and names no pool or worker count, so vitest's defaults apply (a forks pool, up to the machine's parallelism). The message is vitest's own: a forked worker must report that it has started within 60 s (`START_TIMEOUT` in vitest's pool; the project cannot set it).
- *The output.* In run 1, 11 of 23 Ops files: "[vitest-pool]: Failed to start forks worker for test files ... Caused by: [vitest-pool-runner]: Timeout waiting for worker to respond". The two earlier occurrences (11 of 23 files each, passing on an unchanged rerun) were not sampled.
- *The timing.* The Ops suite run alone on the same machine takes 17.8 s for all 23 files, so a start that takes 60 s is not the suite's own cost.
- *The resource evidence.* A read-only sampler (every 2 s: CPU, free and committed memory, the number and memory of `node` processes) ran through all three `pnpm test` runs of this section. Run 1, Ops failed: CPU 100% for 23 samples, **free memory down to 245 MB** of 15.9 GB, 81% committed, 39 `node` processes, 3.98 GB of `node` memory. Run 2, Ops passed: CPU 100% for 26 samples, free memory no lower than 1047 MB, 78% committed, 29 processes, 3.66 GB. Run 3, Ops passed: CPU 100% for 23 samples, free memory no lower than 2150 MB, 78% committed, 40 processes, 3.54 GB. The machine is a 6-core, 12-thread workstation with 15.9 GB, shared with 26 to 35 Chrome processes and the Docker VM (about 0.7 GB). The unsigned process of the earlier machine finding was not running.
- *What this shows, and what it does not.* The run that failed is the run in which free memory fell to a tenth of a gigabyte; CPU saturation and the number of processes do not separate the runs. That is a correlation in three sampled runs, one of them a failure. It is not a cause, it was not reproduced on demand, and the sampler adds a small load of its own.
- *Bounded comparison (follow-up, 11 October 2026).* One run, chosen in advance, with everything enabled: `pnpm run test:root` (the first half of `pnpm test`; it ran just before, exit 0) and then `TURBO_FORCE=true pnpm exec turbo run test --concurrency=1` in place of Turbo's default concurrency, so that the four packages' suites ran one after another and not together. No timeout was raised, nothing was left out, the Ops pool, the CI workflow and the repository's scripts were left as they were, and the run was not repeated. *Result:* exit 0 in 3 min 16 s, five tasks successful and none cached: Ops Portal 23 files and 220 tests (15.6 s), API 144 files with 4469 passed and 8 skipped (132.7 s), api-client 250, harness 199 passed and 1 skipped; **no worker failed to start**. The same read-only sampler recorded the 87 samples of the run: CPU at 100% in 15 (23 to 26 at the default concurrency), free memory no lower than 1080 MB (245 MB in the failing run; 1047 MB and 2150 MB in the passing ones), at most 78% committed, **at most 15 `node` processes and 2.4 GB of `node` memory (29 to 40 processes and 3.5 to 4.0 GB at the default)**, 26 to 31 Chrome processes and the Docker VM at 961 MB. *What it shows:* with the suites serialised the `node` footprint was less than half, and the Ops Portal started every file. *What it does not:* the Ops Portal also started every file in two of the three default-concurrency runs, a 1080 MB floor cannot be told from the 1047 MB of a passing default run, and one passing run neither reproduces the failure nor refutes it. It is consistent with contention among the concurrent suites and is not a cause.
- *Disposition.* **Unresolved.** No timeout was raised, no test disabled, no worker count or concurrency changed, and the suite was not repeated until it passed (the reruns above were needed for the two other failures). Two bounded resource-management changes would fit the evidence and are **not applied**, because the evidence does not establish the cause: capping turbo's concurrency for `test`, or capping the Ops pool's `maxWorkers`. The owner decides, and such a change would be recorded as a resource-management change with every suite still run. The older timing failures of `execution-budget.db.test.ts` (OB-91) are a separate matter that this evidence does not explain: that file passed in both `test:db` runs. **After the follow-up's comparison the matter is still unresolved**: nothing permanent was changed, CI's concurrency is untouched, and a lower-concurrency `test` script or a cap on the Ops pool remains the owner's decision with this evidence, at a cost in wall-clock time to every run.

**Gate 2 status.** Not passed and not claimed. Evidence reached: *fixture/platform verified* on Windows (a real PostgreSQL 18.6, the technical logins, the test kit), including the follow-up, **and on Linux in CI**: the pull request run for `9eaa152` (11 October 2026, `ubuntu-24.04`) passed every job, which obtains the Linux evidence of OB-24 (the real-`SIGTERM` stops of the API and of the worker, idle and with a message in flight) and OB-62. No route, screen or contract operation exists, and the contract comparison of zero operations proves nothing about identity conformance. **Independent review of the batch (11 October 2026) and what it changed.** One read-only reviewer with a fresh context read the S0.24 code and the S0.23 harness (it could run unit tests and the migration lint, not the database tests). Nothing it reported was taken on trust: each finding was checked against the code and the documents and, where it held, fixed test first, the new test being seen to fail for the stated reason before the change.
- *High, not a defect of the tree:* "`session_guard` is created but never attached". The reviewer read the migration while one of my break checks was running on it (a check removes a line and restores the file by hash); the migration of the tree creates both triggers (`session_guard` and `staff_identity_guard`), and `session-schema.db.test.ts` proves them on a migrated database. The rule that follows is kept: no break check runs while a reviewer reads. Its secondary point held: the guard let `last_activity_at` jump to any future time, which disables the idle limit (`judgeSession` treats it as not idle). The trigger now refuses an activity more than five minutes after the database's own clock, and one that moves back.
- *Medium, held:* the issuer could not tell which credential the caller verified, so a session could be issued on a credential that was replaced after the verification and then outlive the replacement. `IssueSessionRequest.verifiedCredentialAt` was compared under the identity lock with the moment the identity's credential was established (`CREDENTIAL_CHANGED`); the audit that followed (§7.17, F02) showed that a moment cannot tell two credentials apart, and it is now the credential's generation (`verifiedCredentialGeneration`). A replacement between discovery and lock restarts and then refuses; a request that states none, or one that is not a whole number of one or more, is a `TypeError`. What the writers of a credential must do for this to hold is OB-128.
- *Low, held, fixed test first:* two `Authorization` header lines are merged by Node and the first used, so two bearer credentials were not refused as ambiguous like two session cookies (now judged from the raw header lines); the schema allowed a browser session with no CSRF hash (`session_csrf_by_principal`: a hash exactly when the session is not a rider's); `terminate` raised `23514` and rolled the whole revoking transaction back after the database clock stepped back past a session's issue time (`greatest(clock_timestamp(), issued_at)`); the test-CA's "outside the checkout" check compared text, and the reviewer showed it accepting a junction into the checkout, `\\?\E:\…` and `\\localhost\E$\…` (all three are refused now, wherever the path leads; a read-only probe on this machine confirmed the extended-length, case-different, `\\localhost\E$` and `\\127.0.0.1\E$` spellings are refused); the generator left `ca.srl` in the result directory by OpenSSL's default (`-CAserial` keeps it in the work directory), removed only the three known files on a failure, and its policy checked no name constraints (see S0.23 above).
- *Low, reported and not changed:* that activity is recorded before a later step refuses the request (finding 13); that the floor checks would land after CSRF (OB-130); and that a staff context can read its own `credential_hash` (finding 14).
- *Checked and sound, as the reviewer found:* the lock order policy, then identity, then session, and the bundle lock held across the read and the insert; nothing written before the revalidation passes; coalesced activity only moves forward; expiry and idleness expire at equality and every judged time is a millisecond `Date`; cookie and bearer kept apart, and no token in a log, an event or a parameter; fail-closed composition; each policy a single `CASE` with a closed `ELSE`, narrower than the registry.

**Findings and decisions for the Product Owner** (nothing here was defaulted or invented):

1. **Where the authenticated-API bucket sits in the refusal order.** permission-enforcement.md §5.1 puts "rate limit" first, before authentication; the authenticated bucket is keyed on the *active session*, which exists only once the credential has been verified, and a limiter keyed on an unverified credential lets any caller invent keys and fill `rate_limit_admission` (OB-110). It is applied by the authentication guard, right after the session is found and before CSRF, authorization and validation. The pre-authentication buckets are keyed from the body at step 1, as written. The owner confirms or changes the wording of §5.1.
2. **`SETTING_MISSING` and `SETTING_INVALID` have no decided HTTP status** (`ERROR_STATUS` holds `null`); a setting that is missing or invalid is an unexpected `500` today. *(Decided by the owner on 12 October 2026, decision B, and built: the existing fixed, code-less `503`; [§7.18](#718-the-gate-3-completion-batch-12-october-2026).)*
3. **Forty-one status inconsistencies in operations outside the thirty-eight of this slice** (statuses declared in the contract that disagree with the axis table's rule, errors-and-enums.md §4). They are later slices' and untouched; each slice that builds one of those operations resolves its own.
4. **`Expect: 100-continue` is not handled**, and a refusal that keeps the connection open drains the rest of the body, bounded by the request deadline; a slot is given back when the response is over, so a handler that goes on after its client has gone is bounded by its budget only.
5. **The limiter is composed without a metrics registry**, so `rate_limited_total` is not counted until S0.68 (OB-107).
6. **Two behaviours changed on purpose:** a body that is not `application/json` is now refused `415` at the transport, and a small malformed JSON body is answered at the validation step, after the guards, as the refusal order requires (`AC-SLICE-000-130`).
7. **The minimal `staff_identity` carries `credential_hash` and `credential_established_at`**, because S0.31 (which lists no migration) writes the credential and S0.32 adds only the failed-attempt count and lock time; (and, since §7.17, `credential_generation`), and the runtime holds `UPDATE` on those three columns **now, before anything writes them**, because a row lock (`FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, the identity lock of §13.10a) needs an `UPDATE` privilege on at least one column. The registry allows exactly this for the `authentication` capability ("`UPDATE` of the credential record only"). The owner confirms.
8. **`session.state` is not a column:** a session is active while `terminated_at` is null, so there is no second source of truth. The port's `NewSession.surface` was removed (it is derived from the principal type) and `PrincipalSummary` gained `bundleId` and `authorizedHubIds` and `IdentityDirectory` gained `readIdentity` (the non-authoritative discovery read).
9. **`SessionStore.terminate` by bundle takes `belowRevision`**, the filter a reduction needs (S0.27 calls it); the browser session's `csrf_token_hash` is created by the issuer with the session (S0.25 validates against it).
10. **The own-clock rule now flags `new Date()` with no argument**, not every `new Date(...)`: a date built from a value reads no clock, and the database's `timestamptz` text is read through `timestampOf`.
11. *(Built in S0.26 and S0.27: [§7.18](#718-the-gate-3-completion-batch-12-october-2026).)* **The request-time authority checks are S0.26's and S0.27's, not S0.24's** (a below-floor session is still accepted by authentication, and nothing is served yet because authorization refuses every route that needs a principal). The same holds for the lock rule of a state-changing request: authentication judges the session once, in its lookup, which takes no policy lock (a read-only request takes none, §13.10a); the shared policy lock on the acting session's bundle and the re-check of the session under it are S0.26's.
12. **Mutation checks.** The owner asked for no broad mutation campaign. Break checks were run on the **new code of this batch only** (the guards of S0.22, the sessions code, the migration, S0.21's earlier set, and the changes the review caused), each mutant restored by hash, about 175 mutants in all; the survivors were either equivalent (one, the order in which a bearer and a cookie are returned after the ambiguity check) or closed by a test. If that is more than the instruction meant, say so.
13. *(Decided by the owner on 12 October 2026, decision A, and built in S0.26: [§7.18](#718-the-gate-3-completion-batch-12-october-2026).)* **Any request that authentication accepts counts as activity, even one a later step refuses.** The activity is recorded (coalesced) in the authentication step, before the authenticated-API bucket, CSRF and authorization run, so a request answered `429` or `403` still extends `last_activity_at`, and a screen that polls an endpoint it is refused keeps a session alive. `authentication-guard.db.test.ts` states the behaviour. Whether a refused request should count is a product decision; until it is made, the Ops Portal must not poll while it is unattended (S0.38 onward).
14. **A staff context could read its own `credential_hash` (closed in §7.17, F04; kept here as the record of the finding and of the choice the owner still has).** `staff_identity_select` admits a staff member's own row and the runtime login holds a table-wide `SELECT` (one login serves the staff context and the `authentication` capability, so a column grant cannot tell them apart). The registry allows self rows, and nothing reads the column for a staff context, but domain-model.md §6.8 says a credential is never retrievable, and only the absence of a defect in a handler keeps it so. A table of its own for the credential, whose policy admits the `authentication` capability alone, is one fix: a classification in the registry and a migration. The fix made (§7.17) is narrower and needs neither: the runtime has no `SELECT` on the column at all, and the `authentication` capability reads it through one `SECURITY DEFINER` function that refuses every other context. The owner may still prefer the table (it leaves the identity row with no column the runtime may update for the identity lock, which is why it was not taken).

It is the signature of the earlier occurrences ([§7.15](#715-gate-2-audit-corrections-11-october-2026-disposition)), in a package this batch did not touch, and **it is not the corrected worker `SIGTERM` test**, which is a different suite and was not involved. Nothing was raised, disabled or reconfigured, and the command was run once more and not again.

The repeat, which passed: CPU at 100% in 33 of 101 samples (mean 58%), free memory no lower than 1165 MB, at most 88% committed, at most 44 `node` processes and 3.6 GB of `node` memory, 33 Chrome processes: the profile of the passing default-concurrency runs of §7.15 (29 to 40 processes, 3.5 to 4.0 GB). That profile does not separate a passing run from a failing one, so **the cause is not established**; it is consistent with contention among the four suites that turbo runs at once and is not shown to be it. Capping turbo's concurrency for `test` or the Ops pool's `maxWorkers` remains the owner's decision, with this evidence, at a cost in wall-clock time to every run.
- *`execution-budget.db.test.ts` did not fail* in this gate, so there was no failure to capture (its 15 tests passed within `test:db`). Over `test:db` (the sampler was started 40 seconds into its 8 minutes) it saw CPU below 99% throughout (mean 32%) and free memory no lower than 2536 MB. It read source and ran isolated probes; it did not run the database, browser or end-to-end suites. Nothing in it was taken on trust: each finding was checked against the code and, where it could be, reproduced (F01 against a real PostgreSQL, F05 over sockets, F06 on what Playwright writes) before it was fixed, test first, and the new code was held to deliberate breaks, restored by hash. **This section is the record; there is no separate handoff.** Nothing is committed, staged or pushed, and Gate 3 is not claimed.

### 7.18 The Gate 3 completion batch (12 October 2026)

**Authorization and scope.** The owner's instruction of 12 October 2026 authorizes, as one bounded batch with internal checkpoints: finishing S0.23 (trusted HTTPS harness) as far as the approved environment allows, S0.25 (CSRF, Origin and Fetch Metadata), S0.26 (authorization), S0.27 (the bundle-change primitive and its races; **S0.27 is the exit task of Gate 3**), and the step-by-step owner instructions for S0.28 (independent manual evidence, needed by S0.43, **not** a substitute for S0.27). No task is renumbered and no gate membership changes. S0.29 and every Stage 4 task are not started; no real sign-in, recovery or administration operation is added, so **fixture/platform evidence stays distinct from real-operation acceptance**. The new work is left unstaged, uncommitted and unpushed; no merge, deployment, dependency or toolchain change; `melarc_dev` and every `.env` are untouched; no CA or private key is generated on the owner's Windows machine and no trust store is changed.

**Baseline.** One scoped checkpoint commit of the reviewed closeout of §7.16 and §7.17 was authorized and made before any new code: `138d02ccada3399793ea914863c490afb74ce469` (parent `0cb2d6d21cbc3a4f3846ee5c0f4a587bde94f02a`, branch `feat/slice-000-gate-3`, 132 paths staged by explicit list: 51 modified and 81 new; unsigned, because no signing is configured). Before it, the working tree matched `melarc-s0.20-s0.24-review-corrected-source.zip` (SHA-256 `1d417900752eee14661e45b3c9a1dd10803805a1b323fa34563227fcff1f4278`) **file for file** (825 files; the manifest compared by hash), and no archive, `.env`, key, `tmp/`, Graphify output or local tool setting was in the commit. Nothing is pushed. While restoring it, one defect of an earlier edit of this plan was found and repaired: the heading of section 8 (the pinned tests) had been dropped from the plan by that edit.

**The owner's decisions of 12 October 2026, and how each is applied.**

| | Decision| Applied as| Where it is normative / proved|
|---|---|---|---|
| A| **Idle activity.** A failed CSRF check, a denied authorization and a rate-limit refusal do not extend the browser idle lifetime; unattended background polling does not keep an otherwise idle session alive. Not "every 4xx is inactivity": an authenticated, authorized action that receives validation or state-conflict feedback is still activity. Qualifying activity is defined **in server-side route policy**, never by a client header; absolute expiry is unchanged; the activity write is integrated with fresh session-state checks so that it cannot revive a terminated or expired session| Every route that needs a principal declares its activity policy (`qualifying` or `background`); a route with none stops the API at start. The authentication step **no longer writes activity**. A request records activity only **after** rate limit, authentication, CSRF and authorization, and only if the final outcome is not an authentication, CSRF, authorization or rate-limit refusal, by the session's row lock and then one conditional statement on the database's own clock (`terminated_at is null`, `now < expires_at`, not idle) whose affected-row count is read: a session ended, gone idle or expired during a lock wait is not revived, whether the other transaction changed the row or only locked it ([§7.19](#719-independent-review-of-the-gate-3-completion-batch-12-october-2026-disposition), V01)| SECURITY_DESIGN.md §13.3; plan S0.24 (activity coalescing), OB-131; proved on a fixture route in `activity.db.test.ts` and the pipeline tests. **Obligation for future routes:** every polling or refresh route declares `background`; the first such route is a Stage 5 task's, with a test that it does not extend idle|
| B| **Missing or invalid required settings.** The runtime `SETTING_MISSING` and `SETTING_INVALID` failures map to the existing fixed, code-less `503`; no invented public `Error.code`, no setting value in a response or a log, no guessed `Retry-After`. The unknown-commit answer stays the separate code-less `500` with its fixed text and no `Retry-After`; an uncertain mutation is never retried automatically| The two error classes of the settings reader are operational failures of the platform filter| `operational-failure.ts`; `errors-and-enums.md` §4 and `ERROR_STATUS` (the two codes stay catalogue codes of the hub-settings paths of later slices, and the runtime failure does not use them on the wire)|
| C| **Authority floor.** A genuinely invalid, below-floor session is `401 SESSION_INVALID` **in authentication, before CSRF**; the stated refusal order is aligned. Kept distinct: an instance below `minimum_revision`, and an instance older than the session's `policy_revision`: both are the operational `503`, end no session and keep the readiness behaviour (`policy_superseded`). Only an instance qualified to evaluate current policy applies the invalid-session termination rule. Planned policy locks, authoritative revalidation and the mutation transaction boundary are preserved: the early check replaces neither the locked check nor the lock order| The authentication step compares the session with the bundle's `reduction_floor` and, for a Vendor or a Rider, with the fixed policy's `minimum_revision` and this build's compiled revision, without a lock (a read is ordered before a reduction it races). **What was built.** Each task was built test first and then held to deliberate breaks of its own code (the "Break caught" comments in the tests; the counts are below). The state cells of the obligations this batch ran or changed (OB-01 to OB-07, OB-09, OB-12, OB-20, OB-21, OB-28, OB-63, OB-65, OB-72, OB-73, OB-75, OB-100, OB-130, OB-131) are updated where they stand and are not restated here.

- **S0.25, CSRF, Origin and Fetch Metadata** (`platform/auth/csrf/`, `platform/routes/csrf.guard.ts`, `platform/http/cors.ts`; step 3 of `AC-SLICE-000-130`). One pure decision in a fixed order, the first failure the one the audit names and every failure outwardly the same `403 CSRF_VALIDATION_FAILED`: the `Origin` must equal, as the string a browser writes, an origin configured for the surface (a missing, repeated, `null`, malformed or unlisted value is refused; the header is read from the raw lines, because Node joins repeated ones); Fetch Metadata is read where the browser sends it (`Sec-Fetch-Site` `same-origin` or absent; anything else, a repeated line included, is refused); and for a cookie-authenticated request the synchronizer token is compared in constant time with the hash the session stored (a missing, repeated or wrong header, and a session that holds no hash, are mismatches). The guard decides three cases by what the request is authenticated with and never by anything the client says: a browser pre-session mutation (an `anonymous` route, judged against the origins of the surfaces it serves), a cookie session (judged against its own surface's origin: a staff session is the Ops origin's, a vendor session the Vendor origin's) and a native operation (an `anonymous` route declared `native`, or a Rider bearer session: no Origin, token or Fetch Metadata is required). Safe methods pass; a route that needs a principal and holds no session is refused (this guard must never be the one that lets such a request on); a route that states no client is held to the browser rule on both surfaces. `auth.csrf.rejected` carries the route as matched and the check that failed, never the token, its hash or the `Origin` as sent, and a failure to record it never decides the answer. Credentialed CORS answers a configured origin with the configured string (never the request's own, never `*`), gives an unlisted origin no header and refuses its preflight (`403`, no error code), answers a preflight itself before routing with a fixed list of methods and headers, and sends `Vary: Origin`. Tests: `csrf-decision.test.ts`, `cors.test.ts`, `csrf.guard.test.ts` and, over real HTTP with real sessions, `csrf-guard.db.test.ts`.
- **S0.26, authorization** (`platform/authorization/`, `platform/routes/authorization.guard.ts`, `platform/auth/sessions/`). *The guard* (steps 4 to 7): the surface gate (the route names the surfaces it serves; a Vendor session on an Ops-only operation fails before ownership is considered), the permission from the **snapshot** the session was issued with (never the live bundle, a role or a bundle's name), the scope of **the grant that authorizes this operation** intersected with what the session reaches (`effective-scope.ts`: `own` is the session's hubs, `all` the explicit all-hub mode, `none` and a `self` operation an empty set, and an empty set means no rows, never all rows), the tier (`tier-policy.ts`: `A < S < P`, a grant with no tier meets no requirement, `INSUFFICIENT_AUTHORITY` is a held key at too low a tier and `PERMISSION_DENIED` a key not held, never both; the route declares it, `tier: { minimum, rule }`, and the guard decides it at step 6, before the scope and the validation: [§7.19](#719-independent-review-of-the-gate-3-completion-batch-12-october-2026-disposition), F01) and the existence rule for a record named in the path (`record-scope.ts`: `404 NOT_FOUND`, or for staff on a hub-scoped entity `403 HUB_SCOPE_VIOLATION` by the scope probe; a Vendor and a Rider are answered `NOT_FOUND` by the same code path as a record that does not exist; `RECORD_ENTITIES` is empty until a slice adds a table that an operation addresses by id). The decision is kept beside the request (`AuthorizedRequest`). Route declarations now state their surfaces, an activity policy, optionally a record and optionally a tier, and a route that needs a principal and states no surfaces or no activity policy stops the API at start. *The runner:* `OperationRunner.read` takes no policy lock and refuses a state-changing request; `OperationRunner.mutate` runs the S0.7 toolkit (the shared lock on the acting session's bundle and, for a Vendor or a Rider, on the fixed policy; the session read again under them and judged on one fresh database instant), so a session that a reduction ended while the request waited is `401` and nothing the use case would have written is written (`OB-131`). *The authority floors* (decision C, `session-authority.ts`): authentication compares a session with its bundle's `reduction_floor` and, for a Vendor or a Rider, with the fixed policy's `minimum_revision` and this build's compiled revision, without a lock; a genuinely below-floor session is `401 SESSION_INVALID` before CSRF is considered and is ended `AUTHORITY_CHANGED` with one enhanced `auth.session.authority_revoked`; an instance that cannot be sure of the policy (no compiled revision, none seeded, below the floor, older than the session) answers the operational `503`, ends nothing, and `/readyz` reports `policy_superseded` (`policy-readiness.ts`). *Activity* (decision A): authentication no longer writes it; `SessionActivityInterceptor` records it after the guards by the route's declared policy and the outcome, through `ActivityRecorder`: the session's row lock first, then one conditional statement on the database's clock that finds the session live (a refusal of authority, a failure of the platform and a `background` route never extend it; a validation or state answer to an authorized action does; the absolute expiry never moves). *Evidence:* `authorization-core.test.ts`, `operation-runner.test.ts`, `session-authority.test.ts` and `session-activity.interceptor.test.ts` (units) and `authorization.db.test.ts`, `authority.db.test.ts`, `activity.db.test.ts` and `refusal-order.db.test.ts` (a fixture operation of the test, in no route inventory and no `IMPLEMENTED_OPERATIONS`, proves the whole order, that a refused request has no side effect and that a command's idempotency record, effect and answer are one unit of work).
- **S0.27, the bundle-change primitive and its races** (migration `0017`, `platform/authorization/policy-change/`, `seed-helper.ts`, `migration-lint.ts`). **Decided and recorded: SQL functions, not application code behind a command**, because the registry names the migration login as the identity for a policy change after the seed, a migration is SQL, and the only way into a forced-row-level-security table that this codebase accepts is a `SECURITY DEFINER` function with a fixed search path and a restricted `EXECUTE` (migration `0005` is the precedent). `melarc.change_role_bundle` and `melarc.change_fixed_policy` take the exclusive lock in the canonical order, read the current revision, write the content and the revision and, on a **reduction**, raise `reduction_floor` (or `minimum_revision`) and end every `ACTIVE` session recorded below it with `AUTHORITY_CHANGED` and one enhanced `auth.session.authority_revoked` each, **in the same transaction** (the events are the ones `endForAuthority` writes, and a test compares them); an addition raises the revision and ends nothing; a change of the name alone raises nothing. A reduction is the removal of a grant or a narrowing of its hub scope (`none < own < all`), its ownership scope (`own` and `assigned` are not ordered: a move between them is a reduction) or its tier (`none < A < S < P`, where a null tier is *not applicable* and ranks below every tier: OB-75); a change that cannot be shown to be a widening is a reduction, because that can only end more sessions, never fewer. The functions run at `READ COMMITTED` only, refuse the protocol's violations (an upgrade, a bundle lock after a fixed lock, a lower key after a higher one), accept a correlation id of a fixed grammar and run only as the migration login; the runtime, the worker and the provisioning login have no `EXECUTE` on them and no table privilege is given to anyone. `melarc.lock_policy_keys` takes a seed's or a release step's exclusive keys in one call in canonical order, and the seed now takes its keys with it. The migration lint refuses a direct write of a policy table unless the migration says why (`-- allow-policy-dml:`). A new task capability, `policy_change`, is asserted only by these functions and is in the registry. `changeRoleBundle` and `changeFixedPolicy` (TypeScript) are the door for a caller that changes one object, and `PolicyChangeError` names the database's refusals. *Evidence* (`policy-change.db.test.ts`, `policy-change-races.db.test.ts`, on a real PostgreSQL 18.6): the privilege matrix over every technical login; a reduction against a sign-in and against a state-changing request in both orders (the session of a sign-in that was ahead is ended; one that starts after reads the reduced content; a request already past its lock finishes whole before the reduction proceeds; one that waits meets an ended session and does nothing); additions that retain snapshots, followed by a reduction that ends every session below its floor; two writers that serialise; a writer that does not hold up a distinct key; an exclusive lock that cannot be taken in time leaves nothing; no advisory lock on the connection afterwards; a stricter isolation level refused; the classification matrices; the SQL lock keys equal to the toolkit's, as the server reports them in `pg_locks`; and two steps that take a bundle and then the Vendor policy never deadlock.

`Set-Cookie` forwarded unchanged; `GBT-W9`); `engine-trust.ts`, a store of its own for each engine in the run's directory (Chromium: the NSS database of a home directory made for the run, `HOME` set for the browser process only; **Findings and decisions for the Product Owner** (nothing here was defaulted or invented):

1. **The primitive is two `SECURITY DEFINER` functions under a new task capability, `policy_change`.** Forced row-level security leaves nobody an `UPDATE` or a `DELETE` on the three policy tables (the owner and the migration login included), and the runtime may hold `SELECT` only, so the registry's "writers: seed, migration" had no way to act once the seed had run. The functions are owned by `melarc_owner` and executable by the migration login alone; the capability can be asserted as a label by the runtime logins and reaches nothing for them, because they hold `SELECT` on these tables and no more (`policy-change.db.test.ts` proves it for every login). This is a new security surface; the registry and SECURITY_DESIGN.md §13.10a are updated in the same change. **Approved by the owner on 12 October 2026 ([§7.20](#720-the-owners-approvals-of-12-october-2026)).** The alternative, application code behind a provisioning command, would need the same functions for the writes and privileges to end sessions and write the audit that only the runtime holds.
2. **How SLICE-009's edit operation reaches the functions is undecided, and no privilege was widened.** The runtime has no `EXECUTE` on them and no table privilege (the registry's `api` writer for the policy tables was withdrawn by the decision on OB-73). The slice chooses: one `EXECUTE` grant to the runtime on one function (a reviewed line in `APPROVED_DEFINER_EXECUTE` and in the matrix of `policy-change.db.test.ts`), or a privileged job run as the migration login. This is the conflict, presented and not resolved.
3. **A move between `own` and `assigned` ownership is treated as a reduction**, as is any change whose direction the orders cannot show (`any` ranks above both; the two are not ordered). A wrong guess costs sessions ended that need not have been, never sessions kept. **Approved by the owner on 12 October 2026 ([§7.20](#720-the-owners-approvals-of-12-october-2026)).**
4. **The primitive changes a bundle's name and the complete set of its grants, and nothing else.** It does not change a bundle's audience or its `privileged` flag; a change to either alters who may approve whom, and no document of this slice says how it is made. The slice that needs it decides.
5. **The seed is moved onto the primitive's locking, not onto its diff.** `runSeed` takes every key it creates with `melarc.lock_policy_keys` (one SQL ordering for every writer) and inserts revision 1 and floor 1 into an empty set through `melarc.initialize_reference_data`; an insert is not a change, so it calls neither change function.
6. **The correlation id of a change is a grammar** (`^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._:/#-]{0,127}$`) that checks shape and nothing more: it is validation and no screen for a secret or for personal data, so a caller passes an identifier it generated or the fixed label of a release step and never text that a user supplied (the wording was corrected on the review of 12 October 2026, [§7.19](#719-independent-review-of-the-gate-3-completion-batch-12-october-2026-disposition)). **Approved by the owner on 12 October 2026 ([§7.20](#720-the-owners-approvals-of-12-october-2026)).**
7. **Authentication now reads the authority on every authenticated request**: one read of `role_bundle` and, for a Vendor or a Rider, one of `fixed_permission_policy`, inside the authentication transaction that already exists (no extra connection and no lock). It is an engineering cost that S0.65 measures; development-qualified, not production-qualified.
8. **CI gains a package step and a longer budget.** The `integrated` job installs `libnss3-tools` (`sudo apt-get install --no-install-recommends --yes`) and runs `pnpm run test:e2e:https` after `pnpm run test:e2e`; its `timeout-minutes` goes from 25 to 30 for the added suite. The package is a tool of the runner and not a dependency of the repository, and no trust store of the runner is changed *(superseded for WebKit alone: [§7.21](#721-the-first-hosted-run-of-the-checkpoint-12-october-2026-its-diagnosis-and-the-correction); the owner's decision of 12 October 2026 puts the disposable CA in the system store of the GitHub-hosted runner for WebKit's proofs)*. **Approved by the owner on 12 October 2026 ([§7.20](#720-the-owners-approvals-of-12-october-2026)): the package and the 30-minute budget.** The first hosted run exercises a workflow change this large: if a step is wrong, that run shows it.
9. **`pnpm run test:e2e` runs Chromium over plain HTTP only**; Firefox and WebKit run in `test:e2e:https`, which exists only on Linux (CI, or a machine cleared for key material). On the developer's Windows workstation there is no automated HTTPS run, because Chromium, Chrome and Edge use the operating system's trust store there and a persistent machine-wide trust change needs the owner's exact installation and removal plan first ([§10](#10-owner-resolutions--the-status-of-every-item), row 4). `test:browser` (the shell and components in three engines over plain HTTP) is unchanged.
10. **WebKit's trust mechanism is a candidate** (`SSL_CERT_FILE` for the browser process): whether Playwright's WebKit build honours it is what the first run shows; until it does, WebKit is reported blocked and not green. *(Resolved by the first hosted run: it is ignored, and WebKit's trust is the system store of a GitHub-hosted runner by the owner's decision of 12 October 2026: [§7.21](#721-the-first-hosted-run-of-the-checkpoint-12-october-2026-its-diagnosis-and-the-correction).)* The branded Chrome and Edge smoke is a person's.
11. **`melarc_dev` holds only migration `0000`** (a strictly read-only comparison of its journal table with the folder, 12 October 2026; nothing was changed). No earlier `0016` was ever applied there, so there is no applied history to correct and no forward migration to write; `db:migrate`, when the owner runs it, applies `0001` to `0017` in one run. The folder and the journal agree.
12. **Disposable databases were left on the local server** by runs that timed out (nine marked `melarc_test_*` databases when the gate began; `pnpm --filter @melarc/api run db:orphans` lists them and changes nothing). `db:orphans --drop` was not authorized in this batch; when five of them made one database test fail (the gate record below) the owner authorized dropping exactly those five on 12 October 2026, and only those were dropped. Four remain (`melarc_test_0ad977c7`, `_36dad696`, `_53fec8b3`, `_7500ca4d`; none holds a privilege of the capability role) and one with no marker, `melarc_test_unmarked12c5bfb2`, which `db:orphans` does not list and nothing here touched. They are the owner's to remove. Some are from this batch's timed-out runs; the rest cannot be attributed. *(Superseded: on 12 October 2026 the owner authorized the removal of the ten marked ones, which were removed, and the three unmarked ones were inspected and kept: [§7.20](#720-the-owners-approvals-of-12-october-2026).)*
13. **OB-100: the exact narrow proposal** (decision F). *What the retained requirements say* (SECURITY_DESIGN.md §14.16): a command's `begin`, effect and `complete` are one transaction of the caller; the record is visible to anyone else only at commit, and then already `COMPLETED`; a concurrent duplicate does not see `IN_PROGRESS` at all but waits on the unique index and then replays; a committed `IN_PROGRESS` record exists only if a command was assembled wrongly. *What the fixture shows* (`refusal-order.db.test.ts`): a command that fails after `begin` rolls the record back with its effect and the retry owns the command; a failure in the middle of the write rolls the record and the effect back together; two concurrent requests under one key, the first held open by a row lock and both watched on the server (never timed), leave the second waiting on the unique index until the first commits, then replaying its answer, with the record changed once; a record planted `IN_PROGRESS` (what a defect would leave) is not answered as a success or a replay, and the pipeline answers the fixed code-less `500` of the unexpected failure with nothing changed. **So no client-visible outcome exists for a correct command, and the missing code would be for a defect.** *Proposal:* (1) add no contract error code: the `IN_PROGRESS` outcome of the store is an internal invariant failure, answered by the existing fixed code-less `500` with the request id, logged with the operation and the principal's type (never the key) and counted, so that S0.68 can alert on it; (2) who reclaims such a record is the open part of OB-113 and OB-114 (no identity holds `DELETE` on the table), and the narrowest reading is that the existing retention cleanup ends it after the replay window, which needs the owner's identity and period; (3) if the owner prefers a client-visible answer instead, `STATE_CONFLICT` is the nearest code and would mislead a client that can safely retry, so the contract would need a new code. **Until the owner decides, the dependent acceptance item stays blocked:** the fixture keeps its `it.todo` for the HTTP answer and the code, and no criterion is reported passed on this path. *(Refined by the review of 12 October 2026, [§7.19](#719-independent-review-of-the-gate-3-completion-batch-12-october-2026-disposition): the code-less `500` is for a committed, stranded `IN_PROGRESS` record only, which a defect of whoever assembled the command leaves; a duplicate whose wait runs out of time is the platform's operational failure, and that distinction is tested.)* *(Approved by the owner on 12 October 2026, [§7.20](#720-the-owners-approvals-of-12-october-2026): the code-less `500` is the answer for a committed, stranded `IN_PROGRESS` record only, and there is no automatic reclamation, so the retention-cleanup reading in point (2) is not adopted.)*
14. **Later slices' status disagreements** (41 operations outside the thirty-eight of this slice, §7.16 finding 3) are untouched, as decision F says; each slice that builds one resolves its own.

**Gate of the batch** (uncached, `TURBO_FORCE=true`, Node 24.21.0, pnpm 11.1.3, Windows 11, a local PostgreSQL 18.6; run once on the tree handed over, from 13:47 to 14:05 UTC: `138d02c` plus 128 changed paths, 79 modified and 49 new, unstaged and unchanged from the start of the gate to its end).
