### 7.19 Independent review of the Gate 3 completion batch (12 October 2026): disposition

**What this is.** An independent review of the source package of [§7.18](#718-the-gate-3-completion-batch-12-october-2026) (`melarc-gate-3-completion-source.zip`, SHA-256 `c60b2cf7b723c21eb15fcd1b4b656b6e75496900faa130a2ba2f2c0c77415ade`, 874 files on `138d02c` with 128 changes) returned **FIX REQUIRED**: four source-level findings (F01 to F04), one verification question (V01), recommended answers to the owner's pending decisions and advice on the length of a batch. It ran no PostgreSQL and no browser (its checks were isolated runs of the scope resolver's source with stubbed dependencies and of the negative test's predicate), so each finding was checked here against the code and, where it could be, reproduced against PostgreSQL 18.6 before anything was changed. Each was fixed test first, and each new test was seen to fail for the stated reason. Nothing here is a claim that Gate 3 has passed, and nothing is committed, staged or pushed.

| Finding| Verdict| What changed| Evidence|
|---|---|---|---|
| F01 High: the tier was left to the operation, which runs after validation| **Confirmed, and reproduced**: a caller with the key and not the tier, sending a malformed body, got `400 VALIDATION_FAILED` where `403 INSUFFICIENT_AUTHORITY` is required; the fixture never called `requireTier`| A route declares its tier, `tier: { minimum?, rule? }`, and the authorization guard decides it at step 6. The **minimum** is decided before anything is looked up. A **rule** (`TIER_RULES`, empty until a slice adds one) derives what the target needs from facts of its own record and is asked once the caller can see the record, through the operation's own transaction and so under the caller's row-level security: no privileged read, no role-name comparison, never a value from the request. An unknown rule stops the API at start, and a rule that answers anything but a tier or `null` fails closed. A caller who cannot see the record is answered by step 7 (the ambiguity below). `OperationRunner.mutate` judges the requirement again, under the locks, before the work, and a use case that locks its target calls `OperationRunner.requireTargetTier` after the lock| `refusal-order.db.test.ts` over real HTTP: insufficient tier with a malformed body; below the minimum with a record outside the hubs, an absent one and a visible one, each `INSUFFICIENT_AUTHORITY`; an invisible record answered by the scope; a missing permission wins over the tier; a sufficient tier proceeds; a refusal leaves no record changed, no key spent and no event; a requirement that changed while the request waited (for the row, and for the policy lock) is refused and writes nothing. Units for the declaration, the rule helper, the runner and the inventory. Three deliberate breaks of the new code, all caught|
| F02 High for the reusable boundary: the scope probe equated existence with an out-of-hub record| **Confirmed, and reproduced** with a real RLS fixture (two RED tests)| A miss is `HUB_SCOPE_VIOLATION` only when the probed hub is outside the effective scope the operation runs under. An existing record in a hub the operation reaches that another restriction hides, and any miss under an all-hub grant, is `NOT_FOUND`; a Vendor and a Rider stay probe-free. SECURITY_DESIGN.md §14.4b and permission-enforcement.md §5.1 say so| `authorization.db.test.ts`, with a table that hides rows by hub **and** by owner: visible, outside the hubs (mine and others'), absent, hidden by its owner in an authorized hub, an all-hub caller with another restriction's miss, and a Vendor with the same shape and no probe. One deliberate break, caught|

A failure with any other signature fails the test to be diagnosed. `harness/https-probe.ts` shows, in the same test, that the endpoint answers a client that trusts the CA. FOR UPDATE`s the row and the clock crossing the idle boundary (or the absolute end) while the write waits, the write returned `true` and extended the session; the control passed. PostgreSQL re-checks a waiting UPDATE only against a row that was *changed*, and the earlier tests changed it| `recordActivity` takes the row lock first (`SELECT 1 ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, which waits for every holder and, under READ COMMITTED, locks the latest version), and only then runs the statement that judges on the clock as it is after the wait. One row and no other lock, so the lock order of §13.10a is unchanged. The write waits at most the request's lock time (default 2 s); a longer wait is ended by the database and the recorder logs it| `session-store.db.test.ts`, "a lock that changes nothing, held while the clock crosses a boundary": the idle boundary, the absolute end and a control with the lock released early; the boundary is two seconds away and is crossed by polling the database's clock, with no long sleep and no guarded column changed. RED before, GREEN after, stable over three runs. The two older OB-131 tests in `activity.db.test.ts` only named the blocked statement and were updated to the new one|

**The ambiguity of F01, decided and recorded for the owner.** The specification puts the tier (step 6) before the scope (step 7), and what a *particular target* needs is a fact of its record, which the platform can read only for a caller who may see it. The choice made, which is the one that discloses nothing: a caller who cannot see the record (outside their hubs, or there is none) is answered by step 7 and never learns what the record needs; for a visible record the requirement is decided before validation. The consequence is that a caller below the tier a hidden record would need is told `HUB_SCOPE_VIOLATION` or `NOT_FOUND`, not `INSUFFICIENT_AUTHORITY`. The opposite order would let the answer to "may I?" disclose a fact about a record the caller may not see. Permission-enforcement.md §5.1 states the rule. **Confirmed by the owner on 12 October 2026 ([§7.20](#720-the-owners-approvals-of-12-october-2026)).**

**Boundaries the review asked to keep explicit.** The ordering proved by `policy-change-races.db.test.ts` and `activity.db.test.ts` is a state-changing request against a **bundle reduction**. `OperationRunner.mutate` rereads the session under the shared policy locks and does not lock the session row; a direct revocation (a sign-out, an administrator's) takes identity and session row locks and no policy lock. It is not proof of every kind of revocation race, and the review does not establish that completing an already-authorized request is forbidden. **OB-132 (new):** the intended order of an already-authorized mutation against a direct revocation of its session is defined, and proved, by the operations that revoke it: `signOut` (S0.34) and the sessions administration (S0.37), on the canonical lock order (policy, identity, session). No blanket actor or session lock is added now: it could introduce a deadlock against the multi-principal plan.

**The review's advice on the cost of a batch, and what this pass did with it.** Related tasks stay in bounded batches with a checkpoint for each (no universal one-task rule); `lint` and the affected `typecheck` run early, then focused behavioural tests; a failing regression comes before a fix, and the 90 deliberate breaks of the first pass were more than the agreed cadence needed (this pass made four breaks, of the new code, only to show its tests discriminate); one appropriate gate after production changes settle, and only the document guards after a documentation-only edit; the lower-concurrency local profile (`test:local`) stays explicit and is no diagnosis of the Ops Portal worker-start failures; database setup is profiled before a template database is adopted (not adopted: the aggregate of seven minutes does not say where the time goes, and the optimisation is deferred from this pass); test resource ownership is a harness concern, and the leftover databases that broke a role test were a defect of that test: it dropped a cluster-wide role, which PostgreSQL refuses while any other database holds a privilege of it, and it now **renames** the role inside the transaction it rolls back, which checks the same thing (the catalogue finds no role of that name) and depends on no other database (shown with a throwaway database of its own that held a privilege of the role: the drop form failed and the rename form passed; the throwaway was dropped; no permission to delete was widened, and the cause of the leftovers, runs killed by their own timeouts, is not removed); and only the plan's affected rows are updated, with no handoff file.

### 7.20 The owner's approvals of 12 October 2026

All ten passed. *Removed* with `db:orphans --drop` naming the ten (no pattern and no "all", and without `--disconnect`: a plain `DROP DATABASE`, which the server refuses while any session is connected; none was refused): `melarc_test_0ad977c7`, `melarc_test_239e4876`, `melarc_test_25bf58e9`, `melarc_test_2d5a3475`, `melarc_test_36dad696`, `melarc_test_50edbcff`, `melarc_test_53fec8b3`, `melarc_test_7500ca4d`, `melarc_test_8a58f6d5`, `melarc_test_d092fac1`. *Retained, as the owner required:* `melarc_dev` (the development database, migration `0000` only) and the three unmarked databases `melarc_test_75aca5d6`, `melarc_test_a32692b8` and `melarc_test_unmarked12c5bfb2`. A read-only inventory afterwards listed exactly those four, none with a session. No full test run was needed for the cleanup and none was made.

**The three unmarked databases, inspected read-only** (read-only transactions, rolled back; names and counts only: no row value was read and no credential printed). `melarc_test_75aca5d6` and `melarc_test_a32692b8` are **empty**: the `public` schema only, no table, function or type, only the `plpgsql` extension; owner `postgres`, no comment, no explicit access list, no role holds anything in them, 7.4 MB, no session. `melarc_test_unmarked12c5bfb2` is the same with **one table, `public.precious`, holding one row**. *Likely origin:* negative-case fixtures that tests create on purpose through the administrator's connection with a bare `CREATE DATABASE`, which is why they carry no marker and belong to `postgres`, to prove that the tooling refuses a database it did not make. `reset-tools.db.test.ts` makes `melarc_test_unmarked<hex>` with `create table precious (id integer)` and one inserted row and checks that `db:reset` refuses it and leaves the row: `melarc_test_unmarked12c5bfb2` is that fixture. `orphans.db.test.ts` and `e2e-database.db.test.ts` each create a bare `melarc_test_<8 hex>` the same way, which is what the other two are (the databases do not say which of the two made which). Each of those tests records the name before creating the database and force-drops it in its `afterAll`, so a leftover means that the run ended before `afterAll` ran, or that the drop failed. **Not deleted**: the owner asked that they be inspected first; `db:orphans` cannot remove them (it refuses a database with no marker, by design), so removing them takes an administrator's `DROP DATABASE` by name, on the owner's authorization.

**OB-133 (new): a test database made by a run that fails, is killed or is cancelled stays on the server.** *The defect.* A database test makes its database and removes it in its own `afterAll` (`createTestDatabase().drop()`; the deliberately unmarked fixtures are force-dropped by name). When the run ends before `afterAll` runs (a process killed or cancelled, a worker ended by a timeout, a gate script stopped from outside; stopping the background task that ran a gate did not end its script: [§7.19](#719-independent-review-of-the-gate-3-completion-batch-12-october-2026-disposition)) or the drop itself fails, nothing removes the database. *Evidence on this machine:* thirteen leftovers beside `melarc_dev` on 12 October 2026, ten marked and three unmarked, from runs of this and of earlier batches; six of the marked ones were made by one run of mine that I killed. *Effects:* (a) they accumulate (7 to 9 MB each); (b) a leftover that holds a privilege of the cluster-wide capability role makes any test that drops that role fail, which broke `catalog-invariants.db.test.ts` in the first gate: that test no longer depends on other databases (the rename approved above), which cures the symptom and not the cause; (c) the marker is a constant string, `melarc:disposable`, with no run, process or time in it, so neither the tool nor a person can tell an abandoned database from a run's that is between steps except by what they know; (d) the unmarked fixtures cannot be removed with the supported tool at all. A GitHub-hosted runner is a fresh machine for each run, so this concerns a developer machine. *What exists and stays:* `db:orphans` lists the marked databases and removes only those a person names, one by one, never by idleness, age or pattern (audit F07: no run removes another run's database because it looks idle). *Not built, by the owner's instruction:* any broad or automatic sweeper. *Narrow options for the owner to choose from later, none built, each keeping removal by name and by a person:* record the creating run and process (and the time) in each database's comment, so that a listing can say "made by a process that is gone"; give the deliberate negative fixtures a marker of their own that `db:orphans` lists and removes by name; a start-of-run check that only reports what earlier runs left. *Until then:* whoever stops a run lists with `db:orphans` and removes, by name, only what they know is theirs, and a gate is stopped by ending its whole process tree and not by stopping the task that launched it.

### 7.21 The first hosted run of the checkpoint (12 October 2026), its diagnosis and the correction

**What this is.** The owner pushed the checkpoint `319c1c3` ([§7.20](#720-the-owners-approvals-of-12-october-2026)) to `origin/feat/slice-000-gate-3` and opened [pull request #4](https://github.com/melarclogistics/Melarc/pull/4) against `main` (not a draft). This section records what the first hosted run showed, the owner's decision and the correction. It states the result of **that** run, which the commit made before it could not.

**The run.** [Run 38284306211](https://github.com/melarclogistics/Melarc/actions/runs/38284306211), event `pull_request`, attempt 1, 17:27:17Z to 17:32:14Z. **Tested revision:** GitHub's merge commit `761adfe0b3301d1cea4110ee90ef789be4609418` (parents `33bc158`, the tip of `main`, and `319c1c3`, the head of the pull request); its tree `fac8c66fc4498a6f506fcdd8460da8db523dba2c` is identical to the tree of `319c1c3` (checked by fetching `refs/pull/4/merge`). Jobs: Static checks success (1 min 28 s); Unit, component and process tests success (2 min 42 s); Database tests success (4 min 10 s); Dependency audit success (32 s); Build, contract and browser tests (`integrated`) **failure** (4 min 37 s) at step 11 only, "Browser, API and database journey over the trusted HTTPS origin" (`pnpm run test:e2e:https`, exit 1, 53 s); CI result failure, as the aggregate of that one job. Steps 1 to 10 of `integrated` succeeded: the build (6 s), `contract:check` (2 s), the browsers (52 s), `test:browser` over three engines (83 s), the plain journey (44 s) and the NSS tools. The diagnostics artifact `melarc-diagnostics-761adfe0b3301d1cea4110ee90ef789be4609418-1` (201,666 bytes) was kept. **This is the first hosted Linux run of this tree**: the static, unit and database jobs passed, which include the tests Windows skips. The durations above are the ones the 30-minute budget of the `integrated` job was to be judged by (a failed run: a passing HTTPS suite takes longer).

**What the log showed.** The step's log is readable only to a signed-in account (the session reads the public job, step and annotation data; the log returned 403 and the artifact 401), so the owner supplied screenshots. Playwright's summary: 22 passed, 1 did not run, and a list of failures of which the visible part is nine WebKit tests. With 11 tests an engine (33 in all) that leaves **ten failures: nine visible, and one above the screenshot, in Chromium or Firefox, not yet identified**. The nine are every WebKit test that needs the CA trusted (the ordinary project's headers, isolation and trust tests; the secret project's four cookie tests and its origin test); the second isolation test did not run (serial mode, after the first failed); WebKit's refusal, the negative control, is not among them. So the generator, `certutil`, the per-engine stores and the TLS front worked well enough for 22 tests to pass.

**The diagnosis: WebKit ignores `SSL_CERT_FILE`.** The inference from the numbers is backed by four checks. The pinned WebKit bundle (revision 2359, the WPE build, read as inert data) carries no TLS library of its own, its wrapper sets only `WEBKIT_*` and `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, and it requires the system `ca-certificates` package. glib-networking's GnuTLS backend fills its trust list from GnuTLS's system trust (`gnutls_x509_trust_list_add_system_trust`); only its OpenSSL backend calls `X509_STORE_set_default_paths`, which would honour `SSL_CERT_FILE`, and Ubuntu 24.04's `glib-networking` package ships `libgiognutls.so` and no OpenSSL module. GnuTLS 3.8.3 (the version of Ubuntu 24.04) reads no environment variable for its trust store. **The exact WebKit error text was not seen**: the diagnosis rests on this evidence and on the pattern of the failures, and the next run confirms or refutes it.

**The owner's decision (A), 12 October 2026.** Put to the owner: (A) on a GitHub-hosted runner only, put the name-constrained disposable CA in the system store for WebKit's proofs and remove it when they end; (B) declare WebKit's HTTPS proofs blocked on Linux, visibly, with Chromium and Firefox mandatory. `ignoreHTTPSErrors` was excluded by the owner's rules. The owner chose A. For WebKit alone this supersedes the statement of finding 8 that no trust store of the runner is changed, and the rule "never trust a CA machine-wide" of `e2e/CLAUDE.md` has this one exception.

**The correction**, test first (each new test was seen to fail for its stated reason before the code existed): `harness/system-trust.ts` (new, and the only code that touches a system store: allowed only on Linux with `CI` and `GITHUB_ACTIONS` equal to `true` and `RUNNER_ENVIRONMENT` equal to `github-hosted`, never on a machine declared cleared for key material; `sudo -n install -m 0644 <ca> /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/melarc-e2e-disposable-ca.crt` and `update-ca-certificates`; removal by `rm -f` and `update-ca-certificates --fresh`, both tried whatever the first does and every failure said; an absolute path only); `harness/engine-trust.ts` (WebKit's plan names no environment value, has `scope: 'system'`, and is unsupported with the reason on any machine that is not a GitHub-hosted runner); `harness/https-run.ts` (**two runs**: Chromium, Firefox and WebKit's refusal while the system store lacks the CA, then WebKit's other proofs with the CA in it; both run whatever the first did; the CA is taken out straight after and again in the `finally`, before the directory goes; a CA that cannot be taken out fails the run; the first failure is the exit status; where the store may not be changed the second run is made without it, says so, and WebKit's proofs fail to trust); `playwright.config.ts` and `tests/https-trust.spec.ts` (the refusal is tagged `@untrusted-control` and run alone by the new project `https-webkit-control`, which the other WebKit project excludes: the control is honest only while the CA is not in the system store, refused before and trusted after with nothing else differing; a test holds the partition, and `playwright test --list` shows 1, 5 and 5 tests for WebKit's three projects); and `turbo.json`, **a trap the run would have met**: Turborepo's strict environment passes only the variables listed, `GITHUB_ACTIONS` and `RUNNER_ENVIRONMENT` were not, so the run would have seen `CI` alone and refused to touch the system store; both are listed and `scripts/turbo-config.test.ts` holds them. The documents changed with it: `e2e/README.md`, `e2e/CLAUDE.md`, `DEVELOPMENT.md`, the comments of `ci.yml` and of the harness.

**Evidence of the correction**, from a machine with no Linux, `sudo`, WebKit or CA: the harness's unit suite (21 files, 452 passed and 3 skipped, 42 more than before); the root guards of `turbo-config`, `test-inventory` and `ci-workflow` (370 passed); `playwright test --list` for the projects; `eslint`, the e2e `tsc` and Prettier. **Not run, because it cannot be run here:** the real `sudo` and `update-ca-certificates` path, GnuTLS reading the bundle with a name-constrained CA, WebKit trusting it, and whatever the tenth failure is. The hosted run of the correction is the proof.

**What is still open.** The tenth failure, a Chromium or Firefox test above the screenshot, is unidentified; if the next run fails there, its log is needed. WebKit's trust through the system store is unproven until that run. S0.23 stays blocked until a hosted run passes in full, Gate 3 stays pending, and S0.28 is the owner's, separately. The correction is a commit on top of `319c1c3` that carries this section; whether it is pushed, and the result of its hosted run, are not stated here. The pull request is not a draft, which the owner may change. *(Superseded by the fourth hosted run, below.)*

**The second hosted run (13 October 2026), and a flake it exposed.** [Run 38390504553](https://github.com/melarclogistics/Melarc/actions/runs/38390504553), event `pull_request`, started 11:28:56Z, tested `319c1c3` again: the correction (`52d06f9`) had not been pushed yet. The HTTPS suite therefore failed exactly as before (22 passed, 1 did not run, the same WebKit tests, 52 s), which shows that failure is deterministic and not a flake of the run. The Database tests job, which passed in the first run, **failed one test**: `guard-chain.db.test.ts`, "stores a keyed digest and no identifier" (1496 passed, 1 failed, 1 todo). *The reason, from the log:* the test asserted that the text of each row of the limiter's table does not contain "ada", and the row held a random keyed digest whose hexadecimal text contains "ada" (`…695adae98d…`) and no identifier. It is a defect of the test and not of the product: a word made of the letters a to f occurs in a random 64-character digest about once in 60 rows, so the job fails by chance in some runs of every hundred. *Fixed test first:* `src/test-support/clear-identifier.ts` looks for an identifier as a whole word (no letter or digit before or after it), and its test uses the row of the failing run (it contains "ada" and holds no identifier), the places where a hexadecimal run can hold the letters, and the ways a stored identifier shows (in a column of its own, quoted, in a key, joined with an underscore, in another case, in an address); the database test uses it and also checks the identifier it signs in with. A search of the repository for the same pattern (an absence assertion on a short word made only of hexadecimal letters) found no other. The file's five tests pass against the local PostgreSQL; the full `test:db` was not repeated for this change.

**The third hosted run (13 October 2026): WebKit passes, one failure is still unseen, and the diagnostics were being erased.** [Run 38392018022](https://github.com/melarclogistics/Melarc/actions/runs/38392018022) (11:42:16Z to 11:47:52Z, head `accf510abebec1e8a869b783dcfc0439262c50da`) is the first run that holds both the WebKit correction (`52d06f9`) and the flake fix (`accf510`). Static checks, the unit job, the Database tests (3 min 14 s: the flaky test passed) and the dependency audit succeeded; `integrated` (4 min 45 s) failed at step 11 only, the HTTPS suite (52 s). *What the owner's screenshot of the end of that step's log shows:* the second HTTPS run (WebKit, with the CA in the system store) ended **`10 passed (7.7s)`**, all ten WebKit tests (the trust test, both isolation tests, the headers tests and the secret cookie and origin tests), and the CA was then removed from the system store; **WebKit trusts the disposable CA through the system store, in a hosted run.** The command still exited 1, so its status came from the **first** run (Chromium, Firefox and WebKit's refusal), whose summary and failure were above the screenshot. *At that point they had not been seen, nothing had been chosen as a fix, and the session had no authenticated access to the log (no `gh` and no token; the log endpoint answers 403 and the artifact 401, and the stored Git credential was not used); the log was then supplied, and the next paragraph records what it shows.*

*A retraction.* The session read the size of that run's diagnostics artifact (10 KB, against 201 KB in the first run) as "fewer traces, so no ordinary-project test failed". That inference had no basis and is withdrawn. Playwright removes the output directory of every project it is about to run when a run starts (`createRemoveOutputDirsTask`, Playwright 1.63), and the two HTTPS runs shared `test-results/artifacts`, so **the second run erased the first run's evidence**: the artifact said nothing of what the first run had found. Shown with a browserless throwaway Playwright run: two runs with one shared output directory leave only the second run's file, and two runs with distinct directories leave both.

*The correction, test first* (`harness/https-run.ts`, `harness/https-run.test.ts`): each run writes to an output directory of its own (`--output=test-results/https-1-own-stores` and `--output=test-results/https-2-system-store`), none inside another or inside the plain run's, both below `e2e/test-results`, which the failure artifact of CI keeps (a test reads the workflow); each run prints its exit status when it ends; the command ends with a summary of every run (exit status, did not complete, or not run, and its output directory) and of the run the overall status comes from, the first that did not pass, or the removal of the CA, or the absence of any run; the first non-zero status is still the overall one. The recorders of the secret projects are unchanged and nothing was enabled (no screenshot, trace, page snapshot or report): only the place Playwright writes to changed. `https-run.test.ts` and `secret-evidence.test.ts` pass (72 tests), with `eslint`, the e2e `tsc` and Prettier; the full gate was not run. **This correction is not committed** (the owner's instructions did not authorize a commit), and the failing assertion of the first run is **not fixed**: it is to be fixed only after its cause is established from its log, with no certificate check weakened, no browser skipped and no timeout raised to obtain a green run.

**The remaining failure, from the supplied log, its established cause and the correction.** *What the log shows (supplied by the owner):* **project** `https-chromium`; **file** `tests/https-trust.spec.ts`; **test** the one tagged `@untrusted-control` ("refuses the same origin, with the engine's certificate diagnostic, in a browser of this engine that does not have the mechanism"); **assertion** `expect(failure, 'an untrusted CA must be refused').toBeDefined()`; **actual** `undefined`: `page.goto` **succeeded**, so the browser that was meant not to trust the CA loaded the origin. The first run passed 22 tests and failed this one; the second run (WebKit, with the CA in the system store) passed 10. Chromium's was the only control to fail: Firefox's trust is a profile that a plain `launch` does not use, and WebKit's is the system store, which the first run lacked the CA in; neither depends on `env`.

*The established cause*, from the pinned Playwright 1.63.0 and shown against its real runner. Playwright Test's worker fixture `_browserOptions` (`playwright/lib/index.js`, lines 196 to 210) builds `{ handleSIGINT: false, ...launchOptions, tracesDir, artifactsDir }` from the project's `use.launchOptions` and installs it as `playwright._defaultLaunchOptions` for the worker; the client's `BrowserType.launch` (`playwright-core/lib/coreBundle.js`, lines 63297 to 63304) does `options = { ...this._playwright._defaultLaunchOptions, ...options }`, so an option that is **absent** from the options given is the project's. The control copied the project's `launchOptions` and **deleted `env`** (`delete withoutTrust.env`): `launch` put the project's `env` back, which for Chromium is the `HOME` whose `.pki/nssdb` holds the CA, and Chromium trusted the origin. The demonstration: a Playwright Test project whose `launchOptions.env` carries a sentinel `HOME`, a "browser" that is Node writing only the `HOME` it is handed; a launch with `env` deleted received the **sentinel** (the trusted one), and a launch with `env` given explicitly received its own.

*The correction, test first* (`harness/untrusted-browser.ts`, new): the negative control launches its browser through `withUntrustedBrowser`, which makes a disposable empty home, builds the environment from the **runner's own** and not from the project's (the path, library path, display and locale kept; `HOME` set to the empty home, and the four XDG directories inside it; `SSL_CERT_FILE`, `SSL_CERT_DIR` and `SSL_DIR` removed; every `MELARC_*` variable removed, the TLS directory's among them; the environment is refused if any value left names the run's TLS directory), and hands it to `launch` **as an `env` of its own**. The browser is closed and the home removed whatever happens (a launch that fails included), teardown failures are never swallowed (a passed test fails with `UntrustedBrowserTeardownError`, a failed test keeps its own error and the teardown is reported beside it), and nothing of the machine's normal trust store is touched. **Certificate validation stays fully on:** no `ignoreHTTPSErrors`, no bypass flag, the classifier and the assertion are unchanged, and the control's context is the same. The tests: `untrusted-browser.test.ts` (the environment, and the teardown, on a double) and **`untrusted-launch.test.ts`, which runs the real Playwright Test runner** under a project with trusted launch defaults and the real `launch` merging, a fake browser executable recording the environment each launch really receives: the old control gets the trusted `HOME` back, the helper's launch gets an isolated one and nothing that names a store, and the home is gone although the launch failed. A deliberate break (the helper deleting `env` instead of passing it) fails three tests, among them the real-runner one, and the file was restored by hash. The per-run output directories and the status summary above are kept, and the secret projects' recorders are unchanged.

*Evidence and what is not evidence.* The harness's unit suite passes (23 files, 482 passed, 3 skipped), `playwright test --list` shows the same partition (6, 1, 5 and 5 tests), and `eslint`, the e2e `tsc` and Prettier pass; no full gate and no CI were run. **The Linux browser proof is CI's:** the trusted Chromium launch must load the same endpoint, and the isolated untrusted launch must reject it with `net::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID`. Firefox's and WebKit's controls now go through the same helper (an empty home and no store locator instead of the runner's own environment), which changes nothing they depend on, and the hosted run confirms it. **Not committed** (the owner's instructions authorize a commit and a push only if their earlier authorization covers this follow-up, which it does not; the fix is left ready for approval).

**The fourth hosted run (13 October 2026): every job passed.** [Run 38403274556](https://github.com/melarclogistics/Melarc/actions/runs/38403274556), event `pull_request`, attempt 1, created 13:13:43Z and finished 13:19:14Z, tested the head **`d24bcfaf4a229e575e593566d82add5bbca04241`** (parent `accf510`): the commit that gives the untrusted control an environment of its own, each HTTPS run an output directory of its own, and the command a status summary. *Verified from the run's public data:* Static checks success (1 min 47 s); Unit, component and process tests success (2 min 33 s); Database tests success (4 min 21 s); Dependency audit success (18 s); Build, contract and browser tests (`integrated`) success (5 min 19 s: build 7 s, `contract:check` 3 s, the browsers 61 s, `test:browser` 101 s, the plain journey 47 s, the NSS tools 1 s, **the HTTPS suite 62 s, success**); the failure-diagnostics step skipped; CI result success (8 s). *The tested revision.* A `pull_request` run tests GitHub's test merge of the pull request's head onto its base, and that merge's SHA can no longer be retrieved (the merge ref disappears when the pull request closes). The base then was `33bc158`, an ancestor of `d24bcfa`, so the tree tested is the tree of `d24bcfa` (`7a167b8e5d33887f22f7d5d446f530c286c63b24`), and the merge commit that `main` received, `51b5e392aa528868acaf6bf3f8c44a1d9774d576` (parents `33bc158` and `d24bcfa`), has that same tree (checked). *The pull requests.* The branch's pull requests were #4 (closed 11:28:16Z, head `319c1c3`), #5 (opened 11:28:51Z, closed 12:13:29Z; by their times its runs were 38390504553 on `319c1c3` and 38392018022 on `accf510`) and #6 (opened 12:14:45Z; run 38403274556). **#6 was merged into `main` at 13:19:21Z by the repository owner's account, seven seconds after the run finished; the session did not merge it** (it has no access to do so, and the instruction was not to). The earlier mentions in this section of "pull request #4" for the second and third runs name the pull request that was open when the branch was first pushed; by their times those runs were #5's.

*What follows from the green HTTPS step, and was not read from the log* (the log is readable only to a signed-in account, and no log text of this run was supplied): `pnpm run test:e2e:https` exited 0, and the command exits with the first non-zero status of its two runs, fails on a CA that cannot be taken out of the system store, and fails a test whose teardown fails. So both runs ended with exit status 0, every test passed (33: the trusted Chromium test; Chromium's control, whose verdict `CERTIFICATE_REJECTED` is accepted for Chromium only for `net::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID`; Firefox's 11; WebKit's refusal in the first run and its other ten in the second) and the CA was removed with no teardown failure. The literal summary lines, the per-run counts and the diagnostic text were not read, and are to be added if the owner supplies the end of that step's log.

### 7.22 Carried from S0.29 (batch of 20 October 2026)

**What this is.** S0.29 (setup grants and MFA factors), built test first on `feat/slice-000-s0-29` (from `a876d20`; nothing staged, committed or pushed) on the owner's instruction of 20 October 2026. It adds no operation and issues nothing to a person, so **no criterion moves** and the evidence is *fixture/platform verified*: the database half of `GBT-B14` (OB-14), the by-key port half of `GBT-E5` for the two stores, and the worker's reader of a setup grant (OB-119).

**What was built.**
- *The tables* (migration `0018_setup_grant_and_mfa_factor.sql`; the shape is `platform/database/schema/setup-grant.ts` and `staff/mfa-factor.schema.ts`, whose headers explain each column). Both are owned by `melarc_owner`, forced to row-level security, classified in the registry, and readable and writable under the `authentication` capability alone (`credential_delivery` also reads three columns of `setup_grant`). `setup_grant`: the eight purposes paired with their principal type, a token hash of 32 bytes, an expiry that is null for `BOOTSTRAP_SETUP` alone, one `PENDING` grant per principal and purpose, and lineage that is a pair of **composite foreign keys including the principal** (`supersedes_grant_id`, `continued_from_grant_id`; a predecessor is named once, and a grant carries at most one of the two), written at insert and never updated. `mfa_factor`: a sealed secret (ciphertext, nonce, key version, envelope version), at most one `ACTIVE` factor per identity, the three creation facts immutable, and `revocation_episode_id` written once.
- *Guards, which hold every login including the administrator.* `setup_grant`: a grant is issued `PENDING`; a reissue names a `SUPERSEDED` grant of the same purpose and episode; a continuation names the `CONSUMED` grant of the same episode that produced it, of one of the three purposes that create a factor; only a `PENDING` grant changes state, and only its state and `consumed_at`; consumption only before the expiry and expiry only after it, on the database's clock. `mfa_factor`: created `PENDING`; a `REVOKED` factor never changes; a proven factor never returns to `PENDING`; the enrolment moment is written once; the accepted time step only moves forward; `revocation_episode_id` has its one legal write (null to an episode, in the statement that revokes with an administrator named), and a **constraint trigger deferred to commit** requires a setup grant of the same identity to carry each episode a factor names.
- *Grants.* The API login holds `UPDATE` of `state` and `consumed_at` on a grant and of the seven columns of a factor's life, never table-wide, and no `DELETE` anywhere; the worker's capability role reads `id`, `state` and `expires_at` of a grant and nothing else.
- *The stores* (`SetupGrantStore`, `MfaFactorStore`; plain classes beside no new port). Both join the caller's transaction under `authentication` and refuse any other context before touching a table, offer by-key lookups only (a test lists the methods and fails when one is added without the check), and return no hash and no secret. `SetupGrantStore`: `issue` (expires what has lapsed, supersedes the live grant, inserts with lineage on one database instant and the lifetime of `recovery_link_ttl_minutes`, queues the message of a message purpose in the same transaction and cancels the superseded one's), `consume` (locks the row, then judges and writes in one statement on a fresh database time; `null` for every refusal alike; cancels the message), `supersedePending`, `findById`, `findByTokenHash`. `MfaFactorStore`: `create` (the seed is sealed to its row: `sealedContext` of identity, operation and factor id), `openSeed`, `activate` (locks the identity's factors in id order, revokes the one it replaces, activates), `recordAcceptedStep` (one conditional update, so one of two requests that present a code together is accepted), `revokeBySystem`, `revokeAdministratively` (the one statement the table allows), `findById`, `findActiveOf`, `findLatestOf`.
- *The delivery worker's reader (OB-119).* `SetupGrantRedemptionReader` asks the one question a send depends on, on the database's clock, over three columns; `redemptionReaderOver` routes by kind, and a kind with no reader (the recovery request, S0.50) and any unknown kind is `UNCONFIRMED`. **The worker as composed now claims and sends**, where before this task it claimed nothing: its start-up warning now says only that the reader of recovery requests is not built.
- *The API's composition (OB-38, OB-107).* With a database and local key custody the runtime binds the `SecretCipher` (serving the TOTP seed and the delivery payload and no other purpose) and the issuing side of the `DeliveryQueue`, and provides both stores (`SETUP_GRANT_STORE`, `MFA_FACTOR_STORE`), absent where a port is missing.

**Decisions the documents do not state, taken here and listed for the owner.**
1. *Where the factor's schema lives.* `src/staff/mfa-factor.schema.ts`, beside `staff_identity`, because the foreign key needs that table and the platform may not import a domain; the code that uses it is `platform/auth/mfa/`.
2. *Hash types.* `token_hash` and `attestation_challenge_hash` are `bytea` of 32 bytes, as every other hash in the database is; `domain-model.md` lists the second as text.
3. *Constraints the documents imply and do not list as such:* a purpose belongs to one principal type; an episode only on the two MFA purposes; `continued_from_grant_id` only on `MFA_ENROLMENT`; the attestation hash for exactly the two rider purposes (set only for them, and required by them); an administrative revocation is the administrator, the reason and the episode together, never the identity itself; a factor's created episode only for a re-enrolment, and checked at commit like the revocation episode.
4. *`PENDING` to `EXPIRED` has no scheduler.* The documents say "System" and name no writer. A lapsed grant is marked `EXPIRED` by the next `issue` or `supersedePending` for that principal and purpose, and every reader judges expiry by `expires_at` on the database's clock, never by `state` alone; a grant that lapses and is never followed by another act stays `PENDING` in the table. (OB-134.)
5. *The expiry instant.* The guard judges consumption on its own `clock_timestamp()`, a moment after the store's statement read the clock, so a grant whose expiry falls in those microseconds is refused by the guard with SQLSTATE `23514` and nothing is consumed, instead of the store answering `null`. A refusal either way; recorded rather than hidden. (OB-134.)
6. *"Most recent factor" is the greatest id* (`findLatestOf`; ids are UUIDv7). `resetStaffMfa`'s three states (S0.37) must confirm that or add a column. (OB-135.)
7. *Not constrained, because no document says so:* one `PENDING` factor per identity, and one continuation per consumed grant. Both are suggestions below.
8. *The stores write no audit event.* The actor, the channel and the reason are the operation's to know (`auth.setup_grant.issued`, `consumed`, `superseded`, `auth.mfa.*`); the first operations to call them (S0.30, S0.31) write them in the same transaction.
9. *Update policies do not filter by state* (the guard answers a terminal row with an error, as `session_update` does); insert policies require `PENDING`. The registry's "self" and administrative-key reads of these two tables are not built: the policies admit `authentication` and, to read three columns, `credential_delivery`, and the operation that needs another adds its own policy.
10. *A non-positive or non-integer lifetime refuses to issue* (no default): a setting that says 0 or -5 is not a lifetime.

### 7.23 Carried from S0.30 (21 October 2026)

**What this is.** S0.30 (the bootstrap seed, the resume command and the custody bundles), built test first on `feat/slice-000-s0-29` (nothing staged, committed or pushed) on the owner's instruction of 20 October 2026. It adds no operation and no route, so **no criterion moves** and the evidence is *fixture/platform verified* on Windows: `GBT-E8` (OB-18, OB-49), the Windows half of OB-25, and the database half of AC-SLICE-000-118 and of AC-SLICE-000-93's command. **No custody file and no credential was made on this machine, `melarc_dev` was not touched, and every bundle in a test is a throwaway sentinel in a disposable folder of the temporary directory** (the open owner item about this machine).

**What was built.**
- *The database* (migration `0019_bootstrap_seed.sql`). Four `SECURITY DEFINER` functions of the owner that only the provisioning login may execute, as for the reference seed: `melarc.bootstrap_status` (locks the staff table against any other seed and counts it), `melarc.seed_bootstrap_administrators` (the pair, their two `BOOTSTRAP_SETUP` grants and their six audit events in one statement, once and only into an empty table; the shape is the function's and not the document's), `melarc.bootstrap_identity_state` (finds the identity by its canonical work email and holds it under its row lock) and `melarc.resume_bootstrap_identity` (the six conditions of §3.3a under that lock, then either a fresh `MFA_REENROLMENT` or a new `BOOTSTRAP_SETUP`). Two constants as functions (`reserved_system_actor_id`, `bootstrap_bundle_id`), pinned to the TypeScript values by a test. The `bootstrap` **policy branches** are the second line: the identity insert admits the bootstrap shape and nothing else (origin, status, the reserved actor as maker and checker, the Platform Admin bundle, no hub, no credential), the grant insert two purposes with no issuer, the factor update only the revocation of a `PENDING` factor with no administrator, the audit insert five events by `SYSTEM` tiered as the catalogue says, and reads of the staff table, grants, factors, sessions and the one setting `recovery_link_ttl_minutes`. **The provisioning login holds no privilege on any of these tables.**
- *The commands* (`src/tools/bootstrap/`; `bootstrap:seed` and `bootstrap:resume`, each a process an operator starts as the provisioning login). One transaction under the `bootstrap` capability: the status, the sweep of the bundles of an earlier run that did not commit (only from an empty table, only files named and begun as a bundle), the function, then each bundle **before the commit**. A bundle is created exclusively, made private, **inspected** and only then written (`custody-store.ts`): the mode, the owner and the link count on POSIX, and on Windows the access list saved by `icacls` and judged as a security descriptor (`custody-acl.ts`: protected, nothing inherited, nobody broad, nobody but the user, the local system and the administrators). A commit whose outcome is unknown removes nothing; a refused one removes the bundles. The custody folder is named, absolute and outside any checkout. Nothing printed names a secret, an address or a path.
- *Isolation.* Nothing the API or the worker loads reaches the folder; no operation, path or tag of the contract and no screen names the commands; the capability is opened only there (`bootstrap-isolation.test.ts`). `.gitignore` and `scripts/package-source.ts` refuse `melarc-bootstrap-*.bundle`.
- *Corrections to what stood.* The `BOOTSTRAP_SEED` basis of `staff.identity.created` now needs the `bootstrap` capability (it named `seed`, which writes no identity); the registry rows, the capability matrix, `APPROVED_DEFINER_EXECUTE`, `COMPOSITION_ROOT` and the documents say what the commands are.

**Decisions the documents do not state, taken here and listed for the owner.**
1. *The reserved system actor is `5eed0000-0000-4000-8000-0000000000a1`* (the bootstrap task's technical principal is `...b1`; neither is the id of any record). Nothing reads it to tell a bootstrap identity: the rules read `origin`.
2. *The event of the resume (AC-SLICE-000-93 asks for an enhanced one under the reserved actor, and the catalogue names none).* The command writes the catalogue's own events for what it does: `auth.setup_grant.issued` (ordinary; its row already lists the controlled provisioning channel), `auth.setup_grant.superseded` (ordinary) and the enhanced `auth.mfa.revoked` for each stale `PENDING` factor it revokes. **Where it revokes none, no enhanced event is written.** The writer holds the tier of an event to the catalogue, so an enhanced `auth.setup_grant.issued` would be a change of the contract. The owner names an enhanced event, or accepts this.
3. *A live setup grant refuses the resume* (`LIVE_GRANT`): an identity whose continuation is still inside its thirty minutes is not stranded, and ending a person's live enrolment is not the command's to do. Only an offboarded identity refuses on its status (the section says no more); a suspended one is resumed.
4. *The resume's `MFA_REENROLMENT` carries no episode and no issuer*: no administrator reset the identity, and the lifetime is `recovery_link_ttl_minutes`, read and never defaulted.
5. *"An explicit all-hub grant" is the Platform Admin bundle's own `all` grants.* The seed writes no per-identity hub row (`HubAssignment` is SLICE-009, D-10) and no primary hub (the HQ roles hold none). S0.9 seeded `staff.identity.create` and `staff.identity.approve` for Platform Admin as `own`, so a bootstrap administrator with no primary hub reaches no hub by those two keys: S0.35 (the first operation that uses them) must settle it with the owner.
6. *The bootstrap policies hold no subquery of the staff table.* The delivery worker reads three columns of `setup_grant` and has no privilege on `staff_identity`, and PostgreSQL evaluates every permissive policy of a table for the login that reads it, so a policy that looked the identity up would break the worker. That the principal of a grant is a bootstrap identity is the functions' own check, under the identity's lock. The credential, hub and principal conjuncts of the policies are also implied by the tables' own checks; they are kept, and tested one at a time (row-level security is judged before a constraint).
7. *Two engineering choices.* The commands' arguments are `--custodian "Full Name <work@email>"` twice (seed) and `--custodian <work@email>` once (resume); one leading `--` is dropped, as `pnpm run script -- args` passes it. The bundle is a text file with a magic first line (`MELARC-BOOTSTRAP-BUNDLE v1`), named by 128 bits of randomness and nothing else.

### 7.24 Carried from S0.31 (21 October 2026)

**What this is.** S0.31 (the three credential setup operations), built test first on `feat/slice-000-s0-29` (nothing staged, committed or pushed) on the owner's instruction of 20 October 2026. **These are the first routes of the product**, so for the criteria below this is the first *real-operation* evidence: AC-SLICE-000-25 and -43 (a route declares how it is reached; anonymity is declared), -88 (two completions of one grant have one winner), -92 and -93 (the bootstrap pair walked from the secret to an `ACTIVE` factor, and the stranded administrator recovered by the provisioning command and by nothing else), -94 (a wrong code leaves the factor `PENDING`), -120 (the resume refuses once a factor is `ACTIVE`), -125 (the setup operations share the recovery bucket, under a purpose-qualified digest) and the setup half of -87 (the password's two bounds). The screens are S0.43's. **No custody file and no credential was made on this machine and `melarc_dev` was not touched**: every identity, grant, password and seed is a throwaway of a disposable database.

**What was built** (`src/platform/auth/staff/`).
- *The service* (`staff-setup.service.ts`, one class, three operations). **The principal comes from the grant and from nothing a request says**: the grant is found by the hash of its token, which names the identity. **Every refusal of a grant is one answer** (`SETUP_GRANT_INVALID`, one message) whether the token is unknown, malformed, spent, superseded, expired, of another purpose, for another kind of principal, for an identity that is not `ACTIVE`, or for one that already holds a credential. **A token that can never work costs no hash**: the grant and the identity are read first, in a short transaction of their own. The password is judged by the credential rule before the grant (`VALIDATION_FAILED` naming `/password` and its rule, never the value), hashed outside any transaction in a hash slot (`runAdmitted`; a request that finds none is `RATE_LIMITED` and changed nothing), and only then does the one transaction of the act open: the identity is locked (the platform's order: identity, then grant), the grant is consumed, the credential is written by one conditional statement, the audit events are written, and for a privileged bundle the factor is created, the earlier `PENDING` factors are revoked, and the `MFA_ENROLMENT` continuation is issued **in the same transaction as the consumption**; all of it commits or none of it (a failure creating the factor leaves the grant open and no credential). `completeMfaEnrolment` proves the code against the seed opened in memory for that and refuses a wrong one by **rolling back**, so the grant stays open and the factor `PENDING` (AC-94); `beginMfaReenrolment` consumes the authorisation, revokes the unusable `PENDING` factor, creates the new one in the reset's episode and issues the continuation. **No operation issues a session or sets a cookie**, and no event, log line or response holds a password, a token, a seed, a code or the provisioning URI beyond the one answer that is its purpose.
- *The routes* (`staff-setup.controller.ts`). `POST /auth/staff/setup/credential`, `/mfa` and `/mfa/begin`: `@Anonymous` with the `rate_limit_recovery` bucket keyed on the **purpose-qualified SHA-256 digest of the bounded token** the body carries (`staff-setup-limit.ts`; an invented token has a key of its own and the limiter digests the key again before it stores anything), browser surface `OPS_PORTAL` only (a missing, `null`, foreign or Vendor-PWA `Origin` is `403` before the token is examined), `200`, `no-store`. Where the application has no database or no local key material the service is absent and the routes answer the platform's fixed `503` (`StaffSetupUnavailableError`).
- *The bindings* (`app.module.ts`, database and local key custody): the Argon2id `Hasher` (a missing pepper stops the application at start), the bounded `HashAdmission` (the slots and the memory budget of the configuration, fitted to the libuv pool the process has) and the RFC 6238 `TotpVerifier`. `runAdmitted` moved out of the adapter file (`run-admitted.ts`, re-exported), because only the composition root may import a `*.adapter.ts`. `IdentityDirectory` gained `establishCredential` (one conditional `UPDATE ... where credential_generation = 0`, the generation from 0 to 1, never a replacement) and `accountLabel`; the summary gained `origin`; the factor store gained `findPendingOf` and `hasBeenProven`; `bundleIsPrivileged` reads the one fact of a bundle the setup needs.
- *The description* states what each operation takes and gives in code (`staff-setup-schemas.ts`, `DescribeErrors`, which reads the statuses from `statusOf` and never types one beside a code), and `contract:check` compares it with the contract: **3 operations compared, no findings** (it found five kinds of drift before the description was written, which shows it compares). `api-client:check` is current.

**Decisions the documents do not state, taken here and listed for the owner.**
1. *A request whose password fails the credential rule is `400` before its grant is judged*, and an unknown token with a valid password is `422` without a hash: the refusal order puts validation before the use case, and neither answer then depends on whether a token is real.
2. *A valid token that finds no free hash slot is `429` and consumes nothing* (§13.4c), so a caller can be told "too many" for a real token and "invalid" for an invented one only when the slots are full. The token is 256 bits, so this reveals nothing to anyone who does not already hold it.
3. *A wrong code answers `MFA_PROOF_INVALID` only on a grant that is the enrolment's own*; any other grant is `SETUP_GRANT_INVALID` with the right code or a wrong one (a test pins the wrong one, which a campaign found unpinned).
4. *The audit actor of these events is the staff identity whose grant it is* (a `SYSTEM` pre-session transaction may name whom it authenticated). The events are `auth.setup_grant.consumed`, `auth.credential.changed` (the generation, never the value), `auth.setup_grant.issued` (channel `RESPONSE`), `auth.mfa.enrolled`, `auth.mfa.revoked` (superseded or replaced), `auth.mfa.reenrolment_begun` and `auth.bootstrap.completed`, **once per bootstrap identity, at its first proof** (origin `BOOTSTRAP` and never proven before), not again after a reset. A failed proof writes no event: it rolls back, and `auth.mfa.failed` belongs to the sign-in.
5. *A re-enrolment is not refused for an identity that holds an `ACTIVE` factor*: proving the new one revokes the old (`REPLACED`, an enhanced event). The grant is issued by a reset that has already revoked the factor, and the resume command refuses an `ACTIVE` identity itself (AC-120).
6. *The otpauth URI names the account by the work email as entered and the issuer `Melarc`.* The issuer is a constant of the service; a deployment-specific issuer would be a setting nobody approved.
7. *`completeCredentialSetup` supersedes any earlier `PENDING` factor* so that no identity ends a setup with two.

### 7.25 Carried from S0.32 (21 October 2026)

**What this is.** S0.32 (`staffSignIn`), built on `feat/slice-000-s0-29` (nothing staged, committed or pushed) on the owner's instruction of 20 October 2026. It is the first operation that **issues a session**, so for the criteria below this is the first *real-operation* evidence: AC-SLICE-000-01 (an Ops Staff member signs in), the first step of -02 and -32 (a privileged identity is given a challenge and no session, whether or not it holds a factor), -04 (every failure is answered alike), -77 (a fifth wrong password locks and nobody is told), -78 (a lock ends on its own and a correct sign-in resets the count), -81 (a refused request is neither verified nor counted), the first half of -91 (the password step's causes in the audit) and the password half of -87. The second step is S0.33's. **No custody file and no credential was made on this machine and `melarc_dev` was not touched**: every identity and password is a throwaway of a disposable database.

**What was built.**
- *The database* (migration `0020_mfa_challenge_and_lockout.sql`, generated part from `src/staff/mfa-challenge.schema.ts` and `staff-identity.schema.ts`, the rest by hand). `mfa_challenge` (forced row-level security, the authentication capability alone; `SELECT`, `INSERT` and an `UPDATE` of `state` and `attempt_count` for the runtime and no `DELETE`; an insert guard that holds the challenge to the credential its identity holds now, an update guard that keeps everything but the state and a count that rises by one, lets only a `PENDING` challenge change, expires one only after its time and consumes one only before it) and `failed_attempt_count` and `locked_until` on `staff_identity` (checks: never negative, a lock needs failures and a credential; the runtime reads and updates exactly these two columns).
- *The ports and adapters*. `IdentityDirectory` gained `findStaffForSignIn` (the identity and whether a lock is in force **on the database's clock**), `readCredentialHash` (the definer function of migration 0016, the authentication capability alone), `recordFailedAttempt` (**one atomic conditional update**: add one unless a lock is in force, restart from one when a lock has run out, set the lock at the policy's count, and say whether this update tipped it), `clearFailedAttempts`, `rehashCredential` (the hash alone, only while the generation is the one verified) and `displayName`. `establishCredential` now clears the count (the contract of the setup). The `MfaChallengeStore` issues a challenge on the database's clock and ends the identity's other live challenge. `runAdmitted`, `commitThenRefuse`, the session issue protocol and the cookie writer, built earlier, are used as they stand.
- *The service* (`staff-sign-in.service.ts`). The schema and the bounds of the address and the password (the address is canonicalised first and only then checked to be an address); the rate limit has already been applied in the guard, keyed on the **canonical address whether or not it is anybody's** (`staff-sign-in-limit.ts`); then **a hash slot before anything identity-dependent** (none free is `RATE_LIMITED`, verified by nothing and counted nowhere, no dummy either); then one lookup with the two settings the count needs (the same statements for every request), and **one verification derivation** (Argon2id): the real one when the password was reached (the identity exists, is `ACTIVE`, holds a credential and is not locked), a dummy otherwise; a correct password at an older cost adds one more, the replacement hash (OB-39); then the bookkeeping. **Every refusal is `422` `INVALID_CREDENTIALS`, one message, and a lock is never announced.** A refusal that must persist is **returned, not thrown** (`commitThenRefuse`): the count and the events commit and only then is it answered; a record that cannot be written is a `5xx` and never an ordinary wrong password. An Ops Staff member is given the session of the S0.24 protocol with the count cleared in the same transaction (`200`, `melarc_session` and `melarc_csrf`, no `Max-Age`); a privileged identity is given a challenge on the credential that was proved and **no cookie** (`202`). A password that expands past 128 after NFKC is a wrong password that is **never derived and never counted**. A stronger hash the hasher says may replace the stored one does so in the success transaction, on the same generation (OB-39).
- *The route and its description*. `POST /auth/staff/sign-in`, browser surface `OPS_PORTAL` only, with its schemas, cookies and errors stated in code; `contract:check` compares **4 operations with no findings** and `api-client:check` is current. `CurrentSession` (`current-session.ts`, `session-schemas.ts`) is built once for the sign-ins and `getCurrentSession`.

**Decisions the documents do not state, taken here and listed for the owner.**
1. *A privileged identity's challenge ends its earlier live challenge* (`UNUSABLE`; the catalogue calls it superseded): asking for another challenge buys no further wrong codes, and a code can be tried on one challenge of an identity at a time. (The review of [§7.27](#727-the-adversarial-review-of-s029-to-s033-21-october-2026), finding 1, shows its cost: a holder of the password can end the user's live challenge as often as the sign-in limit allows.)
2. *The audit of an identifier that is no principal is the SHA-256 of a namespaced canonical address* (`identifier_kind` and `identifier_digest`), as audit.md says "a hash and the identifier's kind". It is **not keyed** (no approved key purpose exists for it), so a reader of the ledger could test a guess against it. The owner names a keyed digest, or accepts this.
3. *An over-long password is recorded as `WRONG_PASSWORD` at the factor `NONE`*: the closed set of causes has no word for it, and the request never reached the password. It is answered and counted as the contract says (answered `INVALID_CREDENTIALS`, never derived, never counted).
4. *The identity changed between the proof and the issue* (its credential replaced, it was suspended, its bundle became privileged): a replaced credential or a status that cannot sign in is `INVALID_CREDENTIALS` with the cause `INELIGIBLE_PRINCIPAL` and nothing counted; a bundle that became privileged is carried out again as a privileged sign-in and given a challenge. The privilege is decided on a read and again under the identity lock.
5. *The password step's two settings are read for every request alike*, so that the branches the work-shape test compares send the same statements; the branch that reached the credential sends only the two more it must (the hash and the count).
6. *A locked identity runs one dummy derivation* (it takes a slot), as §13.4b says, and a request refused by the limiter or by the slots runs none.
7. *Setting a credential clears the count*, though an identity with no credential cannot have been counted by a sign-in: the contract of `completeStaffCredentialSetup` says so, and the migration's check allows a count on an identity with no credential.
8. *The limiter reads a row up to five seconds ahead of the statement's clock as leaving at the end of the window* (the finding of the gate, below), where it used to fail the request closed. The tolerance is an engineering value (`CLOCK_SKEW_TOLERANCE_SECONDS`), development-qualified, which S0.65 calibrates with the others.

### 7.26 Carried from S0.33 (21 October 2026)

**What this is.** S0.33 (`completeStaffMfaSignIn`), built on `feat/slice-000-s0-29` (nothing staged, committed or pushed) on the owner's instruction of 20 October 2026; it is the last task of the authorized run, and the adversarial review of S0.29 to S0.33 follows. It is the operation that turns the challenge of S0.32 and a TOTP code into the **only privileged session the product can establish**, so for the criteria below this is real-operation evidence: AC-SLICE-000-02 and -32 (a privileged identity has no session before a factor is proved), -03 (single-use and short-lived; its clause that a challenge presented as a session is refused as one completes with S0.34's first authenticated route), -79 (a wrong code is refused and counted twice), -80 (a lock reached at the second factor is announced, to someone who proved the password), -91 (the second half: every cause in the audit, one answer), -94 (a PENDING factor cannot answer the second step), -123 (no ACTIVE factor: `403 MFA_ENROLMENT_REQUIRED`, nothing counted) and -126 (six digits, single-use, one step either side). **No custody file and no credential was made on this machine and `melarc_dev` was not touched.**

**What was built.**
- *The route* `POST /auth/staff/sign-in/mfa` (`staff-mfa-sign-in.controller.ts`): a browser pre-session mutation of the Ops Portal only (`403 CSRF_VALIDATION_FAILED` for any other Origin, before the code is examined or counted), limited in the privileged MFA bucket (`rate_limit_privileged_mfa`) under the challenge reference of the body, answered `200` with the session and the two cookies. It needs no session and no synchronizer token: there is no session to hold one. `contract:check` compares **5 operations with no findings**; `api-client:check` is current.
- *The service* (`staff-mfa-sign-in.service.ts`). The decision runs in one transaction that **commits what it wrote whatever it decides**, so that the bookkeeping of a refusal survives it. **It computes no hash** (the caller has proved the password) and takes no hash slot. It reads the challenge, takes **the identity's lock and then the challenge's** (the order of the session issue), and judges the state on the database's clock read after the locks: a challenge that is not there, is consumed, ended or superseded is `CHALLENGE_UNUSABLE`; one past its time is `CHALLENGE_EXPIRED` and is marked so; an identity that can no longer sign in, or that holds another credential than the one proved, is `INVALID_CREDENTIALS` and ends the challenge; a lock in force is `CREDENTIAL_LOCKED`, **neither verified nor counted**; no ACTIVE factor is `403 MFA_ENROLMENT_REQUIRED`, **not a wrong code and counted nowhere**; only then is the code verified against a seed opened in memory for that alone. **A wrong code, or one whose step was already accepted, counts twice** (on the challenge, whose third ends it, and on the identity's count shared with the password, which may set the lock) and writes `auth.session.failed` (`WRONG_MFA_CODE` at the factor `MFA_CODE`) and the enhanced `auth.mfa.failed`. **A correct code issues the session through the S0.24 protocol, and the proofs it spends commit with the session in one transaction**: the challenge is consumed, the step is recorded by the one conditional update that moves forward only, the identity's count is cleared and `auth.mfa.completed` is written. A request that loses a race for the challenge is `CHALLENGE_UNUSABLE`; one that loses a race for the step is a replay and is counted as a wrong code; one whose identity became ineligible between the proof and the issue is `INVALID_CREDENTIALS`.
- *The store and the directory.* `MfaChallengeStore` gained `findById`, `lockForDecision` (the row under `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, with the expiry judged by the database's clock), `recordWrongCode` (one conditional update: the third ends the challenge, none counts on an expired one), `consume` and `end`, each a conditional update on a `PENDING` challenge. `IdentityDirectory.isCredentialLocked` reads whether a lock is in force on the database's clock.

**Decisions the documents do not state, taken here and listed for the owner.**
1. *The second step takes no hash slot and computes no hash*: the password was proved at S0.32 and nothing here derives anything, so there is no derivation to admit; the limiter is the guard against guessing codes.
2. *The limit is keyed on the challenge reference as presented (a UUID in lower case), not on "the MFA challenge and principal"* ([settings.md](../../contracts/settings.md): `rate_limit_privileged_mfa`). The principal is not known before the body is read and the database is asked, and a limiter that waited for that would count nothing for a reference that names no challenge. The key is taken for **any well-formed reference, whether or not it names a challenge**, so the answer does not tell a real challenge from an invented one. **What this leaves open:** a caller who obtains fresh challenges (each needs the password) is bounded by the identity's shared count and its lock, and by the sign-in's own limit, and not by this bucket.
3. *Locks are taken identity first, challenge second.* The session issue takes the identity's lock first and this operation's steps then update the challenge; taking them the other way round would let two requests for one challenge wait for each other. A deterministic test pins the order (`staff-mfa-sign-in.service.test.ts`).
4. *A challenge that is not there, consumed, ended or superseded is answered alike (`CHALLENGE_UNUSABLE`); one past its time is `CHALLENGE_EXPIRED`.* The first four are not told apart so that a reference does not show whether it was ever issued; an overdue challenge is `CHALLENGE_EXPIRED` because the contract declares both codes and a challenge that is still held can say that it lapsed.
5. *An identity that was suspended, or whose credential was replaced, after the challenge was issued is `INVALID_CREDENTIALS`*, its challenge is ended (`UNUSABLE`) and nothing is counted; the audit cause is `INELIGIBLE_PRINCIPAL`.
6. *A lock is announced here, and the challenge stays `PENDING`.* The caller holds a live challenge, so the password was proved (AC-SLICE-000-80); the answer is `CREDENTIAL_LOCKED`, the code is neither verified nor counted, and nothing is written but the audit event.
7. *`MFA_ENROLMENT_REQUIRED` leaves the challenge `PENDING` and uncounted*, however often it is asked (AC-SLICE-000-123), and is audited with its own cause. The challenge is not consumed: it ends by its time.
8. *`auth.mfa.failed` and `auth.mfa.completed` name the `StaffIdentity` as their object*, with the factor and the challenge as related identifiers: [audit.md](../../contracts/audit.md) §5.4 states the events and not their object.
9. *A step already accepted counts like a wrong code*, whether it is found by the verifier (inside its window) or by the conditional update that records the step (a request that lost the race): both are `MFA_PROOF_INVALID`, counted on the challenge and on the identity.

**The break campaign** (30 single breaks of the service, the controller, the limit, the challenge store and the directory's lock reader, each applied to the real file, run against the focused tests and restored by hash). **25 caught, 4 survived and 1 did not apply** (its find-text was not the formatted source; corrected and rerun). Each is now pinned alone by a unit test that makes the neighbouring layer say yes, and all three are caught. The mutant that did not apply (B17, a lost race for the challenge answered as a failure) is caught on its rerun. **Result: 30 of 30 caught.** The service, the controller and the limit were written before the tests that pin them had been run red (the order recorded for S0.32); the campaign is the proof that the tests catch what they claim.

### 7.27 The adversarial review of S0.29 to S0.33 (21 October 2026)

**What it was.** The owner's instruction ended the run of S0.29 to S0.33 with a deep adversarial review of everything built, to be fixed and left green. It was made in three ways: my own reading of the migrations (`0018` to `0020`), the stores, the three services, the controllers, the limits, the directory adapter, the bootstrap tools and the worker's reader; **three read-only reviewers** started with different lenses (the database layer, the application flows as an attacker, and the tooling, the tests and the documents), who ran nothing and reported findings; and **tests that send hostile input to every route**. **No finding was acted on because it was reported.** Each was read in the code first, and every one that is a behaviour was reproduced by a test that failed against the code as it stood (RED) before it was corrected (GREEN); the tests that were written after a correction were proved by removing the correction. One reviewer was cut off by a session limit and resumed, and all three finished.

**Defects found and corrected** (each with the test that failed first):

| #| Defect| Where it was found| Correction and evidence|
|---|---|---|---|

RED: five unit tests and two route tests; the permanent hostile-input suite (below) found exactly this one and no other when the correction was taken out|
| 2| **The sign-in's rate limit could be skipped.** The limiter takes no key from a text longer than 1280 bytes, and the service trims before it judges, so `"<2000 spaces>alice@example.com"` was looked up, derived against and counted like any address, with no limit (AC-SLICE-000-81)| Flows reviewer, read in the code| The service refuses any address past the bound as `VALIDATION_FAILED`, before any work (`MAX_ADDRESS_BYTES`, shared with the limit and tied to it by a test). RED: the route answered `422` and derived|

**Gaps in tests and documents corrected.** The entry scripts and the composition root of the bootstrap commands were run by no test: `bootstrap-tools.process.test.ts` runs the built scripts (the arguments as `pnpm` passes them, the refusals that come before a database or a folder, a real folder judged by the platform's adapters, an unreachable database, no file written, nothing sensitive printed). A password with a NUL byte is held by the hasher as the whole text (a test). The documents said that the commands set ownership on POSIX (they set the mode and check the owner), kept "an archive root" out (only checkouts are recognised), called a swept bundle a secret for nobody (true only of its own database), and did not say how to set the folder (the scripts read no `.env` for it): [MIGRATION_AND_SEEDING.md](../../architecture/MIGRATION_AND_SEEDING.md) §3.2, [DEVELOPMENT.md](../../DEVELOPMENT.md), the vocabulary's messages and the registry's rows for `MfaChallenge` and `StaffIdentity` are corrected. The schema header of `mfa_challenge` claimed a guard on the lockout columns that does not exist and now says so.

**Findings the review leaves for the Product Owner** (nothing here is built, and each is a decision or a design addition):
1. *A holder of the password alone can keep a privileged user from completing the second step.* Every correct password step ends the identity's other live challenge ([§7.25](#725-carried-from-s032-21-october-2026), decision 1), so a thief who has the password and can sign in ten times a minute can end the user's challenge each time, with no failure counted and no lock. The reviewer notes that the ending is not needed to stop extra guesses (wrong codes already count on the identity across challenges). Recommended: decide decision 1 with this in view.
2. *`RATE_LIMITED` is consumed before the Origin check, and the limit is per address.* Ten requests a minute with no `Origin` header, or with any (a non-browser client can send one), use up a victim's bucket and answer `RATE_LIMITED` to the victim. This is the refusal order of [permission-enforcement.md](../../features/identity/permission-enforcement.md) §5.1 (the limit first) and the keying of AC-SLICE-000-81, so it is a property of the design and not a defect of the code; but [openapi.yaml](../../contracts/openapi.yaml) says of `staffSignIn` that a missing or unlisted `Origin` is "answered before the password is examined and without counting it", and the limiter does count it. **Whether "counting" there means the failed-attempt count only, or the limit too, is for the owner to say**; if it means the limit, the Origin check would have to come before it, which the refusal order forbids. Per-source ceilings are the edge's (S0.20, S0.65).
3. *An unauthenticated request makes one audit row* (an unknown challenge reference, an unknown address), and the second step's limit has a key for each reference an attacker invents. Specified behaviour and volume only; bounded by the edge.
4. *The session's view is read in a second transaction after the session has committed*, so a failure there (pool saturation, a deadline) answers an error with no cookie after the proofs were spent and a session nobody holds exists. Recommended: an after-create hook in the session issue (S0.24's protocol) that returns the view from the issuing transaction. Not built here because it changes a protocol that the Vendor and Rider sign-ins will share. **Corrected afterwards by the owner's audit: the optional `project` hook of the issue (A04, [§7.28](#728-the-independent-audit-of-s029-to-s033-21-october-2026-disposition)); the Vendor and Rider sign-ins use it too.**
5. *Guards the database does not hold, that its documents imply* (each is one writer's mistake away, none is a live defect): the lockout columns are not reset by the database when a credential is replaced ([domain-model.md](../../contracts/domain-model.md) §6.8 says they reset whenever it is established or changed; recommended: the identity guard resets them by construction when the generation moves); an `MFA_ENROLMENT` grant may carry no lineage and two may name one source (recommended: a unique index on `continued_from_grant_id` and a rule that the purpose carries one); an `ACTIVE` factor may have no recorded step, so the code that proved it could be replayed (recommended: a check); a lapsed grant may be marked `SUPERSEDED` (the guard allows it where the store never does); no lifetime is bounded at insert. **Recommended: one hardening migration, after the owner agrees the list.**
6. *The `bootstrap` branch of the identity insert policy admits an ACTIVE Platform Admin with no maker or checker to any login that holds `INSERT` on `staff_identity` and sets the label.* Today only the provisioning login reaches it, through the definer function, and the API holds no `INSERT`; when the task that builds `createStaffIdentity` grants it, the branch becomes reachable from the API by label, which the registry's accepted residual risk covers and MIGRATION_AND_SEEDING.md §3.2's "structurally unavailable" does not. Decide at that grant.
7. *Still open from earlier in the run*, and unchanged: decisions 1 and 2 of §7.25 and decision 2 of §7.26 (a challenge's key); the unkeyed digest of an unknown identifier; the retention of `mfa_challenge`; OB-136 (the event of the resume command); the failures of `csrf-guard.db.test.ts`, `delivery-worker.db.test.ts` and `rate-limiter.db.test.ts` that §7.25 records as unexplained; **the Ops Portal's worker-start timeout, which failed one of two full `pnpm test` runs of this review and passed the other**; the **Linux, WSL2 and CI evidence** (the POSIX mode inspection and four tests of it are skipped on Windows); and **a `python` process (process 20568, started 20 October 2026 at 17:33 by a parent `python3.exe -`, about 49 800 seconds of processor time) that uses a core of this machine and that I did not touch**: I cannot prove it is the debris of an earlier session's script, and `Stop-Process -Id 20568` is the owner's to run once they have looked.
