## 11. Decisions of 9 October 2026 and where each is recorded

The Product Owner approved the decisions below on 9 October 2026. Each fact has one owning document, so this section names the document and states only what the plan itself does with the decision; it does not restate the rule. The earlier pending proposals and their exact diffs are replaced by the applied text.

### 11.1 `listReasonDefinitions` as the 38th Slice-000 operation

**Approved (decisions 1 and 2).** `listReasonDefinitions` (`GET /reason-definitions`, permission `settings.reason.read`) is the 38th operation the slice builds, with its branch applicability and the authoritative `StaffIdentity.mfa_reset_state` projection. The request body of `upsertReasonDefinition` is a separate `ReasonDefinitionWrite` schema (**W1**) that carries every writable field and none of the response-only metadata; the general `ContractValidator` is unchanged.

**Where it is recorded.** [contracts/openapi.yaml](../../contracts/openapi.yaml) (version 5.77: the `operation` and `branch` filters, the `400`, `ReasonDefinition.permittedOperations`, `ReasonDefinitionWrite`, `StaffIdentity.mfa_reset_state`); [domain-model.md](../../contracts/domain-model.md) §3.9 (the branch-qualified registry entries and the four changed seed rows) and §6.8 (the projection); [state-machines.md](../../contracts/state-machines.md) §18 (one rule decides both the projection and `resetStaffMfa`); [permissions.md](../../contracts/permissions.md) §7 (scope in practice); [ops-portal.md](../../surfaces/ops-portal.md) (the five routes that take a reason); [SLICE-000.md](../slices/SLICE-000.md) §1.1 and §7; [permission-enforcement.md](../../features/identity/permission-enforcement.md) (`AC-SLICE-000-132`); [IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md](../IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md) §4c (what `SLICE-013` owes).

**What the plan does with it.** The operation joins **S0.35** as a fourth read, in `src/settings/`; S0.35 also builds the one eligibility function behind `mfa_reset_state`, which S0.36 returns on every `StaffIdentity` and S0.37's `resetStaffMfa` calls. **S0.41 Needs S0.35**, and S0.44, S0.52 and S0.60 reach it through S0.41. `AC-SLICE-000-132` completes at **S0.59**, because its Rider-session clause needs a Rider session. The slice's counts are now **38 operations and 126 criteria**; the contract has **172 operations and 175 schemas**. No catalogue mutation is added and `upsertReasonDefinition` is out of scope: the refusals it owes are obligation OB-34 and the `SLICE-013` row of §4c.

**One clarification the projection made explicit.** `NOT_ELIGIBLE` includes an identity that is not `ACTIVE` or `SUSPENDED`. A `PENDING_APPROVAL` or `REJECTED` identity holds no factor and was already not eligible; `OFFBOARDED` is terminal and was not named by the earlier text of `resetStaffMfa`. [state-machines.md](../../contracts/state-machines.md) §18 now states it, and the Product Owner should confirm it (it is listed in the handoff of the P0 commit).

### 11.2 The local QR primitive before staff enrolment

**Approved (decision 3).** The reusable QR encoder and its independent test decoder are **S0.39c**, built before S0.43 and reused at S0.60. Staff enrolment shows the QR and the secret for manual entry together (the manual secret is the accessible alternative). Both are transient credentials: no remote QR service, no analytics, no persistence, no ordinary navigable `otpauth` link, cleared on navigation, completion and expiry, and covered by the sentinel tests of S0.39b.

### 11.3 The reconciliation commit

**Authorized (the message of 9 October).** One scoped P0 checkpoint commit of the reconciliation, preserving unrelated work and excluding secrets, local evidence and archives, **not pushed**; then **S0.1 only**, which is not committed and is not followed by S0.2. The commit hash is reported in the handoff and not written here, because a document cannot contain the hash of the commit that holds it.

### 11.4 Vendor-organisation lifecycle eligibility

**Approved (decision 3).** A vendor account may recover only while its linked `VendorOrganization` is `ACTIVE` or `SUSPENDED`; `REJECTED`, `TERMINATED` and the pre-approval states are answered like an unknown identifier (an administrator gets `STATE_CONFLICT`); recovery reactivates nothing. The rule is recorded in [credential-recovery.md](../../features/identity/credential-recovery.md) §5.7 and AC-121, [state-machines.md](../../contracts/state-machines.md) (the `VendorOrganization` note), [domain-model.md](../../contracts/domain-model.md) (the `RecoveryRequest` invariant), [audit.md](../../contracts/audit.md) §5.4, [openapi.yaml](../../contracts/openapi.yaml) (`requestCredentialRecovery`, `recoverVendorCredential`), [security-test-matrix.md](../../standards/security-test-matrix.md) `GBT-B15`, [SECURITY_DESIGN.md](../../architecture/SECURITY_DESIGN.md) §13.9a and [IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md](../IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md) §4c. `SLICE-008` owes the real transition that rejects or terminates an organisation and ends the account's recovery material in its own transaction; Slice-000 builds and tests the consumer-side guard with a fixture, which is not proof of a termination endpoint. Staff offboarding is unchanged and owed to `SLICE-009`.

### 11.5 Test CA and browser trust

**Approved (decision 4), for an isolated, disposable spike only.** S0.23 opens with a bounded spike that records, per engine (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit, branded Chrome and Edge), which mechanism works and what it proves: a disposable test environment or an isolated browser profile or context that trusts the locally generated CA, with real certificate validation (a negative test with an untrusted CA must fail) and never `ignoreHTTPSErrors` as trust evidence. **This does not authorize a persistent machine-wide trust change**; one needs the owner's authorization of an exact installation and removal plan first. Safari itself stays a manual check.

### 11.6 Where officer operations live

**Approved (decision 3).** Controllers for what an officer does to another principal are thin and live in the permission domain that owns the key's first segment (`staff`, `vendor`, `settings`); `dispatch` serves the two rider reads. The shared session, MFA and recovery logic stays in `platform/auth` behind the S0.1 ports. `dispatch` reads the staff-owned rider data through a read port; there is no second identity store and no duplicated business logic. This is the placement of [§3](#3-rules-every-task-keeps) and [§6.1](#61-operations).

### 11.7 The names and sizes in rows 9b to 9g of §10

**Approved together (decision 3).** The refusal codes for identity-reason management as written in `permissions.md` §7 and `upsertReasonDefinition`; the token of 32 random bytes shown as 43 base64url characters; the floor-timing sentence of SECURITY_DESIGN §13.10; the outcome class `DESTINATION_NOT_ALLOWED`; the readiness reason `policy_superseded`; the table `credential_delivery_job` and its worker capability `credential_delivery`. Each is written in the owning document and in the contract; S0.5, S0.17 and S0.26 use these names.

### 11.8 Deadline ownership and the execution budget

**Decided by the Product Owner on 9 October 2026, closing S0.2** (row 15 of §10; nothing here is implemented yet). The settings are in [DEPLOYMENT_AND_ENVIRONMENTS.md](../../architecture/DEPLOYMENT_AND_ENVIRONMENTS.md) §12.5, "Deadlines", which owns their meaning; this section records who builds what.

- **S0.20 owns the HTTP header and body receipt limits and HTTP admission** (the byte limit, the admission deadline and concurrency, the trusted-proxy setting). They end a slow sender and bound nothing a handler does.
- **S0.6 owns the database and resource deadlines and the shared execution-budget mechanism. S0.20 integrates that mechanism into the request pipeline** (S0.20 therefore needs S0.6).
- **Database timeouts alone do not bound a whole request.** Time outside the database (a provider or verifier call, hashing, the application's own work) is outside them, so a request needs a budget of its own.
- **Enforcing an execution budget is not racing a response against a timer.** The mechanism must say what an expiry does to work already running: cancel what can be cancelled; roll back the open transaction and discard a connection of uncertain state ([SECURITY_DESIGN.md](../../architecture/SECURITY_DESIGN.md) §14.6); and keep a late side effect (a commit, an outbound call, an audit or delivery enqueue) from taking effect, or record it, after the caller was told the request failed. Its tests (S0.6 for the mechanism with a real database, S0.20 for the pipeline over real HTTP) expire a budget mid-work and observe the result on a second connection. This is **OB-37**.
- **Concrete values are qualified at their first use** (§3) and **calibrated in S0.65**, which proposes release values for the owner's approval. S0.2's numbers are provisional, configuration-validated defaults and nothing more.
- **Accepted as written:** S0.2's provisional-default wording, and managed key custody (implementation, rotation proof, recovery proof) as a prerequisite of G3 (OB-36).
- **Not implemented by S0.2:** any future deadline task. No execution-budget setting exists yet; S0.6 chooses it with its mechanism.

### 11.9 The review of S0.3 (9 October 2026)

The owner's review of S0.3 corrected it before it was committed. What the plan itself does with the decisions:

- **The Argon2id profile comes from configuration.** `ARGON2_*` are settings validated at start, with a floor for deployed environments, so S0.3's files include `platform/config/*`, `.env.example` and the DEPLOYMENT table, and its run codes are B D E. The profile, its measurement and the floor are in [DEPLOYMENT_AND_ENVIRONMENTS.md](../../architecture/DEPLOYMENT_AND_ENVIRONMENTS.md) §12.5; confirming the floor is OB-42.
- **Verifying a hash and permitting its replacement are separate decisions.** A stored hash is derived only at a supported profile, and is rewritten only forward: a newer pepper at an unchanged cost, or a larger cost at the same lanes. A changed profile is never assumed to be a stronger one.
- **The envelope version is stored** with every sealed value (the `SealedSecret` port carries it), before any record exists.
- **The production `Clock` adapter is S0.6's**, not left unowned.
- **The real-versus-dummy verification cost difference during a cost migration is documented, not hidden**, and is assessed before a migration is enabled (OB-41). Counting derivations proves their number and not equal work, and nothing sleeps or hashes twice to make branches look alike.

### 7.44 Carried from S0.45 and S0.46 (25 October 2026)

**Why.** The owner asked for Stage 5 (S0.45 and S0.46) to be built to completion and to the fullest, and not S0.47. Stage 5 is the first integrated proof: the real screens against the real API, a real database and the real delivery worker, from the two bootstrap administrators, with no manual database edit.

**What was built.**

- **The harness reaches the database by two closed lists** (`apps/api/src/tools/e2e/arrangements.ts`, run only by the `e2e-database` command as the administrator of its own disposable database): *arrangements* let time pass for something no operation will ever do (`expire-setup-grant`, `expire-mfa-challenge`, `idle-session`, `lapse-lock`, and, since the trusted browser, `age-trusted-browsers`), each taking its values as statement parameters, switching one guard trigger off for one update and on again whatever happened, and **failing when it changed no row** so a journey cannot pass for a lapse that did not happen; *observations* read what no operation shows (`factors`, `sessions`, `setup-grants`, `lock`, `audit-codes`, `trusted-browsers`) and read no secret column. Both are tested without a database (`arrangements.test.ts`).
- **The stack of the journeys**: the two bootstrap administrators come from the real `bootstrap:seed` (the command spawns `bootstrap-seed.js` and `bootstrap-resume.js`), the worker is its own process writing to a capture sink outside the checkout, a TOTP helper takes the earliest step the server still accepts, a custody reader takes a bundle and removes its file, and a message reader takes the next captured message for an address. Passwords, codes, setup keys and links are typed into and read from real pages in specs that run with the recorders off (`*.secret.test.ts`), whose source the evidence policy scans for what would keep them (`attach`, `screenshot`, dynamic imports).
- **The technical journey is retired**: the notes routes and the outbound-call route of `apps/api/test/support/e2e-main.mjs` (which keeps only the three routes the HTTPS specs of S0.23 use), its pool, the `e2e_harness.notes` table and the two specs that used them. A test (`architecture.test.ts`) holds the entry point to no database access of any kind.
- **Nine journeys, one list**: rows 4 and 5, 4a, 1 and AC-115, 2 and 3, 6, 12, 13 and 14 of the demonstration, and the trusted browser. They are registered once (`harness/journeys/staff-journeys.ts`) and run by two thin specs: `staff-journeys.secret.test.ts` over plain HTTP in Chromium (`pnpm run test:e2e`, **a diagnostic**: the cookies are `Secure`, which an engine may or may not honour on a loopback address) and `https-staff-journeys.secret.test.ts` over the trusted HTTPS origin in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit (`pnpm run test:e2e:https`, the evidence of AC-127, **CI only**).

**Decisions the documents do not state.**

1. The journeys are serial: each stands on the people an earlier one made, and a failure stops the rest.
2. A journey changes no row by hand. Time passes by an arrangement; a person is made by the screens.
3. A journey that needs a person nobody has just used takes another (the staff sign-in is limited to ten an address a minute, AC-SLICE-000-81, and the journeys do not step around the real limit): the trusted-browser journey found this when it ran straight after the lockout journey on the same address and was answered `RATE_LIMITED`.

**Findings for the Product Owner.**

1. **Gate 5 is not passed.** What ran is the plain HTTP run in Chromium. The HTTPS run, Firefox, WebKit and the branded smoke need the test CA and run in CI; they are blocked here and recorded as such, never as passed.
2. **The plain HTTP run is a diagnostic and not the evidence of AC-127.** It shows the journeys work end to end; the cookie attributes are proved on the HTTPS origin.

### 7.45 Carried from the trusted browser (25 October 2026)

**Why.** After Stage 5 the owner asked for *remember me* for sign-ins and its related workflow, built to the fullest. Four decisions were taken with the owner before building: it is **a trusted browser that skips the authenticator step** (not a longer session, and not a skipped password); it lasts **seven days, absolutely**; it is offered to **Senior Ops and Platform Admin**, the two bundles that sign in with a second factor; and it is managed by **the person and by a Platform Admin**.

**What was built.**

- **The contract** (`contracts/openapi.yaml`): four operations (`listTrustedBrowsers`, `revokeTrustedBrowser`, `listStaffTrustedBrowsers`, `revokeStaffTrustedBrowsers`), the field `trust_browser` of the second step, `trusted_browser_days` of the challenge, the schemas `TrustedBrowser`, `TrustedBrowserList` and `TrustedBrowsersRevoked`, the cookie `melarc_trusted_browser`, and the extension `x-set-cookies-optional` (a cookie the request decides). 176 operations, 178 schemas, 20 Ops Portal routes; the slice now has 42 operations and 133 criteria (`AC-SLICE-000-133` to `-139`; they were drafted as 130 to 136 and renumbered, because 130 to 132 were already taken).
- **The mechanism** (migration `0033`; `src/platform/auth/trusted-browsers/`): the table `trusted_browser` (32 random bytes, only the hash stored in a column the runtime cannot select; bound to the `ACTIVE` factor and the credential generation; seven days from the database's clock, written once; at most five valid, a sixth replaces the oldest; guard triggers; policies for the `authentication` capability, for a person's own rows and for the one identity an administrator has locked); two definer readers of the hash; the store; the label made from the `User-Agent` by a closed list of browser and system names (the header is never stored).
- **The sign-in**: after the password is proved, a privileged identity whose browser presents a valid credential is answered `200` and the session, with the use recorded and the count cleared in the one transaction, and `auth.session.issued` carries the fact `second_factor` (`NONE`, `TOTP` or `TRUSTED_BROWSER`); every other case is the ordinary `202`, in silence. **A wrong password with the cookie is `INVALID_CREDENTIALS` and counts; a lock refuses a correct one.** At the second step, `trust_browser` makes the credential in the transaction that issues the session after an accepted code, and only there.
- **Ending it**: the person (`SELF`), a Platform Admin (`staff.session.revoke` at tier `P`, a reason of `revokeSession`'s domain, the identity locked first, the enhanced `auth.trusted_browser.admin_revoked` with the count), a reset of the authenticator (`FACTOR_RESET`) and a new authenticator (`FACTOR_REPLACED`); seven days; an identity that is not `ACTIVE`; a moved credential generation. Signing out does not end it.
- **The Ops Portal**: the choice at the second step (a new `Checkbox`, COMPONENT_PATTERNS §7.10), `/account/trusted-browsers` for any signed-in session, and a section of an enrolled profile for a holder of `staff.session.revoke`. The generated client was regenerated.
- **The harness**: the ninth journey, the arrangement `age-trusted-browsers` and the observation `trusted-browsers`.

**Design calls that are mine** (the documents do not state them, or the owner did not).

1. **No reference data was added or changed.** Adding a key or a setting to a database that was seeded before it existed would need a forward data migration, which is a normal capability and a larger change than this feature needs (corrected on 26 October 2026: the earlier text called it a limit of the project). So the administrator's operations reuse `staff.session.revoke`, the seven days are a constant of the contract and not a setting, and the reasons are those of `revokeSession`.
2. **The menu offers `/account/trusted-browsers` to every signed-in session**, in the administration area, because the session lists no second-factor fact to gate it by; the page says plainly that a role with no authenticator has nothing to remember.
3. **An invalid credential is never mentioned**: unknown, expired, removed, another person's, twice, empty, not a token: the answer is the ordinary challenge and no cookie.
4. **The credential is not renewed by use**: using it records `last_used_at` and nothing else.
5. **A trusted browser is made only for a privileged identity**, judged in the issuing transaction; a role that stopped being privileged between the two steps is signed in as it is and given none (a unit test; the table's guard would have refused the insert and failed a correct sign-in).

**Findings for the Product Owner.**

1. **The menu entry is shown to every role** (design call 2). Say if you want it hidden from roles with no authenticator; that needs a fact on the session the contract does not yet carry.
2. **`Checkbox` is a new component pattern** (COMPONENT_PATTERNS §7.10). The task needed it and no pattern named it; confirm it.
3. **The seven days are a constant, not a setting** (design call 1). A setting would need a way to add reference data to a database already seeded, which the project does not have.
4. **A suspended or offboarded person must have their trusted browsers ended by the task that suspends or offboards them.** Today the credential is refused for an identity that is not `ACTIVE`, but a suspension that is lifted inside the seven days would make an old credential valid again; those operations are not built, and their cause (`IDENTITY_NOT_ACTIVE`) is not in the closed list.
5. **`CREDENTIAL_CHANGED` is written by the recovery that replaces a password** (S0.51, not built). It is already *enforced*: the credential generation moved, so the credential is refused; only the recorded cause is owed.
6. **A message to the person when a browser is remembered** (an email, like a new-device sign-in notice) is a suggestion and is not built.
7. **The vendor half of AC-127 is deferred** with the Vendor PWA; the vendor device credential is another thing.
8. **Under the key `staff.session.revoke`, the policies of `staff_identity` now also let the operation read and lock an identity in scope** (migration `0033`, for the administrator's operations). The operations that run under that key and need no identity (`revokeSession` of a rider) do not read one; this is recorded because it widens what a statement under that key can reach.
9. **The Platform Admin and Senior Ops see the section; Senior Ops is refused** with `INSUFFICIENT_AUTHORITY`, because the session lists keys and no tiers.

**Audit of what Slice 000 has built so far (25 October 2026).** The owner asked, after the build, for an adversarial audit of everything done in the slice, with every finding fixed except those that need a decision. It was run by reading the code against the contracts, by mutating the new code (each mutant below was killed by a test, three after a test was added), and by running the whole gate on a tree nobody was editing. Fixed:

1. **A credential name in a log.** The log redaction knew `melarc_session` and not `melarc_trusted_browser` (nor `melarc_vendor_device` inside free text): both are redacted now (`redaction.ts`, `scrub-text.ts`, with tests).
2. **A regression of mine.** Migration `0033` redefined `melarc.staff_locked_facts` from the text of `0030` and so silently undid the corrections of `0031`. It is rebuilt from `0031` and changes only the key list. The lesson: a function that is replaced is copied from the latest migration that defines it, never from the one that introduced it.
3. **A correct sign-in that would have failed.** A role that stopped being privileged between the two steps would have made the table's guard refuse the trusted-browser insert and answer `500`; the sign-in now gives such a role no trusted browser (a unit test).
4. **Duplicate acceptance IDs.** `AC-SLICE-000-130` to `-132` already existed; the new criteria are `-133` to `-139` everywhere (feature, slice, plan, tests).
5. **Contract text that said more than the code does.** The list description claimed a binding check it does not make; the Ops-only self operations did not declare `PERMISSION_DENIED`; the domain model named four of six revocation causes. All corrected in the contract, the code and the domain documents, and the client regenerated.
6. **Checks that had never run.** The `e2e` package had 18 lint errors (most in the S0.45 files of the earlier session) and three files were unformatted; the architecture test still pinned the retired technical-journey entry point; the journeys' failure messages could have printed a grant or a credential (they now carry booleans and digests).
7. **Test debt of the new table and key.** Four bootstrap tests truncated tables without `trusted_browser`; the pins of the policies and definer functions moved with the new `staff.session.revoke` read and lock arms and the two readers of the hash; the Ops shell's browser pins missed the new menu entry; a Vendor and Rider refusal test used the wrong origin. The mutant that let `revokeOne` end an already-ended browser survived until a test was added.
8. **A journey against the real limit.** The trusted-browser journey was answered `RATE_LIMITED` when it reused an address the lockout journey had just used (ten staff sign-ins an address a minute, AC-SLICE-000-81); it takes its own people, and the limit is not stepped around.

Left for the Product Owner, with the findings above:

- **Four tests fail under load and pass alone.** `test/process.test.ts` "startup refusals" (an 8 s bound), the e2e `evidence-policy` probe (about 45 s on an idle machine, over two minutes when the machine was busy), one dialog conflict test in the browser project (30 s) and the Ops Portal's production-build test (a 20 s hook, 3 s alone). None was given a longer bound or a retry, by the rule of this package; run alone, each passes. If CI shows them, the bound is the decision.
- **The administrator's removal states no credential of its own**, as the other staff mutations, so it inherits the contract's default posture: a Rider's bearer credential authenticates as a Rider and is refused at the surface gate with `403 PERMISSION_DENIED`, where the two reads answer `401`. It is the contract's own posture and was left; say if every Ops-only mutation should declare `browserSession` with its token.
- **The database clock of this workstation steps.** PostgreSQL runs in Docker Desktop's virtual machine, whose clock steps forward about 1.07 s every 31 s against this machine's (measured: a 0.48 s and a 0.59 s step, six steps in 90 s). PostgreSQL times a lock wait by that clock, so a `lock_timeout` of 2 s can end a wait after less than one. Five database tests held a row lock for a fixed 1.5 s against that timeout, and one of them failed in about every second full run (below). **Corrected on 26 October 2026**: those tests, and three of the same kind that waited 1 to 1.8 s, no longer sleep (see the corrections below); the virtual machine's time is still the owner's to correct, and is a separate matter.
- **Not run, and not passed:** the HTTPS run, Firefox, WebKit and the branded smoke (CI only), so **Gate 5 is not passed**; the S0.28 accessibility note is still unfiled; the moderate `esbuild` advisory (GHSA-67mh-4wv8-2f99) is still open and below the `high` bar of the audit step.

**The gate on the frozen tree** (25 October 2026, uncached, `TURBO_FORCE=true`). `format:check`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `build`, `contract:check`, `api-client:check` and `db:check` pass. The unit tests pass one package at a time (`pnpm run test:local --continue`): root 1,247 (1,245 passed, 2 skipped), API 5,871 (5,859 passed, 12 skipped, the POSIX-only ones), Ops Portal 2,120, API client 250, harness 538 (535 passed, 3 skipped). The CI form, `pnpm test`, starts every package at once: on this workstation 11 Ops Portal files could not start their test workers in time, and turbo then stopped the API's; that is load, and CI runs it on its own runner. `test:browser`: 364 passed (Chromium). `test:e2e`: 25 passed (Chromium over plain HTTP, the nine journeys among them). `pnpm audit --audit-level high` passes (the one moderate advisory above). `test:db`: 2,960 passed, 2 skipped and **one failed in each of two runs, a different test each time** (`staff-sign-in` "an identity whose bundle became privileged meanwhile", then `staff-setup-operations` "one suspended while the request waited"): each is a 1.5 s hold answered `503` by a lock timeout that ended early, the clock step above, and each file passes when it is run again. Not run: `test:e2e:https`, Firefox, WebKit and the branded smoke.

**Corrections of the audit of 26 October 2026 (G01 to G05, and the decisions it recommended).** An independent audit of the archive of 25 October (SHA-256 `07c164e8…763f1bd`) found five defects of this work. Each was checked against the code and the contract before anything was changed, fixed with a test that failed for its reason, and mutation-checked (the code broken on purpose, the test seen to fail, the file restored by hash). The tree also held the work of Stage 6 (migrations `0034` to `0038`, the recovery and vendor screens), which is another station's and not yet audited: none of it was touched, and the one migration of this correction is `0039`, the next free number (**if the other station also adds a `0039`, the two collide when the trees meet**).

- **G01, one stack for every engine (confirmed).** `HTTPS_PHASES` ran Chromium and Firefox in one Playwright run, so one global setup, one database and one set of one-time bootstrap bundles; the journeys begin by consuming those bundles, so the second engine met a story already told. **Fix:** three runs, each its own invocation and so its own stack: Chromium with WebKit's refusal (which runs no journey), Firefox, and WebKit with the CA in the system store, in that order, each with an output directory of its own (`e2e/harness/https-run.ts`, `https-run.test.ts`, `e2e/README.md`). A test now holds that no run holds two of the secret projects that run the journeys; breaking that (both back in one run) is caught. **What is not shown:** the three runs themselves, which need the test CA and run in CI only. Cleanup failures already fail the run (a CA left in the system store, a stack that cannot stop).
- **G02, expiry judged before the row's lock (confirmed in the SQL, reproduced on PostgreSQL).** `melarc.use_trusted_browser` took the instant before the update that could wait for the row, which a person's own removal holds without the identity's lock, so a browser whose seven days ran out during the wait still stood in for the code. **Fix:** migration `0039` locks the candidate row, takes the instant in a statement of its own, then judges and records; the table's guard refuses a use recorded at or after the browser's end. Tests hold the row from a second connection, **observe** the use waiting (`pg_blocking_pids`, not a sleep), let the end pass on the database's clock and release: the browser asks for the code, a live one is used at an instant after the wait, a committed removal is honoured (`trusted-browser-store.db.test.ts`, `staff-trusted-browser-race.db.test.ts`, `support/lock-wait.ts`); the old definition fails the first two.
- **G03, a retry that removes what was enrolled since (confirmed).** The administrator's removal took no key. **Fix:** it takes an `Idempotency-Key` through the existing store (the receipt, the removals and the event are one transaction), the fingerprint holds the identity, the reason and the note, the contract, the generated client, the screen (the dialog's key, the same on a retry, a new one after the record was checked) and the documents say so. The statement that a concurrent issue is "removed with the rest or issues nothing" is corrected: **a removal ends what exists and is not a ban.** Five new database tests and two screen tests; the receipt removed and the fingerprint ignored are both caught.
- **G04, no audit of the cross-hub list (confirmed).** `listStaffTrustedBrowsers` wrote no `auth.hub_boundary.crossed`. **Fix:** one enhanced event naming the identity's primary hub (read from the identity, never from the request) and the operation, none for the caller's own hub, an identity with no hub or an empty list (the rule of the other lists), written in the read's transaction so a ledger that refuses it fails the read. Five tests; four breaks caught.
- **G05, a success that ignores the cancellation of its flow (confirmed).** The two sign-in screens checked the flow only for the challenge. **Fix:** both screens (and the setup page that navigates, and the failure paths of the setup pages) read `flow.current()` once the answer has arrived and, if it was called off, change nothing, navigate nowhere and show nothing, emptying only the field they read; no sign-out is sent, because it could end a session that is not this attempt's: the next read of the session (`GET /auth/session`) is how the page learns what the server holds. Tested in jsdom with a network that ignores the signal, and **in Chromium** with a `fetch` made deaf to cancellation (a real one aborts the request, and then the late answer never arrives to be refused): a late success after leaving the page, a late success of an earlier sign-in over a newer one, and the second step; the checks removed are caught in both. **Not touched:** the two recovery screens of Stage 6, which the other station's audit should read for the same gap.
- **Decisions of the audit that were applied.** (2) the claim that the project cannot extend reference data is replaced everywhere it was written; (5) the administrator's removal declares the browser session and its token like the read beside it (contract, controller, inventory pin: a Rider's bearer is now `401`); (6) the narrow `staff.session.revoke` read and lock of an identity is kept, and a test as the real runtime login shows it changes nothing; (7) a list shows only browsers still on the credential they were trusted on, and what a task that suspends or offboards a person owes (end the browsers in the status change's transaction, with a cause it adds, and prove that reactivation revives none) is written in the model and the feature, not built; (9) the sleeps that held a lock for 1.5 s (three sites) and the three that waited 1 to 1.8 s (two A06 tests, one holds test) now observe the wait and the database's clock, with the lock bound lengthened for those applications alone and production's untouched; (10) `pnpm run test:local` is the lower-concurrency profile (`DEVELOPMENT.md`). **Kept as they were:** 1, 3, 4 and 8.
- **Still owed, and not claimed:** the hosted Linux run and the three engines' journeys on a revision that contains this tree, which only a pushed checkpoint can give (nothing was committed or pushed); a clean `test:db` on this workstation depends on its database clock, which steps about a second every half minute (§7.45 above); the four load-sensitive tests; S0.28; and Gate 5.

**The gate of the corrected tree** (26 October 2026, uncached, `TURBO_FORCE=true`, the machine otherwise idle, the unit tests by `pnpm run test:local --continue`). `format:check`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `build`, `contract:check`, `api-client:check` and `db:check` pass. Unit: root 1,247 (1,245 passed, 2 skipped), API 206 files and 5,908 tests (12 skipped, the POSIX-only ones), Ops Portal 109 files and 2,199, API client 250, harness 541 (538 passed, 3 skipped). `test:browser`: 382 passed (Chromium, the Stage 6 specs among them). `test:e2e`: 28 passed. `pnpm audit --audit-level high` passes (the one moderate advisory is unchanged). **`test:db` was not clean in its first run and is reported as two runs, not as one:** in the gate, 107 of 108 files and 3,167 tests passed (12 skipped) and one file, `assignable-bundles-route`, did not run its tests because its setup hook timed out at 20 s under the parallel load of the suite (it passes 10 of 10 alone, three times); a second whole run on the same tree passed 108 files and 3,177 tests (2 skipped, the POSIX-only ones). **G01's acceptance, as far as this workstation can show it:** the complete staff story (12 journeys, the bootstrap rows among them) passed in two consecutive Playwright invocations of 5.0 minutes each, each from a database and custody folder of its own; the three HTTPS runs themselves are CI only. **Two things of mine that the first attempt at this gate found, and that are corrected:** the client check failed because the contract's list description was changed after the last regeneration of the client (regenerated, and the check is now current); and the unit stage of that attempt died at process start (`0xC0000142`) while the machine had about 1 GB of memory free, so that attempt was stopped, its logs kept apart, and the gate restarted on a clean machine. **Not run:** `test:e2e:https`, Firefox, WebKit, the branded smoke and the hosted Linux run. **Left on the machine by interrupted runs of mine:** three disposable test databases (`melarc_test_12385707`, `melarc_test_c94162b8`, `melarc_test_d2321058`), not dropped, because dropping is a destructive database operation that this task does not authorize (`pnpm --filter @melarc/api run db:orphans`, then `--drop` with the names, when the owner says so); ### 7.46 Carried from S0.47 to S0.52 (26 October 2026)

**Why.** The owner asked for Stage 6 (S0.47 to S0.52) to be built to completion, then for a deep adversarial review of the whole stage with every finding fixed except those that need a decision, everything green, and a fresh `package:source` archive. Nothing is committed or pushed.

**What was built.**

- **S0.47, the vendor and its setup**: migrations `0034` (`vendor_organization`, `vendor_account`, `vendor_credential` and the vendor part of `registered_device`, under forced row-level security; the secret hash and the browser hash are columns the runtime cannot select; definers read a secret's facts and lock an account in the caller's scope) and `0035` (the re-issue's arms, bound to the account the operation locked); `listVendorAccounts`, `getVendorAccount` and `reissueVendorCredentialSetup` (`src/vendor/`); `completeVendorCredentialSetup` (`platform/auth/vendor/`), which stores the vendor's own secret and registers the browser through a real `Set-Cookie`; the platform router over the staff and vendor directories; the fixture (`db:seed --vendor-fixture`); version 2 of the delivery payload, which carries a vendor's account identifier.
- **S0.48, `vendorSignIn`**: three factors in the contract's order, one answer for every failure but the lock a registered browser is told, the shared lockout, one live session per account, and the limit keyed on the account and the recognised browser by a partition step of the rate limit (`LIMIT_PARTITIONS`).
- **S0.49, the vendor's browsers**: `requestAdditionalDeviceGrant`, `completeAdditionalDeviceEnrolment`, `listVendorDevices` and `revokeVendorDevice`; migration `0036` keeps the grant request's idempotency record on the vendor's behalf (`ON_BEHALF_OPERATIONS`).
- **S0.50, the request**: migration `0037` (`recovery_request`; its guards hold eligibility, the registered channel and the cap of two live links), `requestCredentialRecovery` (one `202` for every caller, eligibility judged under the identity's lock, coalescing inside the guard window or at the cap, the message queued in the same transaction), the `RECOVERY_PRINCIPAL` limit partition, the counter of the refusals, and the worker's reader of a request.
- **S0.51, the completion and the administrators**: `completeCredentialRecovery` (the identity locked, then the request; the credential replaced, the lock cleared, every session ended `CREDENTIAL_CHANGED`, every other link ended and its message cancelled, a staff member's trusted browsers ended `CREDENTIAL_CHANGED`, a vendor's browsers revoked and the completing one registered), `recoverStaffCredential` and `recoverVendorCredential` over the shared `AdministratorRecoveries`, and migration `0038` (their arms, bound to the locked principal; `staff_locked_facts` rebuilt from `0033` with one more key). 34 operations are now implemented (`implemented-scope.ts`).
- **S0.52, the screens and the journeys**: `/recovery`, `/recovery/complete`, `/admin/vendors`, `/admin/vendors/{id}` and *Start password recovery* on the staff detail; `recovery.spec.ts`; the journeys of rows 10a and 11 (`e2e/harness/journeys/recovery-journeys.ts`, with `vendor-browser.ts` as the vendor's client of the real API, since the Vendor PWA does not exist) and the `e2e-database vendor-fixture` command.

**Design calls that are mine** (the documents do not state them).

1. **A vendor's own credential acts run under the authentication capability**, with the account as the actor: the registry gives a Vendor no write on `RegisteredDevice`, `SetupGrant` or the message. The grant request's idempotency record is kept on the vendor's behalf (migration `0036`).
2. **The hub boundary of `VendorAccount` is also a row-level rule** through `VendorOrganization`, with the scope probe reaching the account through its organisation ([data-scope-registry.md](../../contracts/data-scope-registry.md) §8.5, rewritten). The authentication capability now reads `VendorOrganization`, for a vendor's eligibility (the registry row says so).
3. **A vendor's identity lock is its account row**, taken in a statement of its own: a lock over a join re-reads only the locked row after a wait.
4. **The delivery payload carries the account identifier** (version 2) for a vendor's messages only; the queue refuses a vendor message without one.
5. **Each recovery belongs to its surface.** A request is held to the origin of its principal type's surface (the other pairing is `403 CSRF_VALIDATION_FAILED`); a completion presented from the other surface is the one `RECOVERY_TOKEN_INVALID`, so a vendor's browser credential is only ever given to a page of the Vendor PWA.
6. **The fixture** travels by email, to an address of the reserved `.invalid` domain, and answers to the reference seed's hub. No allowance is made: no allowance table exists in this slice.
7. **The Ops menu** lists Vendors third and Trusted browsers fourth; `/recovery` uses the first photograph and `/recovery/complete` the third.

**Findings for the Product Owner.**

1. **A contract change.** The `422` response of `revokeVendorDevice` and `requestCredentialRecovery` named no code that answers `422`, and was removed (no version bump, the client regenerated). Nineteen unimplemented operations have the same pattern and were left.
2. **On a fresh deployment nobody can re-issue a vendor's setup link.** `vendor.organization.approve` is "own hub" for a Platform Admin too (permissions.md), and the two bootstrap administrators have no primary hub, so the re-issue needs a Senior Ops or Platform Admin of the vendor's hub. The vendor page offers it to every holder of the key (the session lists keys, not scopes), and the server refuses a Platform Admin with no hub with `HUB_SCOPE_VIOLATION`. The journey makes a Senior Ops of Accra for it. Say whether a Platform Admin should reach every hub for this key. **Answered on 5 November 2026 and built by task P1:** a Platform Admin reaches every hub for this key.
3. **A pending additional-browser grant survives a vendor's recovery.** The completion revokes every browser, but a `VENDOR_DEVICE_ENROLMENT` grant issued before it stays usable and can register a browser afterwards (it goes to the vendor's own channel). credential-recovery.md ends recovery links only. Suggestion: the completion ends it `SUPERSEDED`.
4. **The sources disagree about a vendor with no registered channel.** The contract makes a registered channel part of eligibility (so `STATE_CONFLICT`), and errors-and-enums.md gives "no deliverable registered channel" to `CREDENTIAL_DELIVERY_FAILED`. The administrator's recovery answers `CREDENTIAL_DELIVERY_FAILED`; the case cannot arise from the fixture.
5. **A re-issue of a vendor's setup needs the account and its organisation `ACTIVE`**; a suspended one is refused. The contract's "Suspension is preserved" is read as "the act changes no state".
6. **The completion that loses a race has hashed already.** A link whose identity is offboarded while the completion waits is refused with the same `RECOVERY_TOKEN_INVALID`, but after the new credential's hash, so not in the timing class of a dead link (AC-SLICE-000-103 asks for the same class). Matching it needs a hash for every invented token, which the design avoids.
7. **The cap of two live links is judged without a lock in the guard**: it holds for every writer because each takes the identity's lock first.
8. **`credential_recovery_requests_excluded_total` counts nothing in the running API**, which binds no metrics registry until S0.68; the tests bind one.
9. **`recovery_request` is narrower than the entity**: no `RIDER` principal and no `OPS_VERIFIED` channel, which arrive with the rider tasks.
10. **Two branches cannot be reached through their routes**: `DEVICE_REVOKED` (a vendor has one live session, on the browser in use, which `revokeVendorDevice` refuses) and `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_CONFLICT` for `requestAdditionalDeviceGrant` (it has no body, so a repeated key is always the same request).
11. **The success page of `/recovery/complete`** says every session ended and the authenticator is unchanged; it does not say that a remembered browser will ask for the code again. A copy suggestion.
12. **The vendor domain uses two staff helpers** (`validated`, `checkedNote`) for its reason and note; and a self-service registration records `registered_by` as null.

**The adversarial review (26 October 2026).** Every safety property of S0.47 to S0.51 was broken on purpose, and each break was caught by a test in the end (S0.47: 35 mutants and 8 on the directory router; S0.48: 15; S0.49: 17; S0.50: 26; S0.51: 25; some were caught only after a test was added, and a malformed mutant was rewritten rather than counted); then the whole stage was read again against the contracts and run on the real stack. Fixed:

1. **A credential written for no one.** The recovery that replaced a password left the staff member's trusted browsers valid on the record (domain-model.md §6.8 names `CREDENTIAL_CHANGED` as the cause the recovery writes): the completion now ends them, with `auth.trusted_browser.revoked`, and state-machines.md has the transition.
2. **The work of the vendor sign-in said whether a stolen browser credential was still registered.** The limit's partition skipped the account read for a browser that was not `ACTIVE`, so a revoked browser sent one statement fewer: both reads are made whatever the first finds, and a work-shape test now compares an unknown account, another account's browser, a revoked browser and a suspended account (S0.48's evidence named it, and it was missing).
3. **Readiness over an inert unit of work.** `/readyz` answered `503` in an application with no database once the Vendor policy was declared: policy readiness now needs the database.
4. **An audit rule that refused self-service.** `auth.recovery.requested` required `initiated_by` of every request; it is now required of an administrator's request (and must be the actor) and refused on a self-service one.
5. **A store that trusted an unknown key.** The recovery store's context check read a key map without `Object.hasOwn`.
6. **A journey that could not be true.** The vendor journey expected a sixteen-character identifier (it is eight) and had a hubless Platform Admin re-issue a hub's setup link (finding 2).
7. **Checks that had not run during the build.** 85 API files and four harness files were not formatted to the repository's width, and the API had 20 lint errors in the new code; all are corrected.
8. **Documents made untrue by the stage**: the area notes of the API, the Ops Portal and the harness, the data-scope registry, domain-model.md §6.8 and the implemented-scope header.

**The gate on the final tree** (26 October 2026, uncached, `TURBO_FORCE=true`, Windows, Node 24.21.0). `format:check`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `build`, `contract:check` (34 operations, no findings), `api-client:check` and `db:check` pass. `test:db`: 107 files, 3,159 passed, 2 skipped, none failed. `test:e2e`: 28 passed (Chromium over plain HTTP; the three recovery journeys among them). `pnpm audit --audit-level high` exits 0 (the one moderate `esbuild` advisory, unchanged). The unit tests, one package at a time (`test:local`): root 1,245, API client 250, harness 535 passed and 3 skipped, Ops Portal 2,186 passed and 1 failed, API 5,905 passed, 12 skipped and 2 failed (the three failures are named below). `test:browser` in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit: 1,107 passed, 15 failed in the first full run.

**What is not clean, by name, and why it is not called a defect.** None of these was given a retry, a longer bound or a skip. (1) The 15 browser failures were all in older files (`shell`, `components`, `dialogs`, `pre-sign-in-dev`), none in the recovery or vendor specs; the five projects they belong to were run again alone and 13 of the 15 passed, and the other two (`dialogs.spec.ts:216` and `:246`, WebKit) passed when run on their own. They are 5 s and 30 s waits that a loaded machine misses. (2) In the full unit run, `SetupMfaCompletePage.test.tsx` (the confirmation screen draws no navigation) and, in the API, `bootstrap-tools.process.test.ts` (`bootstrap:seed` and `bootstrap:resume` as processes, bounds of 20 s and 8 s) failed; both files pass when run on their own (16 of 16, 12 of 12); `process.test.ts` and `contract-check.process.test.ts` passed in that same full run, and had missed their own 8 s bounds in the run that sleep voided. The machine was shared with another project's test run. (3) **The workstation went to sleep for about 90 minutes in the middle of one unit run** (the system log: asleep at 07:18, resumed at 08:51), which voided that run (worker-start timeouts, 5,708 s for the Ops Portal); it was run again whole. **Not run, so not passed:** `test:e2e:https` (the HTTPS evidence of AC-127, which needs the test CA and is CI's), the branded smoke, the Ops Portal's end-to-end journeys in Firefox and WebKit (the browser pass covers the screens in all three engines, the journeys run in Chromium only), and every Linux or hosted check. **Gate 5 therefore stays not passed. Gate 6 is the owner's to pass; what this workstation shows is S0.47 to S0.52 green under `test:db` and `test:e2e`, with the HTTPS and Linux halves CI's.**

### 7.47 Carried from S0.53 to S0.60 (27 October 2026)

**Why.** The owner asked for Stage 7 (S0.53 to S0.60, the rider and the device attestation) to be built to completion, then for a deep adversarial review of the whole stage with every finding fixed except those that need a decision, everything green, and a fresh `package:source` archive. S0.61 (the handset on real hardware) is the owner's evidence and is not buildable. Nothing is committed or pushed.

**What was built.**

- **S0.53, the rider and the roster**: migration `0040` (`rider_identity`, the rider part of `registered_device` with its `public_key`, the one-`ACTIVE`-device index, `setup_grant.idempotency_record_id` with the trigger that ends a sealed replay with its grant, the rider guard trigger, and the definers `rider_pin_hash`, `rider_active_device`, `rider_locked_facts` and `add_rider_fixture`); the rider `IdentityDirectory` adapter and its arm in the platform router; `listRiders` and `getRider` (`src/dispatch/`, `dispatch.read`, scoped through each rider's primary hub, the record's `ETag` the version a replacement takes); the enrolment URI (`platform/auth/rider/enrolment-uri.ts`: the version-1 form, strict parse, published vectors); `registerRiderDevice` and `reregisterRiderDevice` (`src/staff/`), whose grants carry a single-use token and challenge in one 127-character URI, the first with the sealed idempotent replay of SECURITY_DESIGN.md §14.16; the rider fixture (`db:seed --rider-fixture`, `e2e-database rider-fixture`).
- **S0.54, the device-key protocol and the substitute**: ECDSA P-256 over SHA-256 with the signed message `MELARC-RIDER-SIGNIN-V1` + LF + the challenge text (`platform/auth/device-key/device-key-protocol.ts`: a strict SubjectPublicKeyInfo and a strict DER signature), the published vectors made on the pinned JDK by an independent program, the attestation port reshaped (the evidence carries the challenge's digest, the verdict a closed set of eleven integrity causes and six unavailable ones), and the substitute verifier that a local run and the tests use and a production build refuses.
- **S0.55, the JVM verifier** (`apps/attestation-verifier`, Kotlin, Gradle wrapper 8.14.5 with dependency verification, the vendored `android/keyattestation` v0.4 at commit `621149c4`): the ten-step policy, strict revocation-list and request parsers, independent BouncyCastle fixtures (84 cases), ten real chains, mutation rounds, `pnpm run verifier:start|stop|status|test` and the CI job `verifier`.
- **S0.56, the HTTP adapter**: `service.attestation-verifier.adapter.ts` calls the verifier outside any transaction under `budget.effect`, refuses a redirect, reads the answer with a strict reader, and counts three metrics; the configuration refuses a missing caller secret in production on any host.
- **S0.57, `completeRiderDeviceEnrolment`**: the grant is looked at first (no evidence is read for a grant that cannot be used), the verifier is asked outside any transaction, the PIN is hashed only after `VERIFIED`, and one transaction under the rider's lock reads the grant, the rider's status and its devices again, consumes the grant, ends an `ACTIVE` device as `REPLACED` (its session `DEVICE_REPLACED`), registers the new one and sets or replaces the PIN. No session is issued.
- **S0.58, `revokeRiderDevice`**: a reason and no version and no verification, the rider's live session ended with the device.
- **S0.59, the challenge and the sign-in**: migration `0041` (`rider_sign_in_challenge`), `requestRiderSignInChallenge` and `riderSignIn` (`platform/auth/rider/`), `BUILD_FIXED_POLICY` `{ VENDOR: 1, RIDER: 1 }`, the Rider session (no idle rule, one live session, the old handset a plain `401`). 42 of the slice's 42 operations are in the implemented scope.
- **S0.60, the screens**: `/admin/riders`, `/admin/riders/{id}`, `/admin/riders/{id}/device/register` and `/admin/riders/{id}/device`, the `Textarea` primitive, `withNote` on the reason dialog and `unknownText` on the shared outcome notice (`COMPONENT_PATTERNS.md` §7.11, §12.9, §20.3, §33.2), the guards `rider-shape.ts` held to the contract, and `riders.spec.ts` with the stateful stand-in `rider-api.ts`.

**Design calls that are mine** (the documents do not state them).

1. **A `SUSPENDED` or an `OFFBOARDED` rider is given no device** (the first binding and a replacement are `STATE_CONFLICT`; an enrolment already begun is refused when the grant is used). `INACTIVE` and `TEMPORARILY_UNAVAILABLE` may be enrolled so that the handset is ready when the status is lifted. The specifications say who binds a device and are silent on the rider's status; `DEVICE_BINDABLE_RIDER_STATUSES` is the one place the line is drawn. The screens offer a binding only there.
2. **A rider who holds or has held a device is refused a first binding** (`STATE_CONFLICT`, pointed at the replacement): a revoked rider is bound again by `reregisterRiderDevice`, which is why a replacement works for a rider whose only device was revoked.
3. **The challenge is bound to the number, the purpose, the service and the device it was issued for.** A mismatch of the first three is `CHALLENGE_UNUSABLE` and ends a still-`PENDING` challenge; a challenge issued for another device is a failed proof; any other presentation ends it, in the transaction of its outcome. The audience is `melarc-api/<APP_ENV>`.
4. **One bucket for both sign-in operations**, `rate_limit_rider_challenge` (20 a minute), keyed on the canonical number whether or not it is a rider's; each sign-in attempt therefore costs two of the twenty.
5. **Exactly one Argon2 derivation for every request admitted to a hash slot**: real where the PIN is the deciding factor or was reached, a dummy otherwise; the reads before it are the same statements on every branch (the nil identifier names no rider).
6. **The verifier's `413` is `EVIDENCE_MALFORMED`** (the chain's size is the caller's), other `4xx` answers are an interface break, and a `VERIFIED` verdict for another key is `INTERFACE_BROKEN`.
7. **The report of a loss has no note**: `DeviceRevocation` is a reason and nothing else, so the dialog shows none (`withNote={false}`).
8. **The replacement's verification note is a `Textarea` that is held to one line** (the audit's rule for a note), which makes the field a multi-line control that refuses a line break.
9. **The Ops menu** lists Riders fourth (the `Bike` icon, with the rider as the one icon of the family that means a rider) and Trusted browsers fifth.

**Findings for the Product Owner.**

1. **The seeded Platform Admin cannot find a rider it may bind.** `dispatch.read` is `own` for a Platform Admin and the two bootstrap administrators have no primary hub, so their roster is empty although they hold `staff.device.register` at `all`: the officer who may register a device in every hub cannot find the rider in a hub that is not theirs. The page offers the acts to every holder of the key (the session lists keys, not scopes) and the server decides. Say whether a Platform Admin should read every hub for `dispatch.read`, as for `staff.read` (the decision of 25 October 2026). **Answered on 5 November 2026 and built by task P1:** a Platform Admin reads every hub for `dispatch.read` (OB-S1-75).
2. **A rider whose access has ended is given no device** (design call 1). The specifications say who binds a device and are silent on the rider's status. Say whether `INACTIVE` and `TEMPORARILY_UNAVAILABLE` riders should be enrolled (they are), and whether the handset of a `SUSPENDED` rider may be replaced (it is refused).
3. **A rider's sign-in challenge is bound with unkeyed digests, and the audit's identifier digest for a number that matched no rider is unkeyed too.** The space of telephone numbers can be enumerated, so `phone_hash` is a binding and not a privacy control, and neither is the `identifier_digest` of `auth.session.failed` (the staff sign-in's digest of a work email is the same class). The table is readable by the authentication capability alone, which is what keeps it private. Say whether a keyed digest is wanted.
4. **`rider_sign_in_challenge` rows accumulate and nothing deletes them.** Every challenge request writes one, a number that matched no rider included, because the domain model says an unknown number's challenge is created and behaves like any other. Growth is bounded by the per-number bucket (20 a minute) and the edge, not by a retention; the retention cleanup of S0.19 is not extended to the table. Say who owns the retention (it belongs with OB-113 and OB-114).
5. **The hashes of the challenge are `bytea`, and the audience is mine.** The domain model says `text` for `nonce_hash`, `phone_hash` and `device_context_hash`; the table holds 32-byte digests as `bytea`, with a CHECK. The audience is `melarc-api/<APP_ENV>`; the model says only "the environment and service".
6. **No audit event for a challenge request.** The catalogue has none, and an event for each request would be the log an attacker fills; `auth.session.failed` records the refusals of the sign-in.
7. **A challenge presented with another number is burned.** "Any other request consumes it" is read to include a mismatched presentation, so a stolen challenge presented with the wrong number ends it as `UNUSABLE`.
8. **A rider with no `ACTIVE` device is told `DEVICE_NOT_ENROLLED` for the right PIN whatever the rider's status.** The order in SECURITY_DESIGN.md §13.4b (step 3) decides by the PIN where there is no proof to check and consults the status only after a valid signature (step 4), so a suspended rider with no device learns the PIN is right.
9. **The wording of three criteria and the build disagree about a Rider session on an Ops-only operation.** AC-26, AC-102 and AC-113 say `PERMISSION_DENIED`; the build answers `401 SESSION_INVALID`, identical to no credential, for an operation whose security is the browser session alone (the credential mode of S0.25, `authentication.guard.ts`: a Rider's bearer is not a credential for it), and `403 PERMISSION_DENIED` for the registrations, which inherit the default security. `listReasonDefinitions`, which takes the bearer, is `PERMISSION_DENIED` as AC-132 says. The tests pin the `401` and read the criteria as satisfied in spirit. Suggested: reword the criteria.
10. **AC-54's residual.** Only `getCurrentSession`, `signOut` and the sign-in exist, so AC-54 is proved for them under a stale verifier (the sign-in needs no trust data); the collection, upload, payment and handover clauses belong to later slices.
11. **`verification_note` has no `maxLength` in the contract.** The audit's note limit (1000 characters, one line) answers `VALIDATION_FAILED`; the screen holds the same limit.
12. **Retry-After of 60 seconds is my figure.** No document states one; the contract and the design say "shortly" and that the grant is still good.
13. **The verifier's `413` is `EVIDENCE_MALFORMED`** (the size of the chain is the caller's), any other `4xx` is a break of the interface, and a `VERIFIED` verdict for another key is `INTERFACE_BROKEN`. **The "actor's authority" of the completion is read as the rider's status**: a QR grant outlives the officer who issued it, and the completion does not ask whether that officer still may.
14. **`revokeRiderDevice` for a rider with no `ACTIVE` device is a `204` that changes nothing and writes no event**: no document says otherwise and the contract declares no code for it. A repeated report is safe.
15. **AC-69's alert is not built.** The verifier exposes `attestation_trust_data_age_seconds` and its failure counters; the rules at 12 and 24 hours belong to the operational alert path (OB-32) and the rehearsal that SECURITY_DESIGN.md §15.2.2 names.
16. **The verifier's pins are newer than the vendored release.** BouncyCastle 1.86 (the ASN.1 nesting guard of GHSA-qp49-qgx5-5m26 is reached before the chain is proved) and Kotlin 2.4.21 (a build-cache advisory) replace the versions the vendored `android/keyattestation` v0.4 was released with, and a KeyMint tag the policy does not know is refused rather than ignored (my reading of "fail closed"; the one expiry exception, the factory attestation certificate, is the specification's own, §15.2.1 step 3). The catalogue header and `PROVENANCE.md` say why. **OB-26, the Linux or CI run of the verifier build, is owed**: it needs the owner's push or a WSL run.
17. **A verifier caller secret is required in production on any host**, loopback included, which tightens the configuration beyond "a missing endpoint or caller authentication".
18. **Stale `422` responses.** The contract's `registerRiderDevice` named a `422` that no declared code answers, and it was removed (no version bump, the client regenerated). Eighteen unimplemented operations (none of them in this slice) carry the same pattern and were left: a 422 response that no declared code answers.
19. **A latent defect of Stage 6, fixed in `0040`.** `registered_device_vendor_shape` let a row with null columns pass its CHECK. The fixture numbers use the ITU-reserved `+999` range, so none can reach a person.
20. **The sealed replay is linked by a column without a foreign key** (`setup_grant.idempotency_record_id`), because the replay's record is owned by another table that the grant's trigger ends with it.
21. **The Ops screens' words are proposals** (`rider-copy.ts`), as are the `Bike` icon for Riders, the `Textarea` pattern (§7.11), the order of the menu (Riders fourth, Trusted browsers fifth), and "Make a new code" for the specification's "issue a new code". The `Textarea` takes one line only for the verification note, which makes the field a multi-line control that refuses a line break.
22. **A flaw in the shared dialog, found by the rider screens' browser test and fixed.** `CommandOutcomeActions` gave the next branch the button the click was on, so a dialog whose "Reload the record" leaves it open (the showcase's) submitted itself again; no screen was affected, because each closes its dialog on reload. Every button has a key of its own now, and `dialogs.spec.ts` holds it (the test failed before the change). It is a change to a shared component made inside this stage: say if you would rather it were a task of its own.
23. **S0.61, the handset on real hardware, is the owner's.** Until it exists the rollout of rider enrolment stays blocked, and S0.70 carries it as *deferred*.

**The adversarial review (27 October 2026).** Every safety property of S0.53 to S0.60 was broken on purpose, one change at a time in the real file, with the tests that should catch it run and the file restored (about 490 breaks: the roster's reads 10 and the directory 13; the two registrations 17; the device-key protocol 13, the enrolment URI 5 and the substitute verifier 6; the verifier's policy 22, its service 63 and the provenance guard 7; the enrolment service 22, its attested path 4 and the device store 12; the revocation 9; the sign-in 46, its judgement 10 and the challenge store, the requests, the device store and the migration 45; the screens 56; the verifier's HTTP adapter and its strict answer reader 74; and the rider controllers' declarations, the number's limit, the digest binding and the status vocabulary 58; then a second pass over every survivor once its tests were strengthened, four of the screens' in Chromium among them). Each was caught by a test in the end, except the ones that change no behaviour. **Caught only after a test was written for it:** the software-root rule of the verifier's policy; the 16 KiB bound of one certificate; a locked attempt that must not be counted; four properties of the challenge store and its table (fix 1); and three behaviours of the screens (a retry offered for a code that must not be sent again, a replacement that could be sent a second time, a record kept after its screen was left); sixteen of the verifier adapter's and its reader's (fix 9); and sixteen of the controller round's (fix 10). **Equivalent, and why:** the enrolment's "grant is not locked again" (the consumption repeats the state and expiry condition); the device store's "any state may be ended" (the row-level policy refuses it first); the verifier's key-prefix check (the parse and the re-encoding repeat it) and the declared length of the revocation list (the counted read repeats it); the sign-in's "credential generation is not compared under the lock" (the count of a wrong PIN repeats the condition and answers the same refusal); the screens' "a dialog that takes no note still sends one" (there is no way to type a note, and an empty one is not sent); and, of four breaks of the dialog foot's keys that only a browser can judge, the three that change nothing anyone can see: the confirm button, or the reload button, left without a key (React never matches a keyed old child to a keyless new one, so one key of the pair is enough), and *Try again* given the confirm button's key (the confirmed command refuses a second send while one is in flight or unresolved). The fourth, *Reload the record* given the confirm button's key, is killed in Chromium by `dialogs.spec.ts`. In the adapter: the fragment of the configured URL (`fetch` drops it), a body read for a 4xx (the status decides), the guard against a 1xx (`fetch` never shows one), the declared length ignored (the counted read repeats it), a least time of zero (`AbortSignal.timeout(0)` and `(1)` both fire at once) and the attested key returned as sent (the reader holds it canonical already). In the controller round: `no-store` on three responses (the platform sets it on every response), the operation name in the fingerprint of the first binding (a constant per route), and a page size in another spelling or a query parameter given twice (the contract's validator refuses both before the controller; the reads suite now says so). Then the whole stage was read again against the contracts, the screens were driven in a real browser (Chromium, the production build and the development server, with an accessibility scan at three widths) and the findings above were written. Fixed:

1. **Four properties of the challenge store and its table that no test held, and one of the sign-in.** The time of a decision is read after the lock is granted and not before it; a failure of a consumption that is not the guard's own is raised as it was and not told as an expiry; the table's row-level security is enabled *and forced*; the policy alone (with the insert trigger stood aside) refuses a challenge that is not `PENDING`; and a request that met the lock, though the lock runs out while its dummy derivation is in flight, counts nothing, because its PIN was never verified. Five mutants had survived; a test for each was written and shown to fail on the break.
2. **A code nobody asked for, found by the browser and not by jsdom.** In the replacement form, a click on *Reload the rider* turned that very button into the form's submit button (React reused the DOM node and changed its `type` before the browser acted on the click), so the browser submitted the form and a code was asked for that no officer had asked for; a new code ends the earlier one. Every branch of the form has a key of its own now, and `riders.spec.ts` holds it.
3. **The same flaw in the shared dialog** (finding 22). `CommandOutcomeActions` gave the next branch the button the click was on, so a dialog whose *Reload the record* leaves it open submitted itself again. No screen was affected (each closes the dialog on reload), and the showcase's was. Every button has a key now, and `dialogs.spec.ts` counts the requests of the conflict test, which failed before the change.
4. **Words that were never shown.** `rider-copy.ts` held words for an outcome nobody knows, but the shared notice printed its own generic sentence, which for a replacement leaves out what matters (a new code ends any earlier one). `CommandOutcomeNotice` takes `unknownText` now, both code screens pass their own, and a test holds each.
5. **Two refusals with nothing to do in them.** The first binding's `VALIDATION_FAILED` and a replacement's `STATE_CONFLICT` fell to the generic text; each has words of its own (the second says to reload the rider).
6. **A code that nobody could find with a keyboard or a reader.** The picture of the enrolment code, and the news that it has lapsed, now take the focus when they appear.
7. **Tests that could not fail, and tests that were missing.** The check that the screens draw no credential used TypeScript's token scanner, which loses its place after a template literal; it reads the syntax tree now. Tests were written for an answer to the report of a loss that is not the contract's `204`, for a rider's record kept after its page is left, and for a dialog that takes no note; and the criteria the screens' tests cite were corrected (the screens have no criterion of their own; the roster is AC-113, the rendering of the code AC-40's clause).
8. **Checks that had not run during the build.** The first `precheck` of the stage found 15 lint errors (in the verifier's adapter, in tests and in the generators) and 17 files outside the repository's width; later runs found unused names and one redundant condition in the sign-in service, and spreads of strings and a control-character pattern in the browser stand-in. All are corrected, and `precheck` passes.
9. **The trust boundary to the verifier had untested branches.** A mutation round on the HTTP adapter and its strict answer reader (74 breaks) left 22 alive; 16 were gaps in the tests and are closed with 19 new ones, and no production code changed: the strictness of three of the four verdict shapes (an unknown member, a version other than 1), a fractional attestation version, a digest with a character before or after its 64, the answer's size (the helper that writes the stand-in's answers sends every body chunked, so no test had ever declared a length: the cap is now held at exactly the cap, declared and chunked, and a server error with a declared enormous page is an unreachable verifier), a verdict body under a 500, a 502 or a 503 without the service's media type (never taken as the service's word), a configured URL that carries a query, and the call's two bounds (the lesser of its time-out and what the budget has left, and aborted with the budget).
10. **The rider controllers' declarations, the number's limit, the digest binding and the status vocabulary had no test of their own.** In 58 breaks, 22 survived the database tests, and 16 were gaps that are closed: `rider-routes.test.ts` holds the limit and the client of the enrolment, the challenge and the sign-in (the enrolment's key space is a rider's device; the other two draw on one bucket keyed on the E.164 number, 16 bytes at most), `rider-vocabulary.test.ts` the statuses a device may be bound to and the forms of a number, a PIN, a key, a signature and a challenge, and `rider-challenge-binding.test.ts` the digests and their comparison (an absent binding equals only an absent one, a different length is not an error, a device is bound whatever the case of its identifier, and the audience names the environment).
11. **Two enumerations that the later rider routes had made untrue.** `route-inventory.test.ts` and `openapi.test.ts` listed the application's routes and documented operations only up to S0.53c, so the unit suite would have failed on `revokeRiderDevice`, `completeRiderDeviceEnrolment`, `requestRiderSignInChallenge` and `riderSignIn`. The survivors of the controller round led to them (the inventory pins the declared surfaces and activity of every route); both are corrected.
12. **Documents made untrue by the stage**: the area notes of the API and the Ops Portal, `domain-model.md` §6.8, the data-scope registry (the challenge table), `COMPONENT_PATTERNS.md` (§12.9, §20.3, §33.2) and the implemented-scope header.

**The gate on the final tree (27 October 2026, uncached, Windows, Node 24.21.0; the tree was 1,613 files, digest `7fbf275ed960`, unchanged in every run). It ended FAILED, and no passed gate is claimed.** Three gates were started. The first (`stage7-final`, stopped at 18:42) and the third (`stage7-final-3`, stopped at about 15:00, when the owner asked why the whole suite was being run again) have not run ([DEVELOPMENT.md](../../DEVELOPMENT.md#the-development-loop-and-the-gate), step 6). The second (`stage7-final-2`, 68:44, with `TURBO_ENV_MODE=loose VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=3` and `JAVA_HOME` set, the only departure from the documented command, made because the default eleven workers drove this machine to 0.4 GB free and to timeouts of operations that take seconds) ran every stage to its end. **Passed:** `db:check`, `api-client:check`, `format:check`, `typecheck`, `build`, `contract:check` (42 operations, no findings) and `lint`, all uncached; `verifier:test` (51 s, `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`); `test:browser` (524 passed in Chromium, 19:22); `test:e2e` (28 passed, 10:32); `pnpm audit --audit-level high` (exit 0; the one moderate advisory is unchanged). **Failed:** `unit` (12:29) and `db` (18:32). In `unit`: root 1,386 (1,383 passed, 3 skipped), Ops Portal 119 files and 2,553 tests, API client 250 and harness 538 (3 skipped) passed; the API had 6,272 passed, 12 skipped and **42 failed, every one a test of the `process` project that starts a child process under an absolute 8-second deadline** (`bootstrap-tools`, `process`, `shutdown`, `delivery-worker`, `contract-check`, the process helpers). In `db`: 3,589 passed, 2 skipped and **4 failed**, three of the same kind (`api-process` twice, `delivery-worker-process` once) and one 20-second timeout (`e2e-database-tool`). **Why this is the machine and not the code, as far as it can be shown:** the gate's own sampler recorded 0.0 GB free in `unit` and 0.1 GB in `db` (3.1 GB at the start, its warning given); the committed memory of the machine was 43 GB on 15.9 GB, with Chrome, VS Code and the WSL VM holding most of it; and another Claude session (a second project, `Denel`, session `denel-e9`) was running its own test suites beside the gate (seen in the process list). **A diagnosis, not a gate** (step 6): the API `process` project alone, 7 files, 102 passed and 6 skipped (the POSIX-only ones), 148 s; the three database files alone, 10 passed and 2 skipped, 70 s; and an earlier full API run (05:56, nothing else of mine running) had passed every process test except the two whose expectations were stale. **Also found by running the whole suite, and corrected before the second gate:** `bootstrap-functions.db.test.ts` listed the definer functions the API login may execute without the three rider ones of migration `0040`; `process.test.ts` and `contract-check.process.test.ts` (the generated route list, 34 operations) were out of date; `route-inventory.test.ts` and `openapi.test.ts` (fix 11). **What this costs the record:** the sleep of the workstation for 88 minutes (07:12 to 08:40) voided one full browser run, which was then run again whole by the second gate. **Not run:** `test:e2e:https` and Firefox and WebKit (CI's), the hosted Linux run of the verifier build (OB-26), S0.61, and the branded smoke. **A passed gate on this tree is owed**: the owner's run (`pnpm run gate`, [DEVELOPMENT.md](../../DEVELOPMENT.md#the-development-loop-and-the-gate) step 5; never with `VITEST_MAX_WORKERS`, [§7.48](#748-the-testing-loop-27-october-2026)), or the hosted run. **Left on the machine:** nine test databases (`melarc_test_05148876`, `_07e38034`, `_19bb3715`, `_2ab38534`, `_5db77b23`, `_7aa6f614`, `_a7ded4c7`, `_e9de3572`, `_fecd2397`), from runs that were stopped; dropped by name on 27 October 2026 at the owner's word, after a check that nothing used them ([§7.48](#748-the-testing-loop-27-october-2026)).

**Rider screens after the renewal correction, and what stays open (1 November 2026).** "Make a new code" takes the earlier code off the screen at the click, and a lost, refused or conflicting answer shows its notice and its way on, both from a visible code and from the lapsed screen. The lapsed notice says only "The QR code is no longer displayed. Make a new code when the rider is ready." (the page drops a code before the grant ends, so it makes no claim about the server), and the first-device page keeps the focus on a control or a notice across those transitions. This ran in jsdom, in Chromium (the production build and the development server) and, for the changed cases, in Firefox and WebKit; it was not part of a gate, and no screen reader was used. **Known and open, not fixed:** (1) on the replacement page a refused renewal from the lapsed screen leaves the focus on the document; (2) on both pages, pressing *Check the rider* or *Reload the rider* replaces the button that had the focus and leaves it on the document; (3) the lapsed notice is still drawn as a danger alert although its news is now neutral. **Accepted:** the Product Owner accepted, on 1 November 2026, the wording of the notice that says the earlier code was taken off the screen ("The earlier code is no longer shown. Taking it off the screen does not end it; making a new code does."); the rest of these screens' words stay proposals (finding 21). The rider experience is not claimed to be free of defects.

### 7.48 The testing loop (27 October 2026)

**Decision.** The owner, on 27 October 2026, after the suites had grown to an hour a gate: the full gate is the owner's manual run (`pnpm run gate`), never an agent's unasked; a task tests what its change reaches, with `pnpm run test:affected`; no paid CI minutes are relied on. [DEVELOPMENT.md](../../DEVELOPMENT.md#the-development-loop-and-the-gate) owns the loop, §3 the cadence.

**Built.** `scripts/affected.ts` with `affected-baselines.ts` (the selector, its record of each target's last green tree, one run at a time on a machine), the gate's refusal of an agent without `--asked` and of a start beside an affected run, and its record of what each passed stage proves. The API's database tests run several files at a time; the 22 files that change or watch what the whole server shares, or whose time bounds need the machine, run alone after them in `test/database/alone/`, each saying why on its first line, and every database file holds the server, shared or alone, for its lifetime (`test/database/support/server-hold.ts`). Role provisioning is one transaction. Every Vitest configuration bounds its workers (`MELARC_TEST_WORKERS`, 4) and the API's refuses `VITEST_MAX_WORKERS`. The gate refuses to start, and the affected run owes the database target that would start the verifier, when no JDK 21 is set up (`scripts/jdk.ts`, added after the run below found none).
